div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES
W,titiVV.

THE BLIND WEAVER. A weaver sat at his loom. A blind old man was he; And he saw not one of the shuttle's threads, Which he wrought so cunningly. But his fingers touched each line, As the pattern before him grew; And the sunset gleam of a smile dvine, Its light o'er his features threw; As plying his work to a slight refrain, • He sang it o'er and o'er again: Light and Darkness and Shade, Shade and Darkness and Light ; We never can tell how the pattern's made, Till the fabric is turned in our sight I And slowly the fabric grew, As his shuttle, from side to side With a cunning twist of his wrist he threw, And its lines were multiplied. But still the surface was rough, And the pattern you could not trace; For the threads seemed blindly broken off, And showed neither beauty nor grace; But he plied his work to the slight refrain. And crooned it o'er and o'er again: Light and Darkness and Shade, Shade and Darkness and Light ;- We never can tell how the pattern's made, Till, the fabric is turned in our sight ! And thus at the loom of life, Like that blind old weaver, sve Are working the threads of our own designs To a pattern we do not see And still with a patient love. That is wiser far than we know, There is One that looks from His throne above, And directs the shuttles throw; 'And spite of our broken threads, HIS great design, hvelayvoeurnlywgrerakcetoshthalel:esihdrrineef!rain. Professor Leone Levi remarked that the econo- mical condition of the people had much to do with their stature and weight, as was shown in the following figures: —Town artisans appeared from the returns to be of an aver- age height of 66.55, the labouring class of 0715, the com- mercial class of 67.79, and the professional 6810. In weight the town artisans again stood lowest with 136.21 b., the other statistics being :—Labouring class 137'8, commercial 143.9, and professional 1521. The general population had an average weight of 145.21 b., and a stature of 67.63 inches. Mr. Augustus Mongredien's essay on "Free Trade and English Commerce" has just been translated into Japanese by Mr. Miyoi Keinosin, and is said to be now on sale through- out Japan at a very low price. The translation is preceded by two short addresses to the reader—one by a Mr. Nomura, who has revised the rendering, and one by the translator. The former states that the leading men of the country know nothing of the true principles of political economy, and that hence they attribute the financial difficulties of Japan to an adverse balance of trade. To correct fallacies such as this, and to assist his countrymen in understanding the relative advantages and disadvantages of Free Trade and Protection, he has assisted in translating Mr. Mongredien's volume. The translation is copyrighted for a term of thirty years, and it is in contemplation to publish shortly translations of some other publications of the Cobden ftlub. THE TRFATMEKT OF ELYDROPROBII.—There seems in creased reason to hope that the large amount of attention which has latterly been given to the virus of communicable diseases will result in the discovery of means whereby hydrophobia may be prevented or cured. A couple of menthe ago, a Brazilian paper gave an account of exceri- mente which had been made in the presence of the Emperor of Brazil and the Minister of Agriculture, with respect to the efficacy of permanganate of potash (Condy's fluid) as an antidote to snake poison. These experiments were made upon dogs, and it was found that an injection of a solution of one part of permanganate of potash in one hundred parts of water into the veins of the animals resulted in the Eubsi- dence of the active symptoms, caused by snake poison pre- viously administered. The poisoned dogs were not only relieved but metered to health. These experiments have since been brought under the notice of the French Academy of Sciences, and have attracted considerable attention in France. It has been suggested as a consequence that pos- sibly the same treatment may be efficacious in regard to rabies. As yet the idea is only in the empirical stage, but French investigators have recently disclosed one or two curious facts which to oar mind, increase the probability that it may really prove _laluable. The first discouraging reflection that presents itself is, that it has been shown by M. Pasteur and others that the virus of hydrophobia acts upon the nervous tissues, and that the distinctions which have apparently been set up between specific action on the tissues and the blood make it seem unlikely that an antidote administered directly to the latter would be effective against disease in the former. An illustration of the distinction referred to is afforded by the circumstance that in the case of cattle apparently, two maladies have been confounded under the name of anthrax. One of these, splenic fever, appears to be communicable through the blood; the other, which has been spoken of as symptomatic anthrax, is com- municable through the tissues and not through the blood. Though these maladies in other respects strongly resemble each other yet it has just been shown by three young ex- perimentalists, MM. Arloing and Cornevin, of the Lyons Veterinary School, and M. Thomas, a veterinary surgeon at Dammartin, that they are associated with specifically dis- tinct bacteria. A carious fact, however; which has appa- rently been placed beyond doubt by the same able inquirers is that the virus of symptomatic anthrax, if introduced directly into the blood, gives the animal immunity from the specific disease; that is, virus which is mortal will, if injected into the veins, act as a vaccine against subsequent inoculation through the tissues. There is a curious analogy between this action and that resulting from the in- jection of permanganate of potash, also into the veins, in cases of poisoning from snake bites. It may be said that snake virus is not necessarily the same as the virus of hydrophobia. As yet the precise nature of the virus of hydrophobia is not known. A few weeks ago however, we stated that a French chemist, M. Gautier, of the Paris Ecole de Pharmacia had discovered that the salivary glands of man, even ia a state of health, secrete a toxical principle analogous to that of the venom of serpents. The difference in this respect between, the saliva of man and the venom of serpents is only one of degree. The poisonous principle of human saliva is increased by angry excitement, and cases are on record of death resulting from the bites of men in such a state. This suggests a possible relation between the virus of rabies and the venom of serpents. The whole group of analogies is, at any rate, sufficiently remarkable to make it appear worth while to try the effect of the permanganate of potash treatment on dogs suffering from rabies.

People glorify all sorts of bravery except the bravery they might show on behalf of their nearest neighbour.— George Eliot. I learned that he that will be a hero will barely be man; that he that will be nothing bet a doer of his work is sure of his manhood.—George Macdonald. A general and intent eent oversight is very different from petty and irritating meddling. The appreciative eye which discovers real merit and rewards it by increasing trust is a potent influence to produce good and true work. Chrysostom said beautifully—so beautifully that the words have been -preserved like a fly in amber: "God has given a man two eyes ; if he lose one he bath another. But man bath only one soul; if he lose that, the loss can never be made up again." We never know through what divine mysteries of com- pensation the great Father of the universe may be carrying out His sublime plan; and those three words, "God is love," ought to contain, to every doubting soul, the solution of 11 things.—Miss Matlock. Depend upon it, in the midst of all the science about the world and its ways, and all the ignorance of God and His greatness, the man or woman who can say, "Thy will be done," with the true heart of giving up, is nearer the secret of things than the geologist and theologian.—George Mao- donald. EARLY RISING.—There is not one man in ten thousand who can afford to do without seven or eight hours' sleep. All the stuff written about great men who slept only three or four hours at night is apocryphal. They have been put upon such small allowance occasionally, and prospered; but no man ever kept healthy in body and mind for a number Of years with less than seven hours sleep. If you can get to bed early, then rise early. If "you cannotego to bed until late, then rise late. It may be as proper for one man to rise at eight as it is for another to rise at five. Let the rousing bell be rung at least thirty minutes before the public ap- pearance. Physicians say that a sudden jump out of bed gives irregular motion to the pulse. It takes hours to get ovOr a sudden rising. . LAU= AND Gnow FAT.—There is not the remotest corner or little inlet of the minute blood vessels of the human body that does not feel some wavelet from the con- vulsion occasioned by good hearty laughter. Thel ife prin- ciple, or the central man, is shaken to the innermost depth, sending new tides of life and strength to the surface, thus materially tending to insure good health to the persons who indulge therein The blood moves more rapidly and con- veys a different impression to all the organs of the body, as it visits them on that partictdareenystic journey when the man is laughing, from what it does at other times. For this I reason, every good, hearty laugh in which a person indulges prolongs his life, conveying as it does new and distinct stimulus to the vital forces. Doubtless the time will come when physicians, conceding more importance than they now do to the influence of the mind upon the vital forces of the body, will make up their prescriptions more with reference to the mind and less to drugs for them, and will, in so doing, find the best and most effective method of producing the required effect upon the patient FRENCH TECHNICAL IttsriTuTEs.—The Ecole des Arts et Metier, at Paris, may be regarded as the parent of the Schools of Art and Science in Great Britain. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 22 1881
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 22 1881
CULTURE, &c.

A QUESTIONABLE EXPERIMENT.—SOOIO Texas farmers are trying the experiment of importing from Russia a cer- tain beetle indigenous to that country, which is represented as being very voracious, and living on grasshoppers, locusts, cotton-worms, and other destructive insects. It will be well to take precautions against "catching a Tartar." ATMOSPHERIC GERMS.—M. Chappuis has undertaken ex- periments to show that ozone has the property of destroying the germs capable of occasioning fermentations, putrefac- tions, and the development of mouldiness. He has filled flasks with beer yeast, and stoppered them, some with cotton which had been exposed to the action of ozone, and the remnant with cotton not so prepared. The latter became turbid in the course of a few days, whilst those stoppered with ozonised cotton remained limpid after twenty days.— Mechanical World. A museum of casts from sculpture, such as there have been several attempts made to establish in England, is to be opened at the Trocadero next month. The principal aim of the founders of this museum has been to collect typical works of French sculpture from the twelfth to the eighteenth century, placing side by side with these various works of foreign art of the same age, so that the student might be able to compare them. At present only the collections belonging to the twelfth and thirteenth centuries have been arranged. The selection of types has been made chiefly by M. Viollet-le-Duc, who is the real founder of the museum, though the work of formation has been carried on under the superintendence of the Commission des Monuments His- toriqucs. FARMERS AND Ecoematv.—Thoughtful men keep asking themselves and others whether Michaelmas, 1881, finds the agriculture of England in any better state than it was a year ago. And it requires the attention of a well-balanced mind in these days in order to form an opinion worth anything. We have, as Lord Derby has well reminded us, a bad habit of rushing into extremes. A few years ago our home and foreign trade was not only increasing, but was springing on by leaps and bounds. Everybody acted and everybody talked as if the tide was likely always to flow, and there would be no ebb. And the making haste to be rich became an unhealthy mania, prevalent not only in trade but in agri- culture. Landlords encouraged by the reports of farming profits diming good seasons, and by the increasing number of would-be tenants, formed not unnaturally a too high opinion of the value of their land'. Visions •of increased rent rolls, which were unlikely ever to fall again, invited them to spend more money in many ways. Merchant princes and retired tradesmen alike were urged by "land hawser" to buy if they could an estate or farm on which to emus:them- selves, and to show old-fashioned landlords and farmers of what land was capable when managed by the help of new lights which successful tradesmen were sure to pour on it. It was of no use for cautious men to drop hints about there being a limit to remunerative outlay. The triumphant reply was always readY, In which there is just enough truth to make it always pass, "the more one gives to a field the more it gives back.' And so fancy farmers became for a short time as plentiful as blackbertles. The sun shone, and under sunshine money was merrily spent, and everything went like a marriage bell. My lord, with his encumbered estates of many thousand acres, lifeowner only though he was, couldn't bear to be left behind in the race. So by the help of land improvement companies, expensive schemes which were to be excellent investments in the long run were carried out. There was a universal forgetfulness of the truth of the old saying, "He that goes a borrowing goes a sorrowing." Economy—become almost extinct amongst landlords, who had temptations of town and turf—soon also was scarcely esteemed a virtue amongst farmers. And although that fatal facility for borrowing which the possession of real estate always gives was not within the tenant's reach, still there are always, in a rich country like England, plenty of men willing to lend on some sort of terms. Besides, the common run of farmers are men who always pay if they can. So landlords spent freely, and tenants in their way followed suit; and, of course, soon it became the turn of the labourers. As the land has in the long run to bear the expense of all the classes who live by it, the burden rapidly became much bigger than it used to be; and a time of reckoning was sure to come, sooner or later. That time came sooner because of unpropitious seasons, no doubt; but a return to a sound condition has been delayed to a much further period by that extravagance of which landowners have been largely guilty, and from which their tenants have not been wholly free. It is high time that an overhauling of our land system took place; and we shall ;sot have farming conducted on a firm basis until the principle of cash payment becomes the rule, and the pledging of credit is the exception.—T. C. S., in the Agricultural Gazette. CROPS AND StOCll IN NORTH LANCASHIRE.—We can now form a pretty tolerable estimate of the crops for 1881; and certainly, taken all round, they are the worst of recent bad years. Wheat and barley are poor in ear, thin on the ground, the grain in many cases discoloured by the weather, and the straw is poor and light. Oats are the crop of the year, and will come near to, if not quite, an average both in grain and straw. Commencing with seed grasses, the crop was light as a whole and not well secured. Meadows did no, give an average swathe, and such was the rainy season at harvest, that most part was got in bad condition, some so washed out as only to be fit for bedding. In many cases, however, fair second crops of seeds have been got, and the meadows are fall of after-grass. Mangels at an early stage were attacked by maggot, and they have experienced two subsequent attacks, so that half to two-thirds of a crop will be the rule. Swedes were troubled with fly, and later on with wireworm : and if the total yield come up to two-thirds of an average, the remaining season of growth will have to be a favourable one. Both mangels and swedes have made excellent progress during the past fortnight of dry weather. Previously they were simply waterlogged. Carrots did not promise well at the early part of the season, but recently they have picked up a lot. Cabbages, too, have not hearted well—too much outside leaf, gross growth, and the hearts lack solidity, and consequently weight. Up to the past few weeks, both fat and lean live stock have made fair prices; but recently both have fallen in price. Best beef carcases have with difficulty made Scl. per lb.; second quality, about 7d.; top price of mutton also, Bd. per lb. With the prospect of scarcity of keep in the coming winter, stores are being forced into the market, and where most are sellers and few buyers, prices have necessarily fallen. It is easy to remember that cwe6rdetaih;ienerwalreatsmiebilese are dearer now than fifty years ago, but it appears to slip out of remembrance that labour is paid fourfold; that rates are higher, and accumulated under the rc:ginze of sanitary, cemetery, and school board; that hours of work for labour are shorter, and that seasons have been persistently bad. Further, that rents have gone up 50 per cent., and that no reductions have been as yet made here. Lastly, that unless the pro- ducer can sell direct to the consumer the middlemen take the lion's share of the profit—B. HABITATIONS FOR STOCK.—In choosing a site for the erec- tion of stables, cow-sheds, kennels, and other animal habita- tions, preference at all times should be given to an elevated position where plenty of light and air are to be obtained The sod should be dry, and the conformation of the locality . such as to favour perfect drainage. Agdes fpoirythoer water should be at hand, and every facility afford dry, and well animal dwellings should be large, lofty, other, but in venti- lated. They should not be placed too. nearf d proper and perfect removal of sewage. To be healthy, such relation as to allow a free circulation o air within an about them. The ends of stables, Sze., should, if possible, stand north and south, so as to expose the two sides of the building to the sun. By this arrangement warmth, dryness, circumstance. such as hills, woods, and buildings, may ren- der another aspect advisable. In that case the next best position for acquiring sun, air, and light must be chosen. CULTIVATION AND FERTILISERS.—It is not alone the naked fallow which enables the succeeding crop to draw more from mother earth. The thorough cultivation which farmers give, and should give, all hoed crops, answers the same purpose. Sometimes after passing through growing corn with the cultivator, it will start into such vigorous growth as to make one think that tke corn had been "taking I a drink," as a man once remarked. And so it had, but the drink was ammonia, which the loosened soil had absorbed from air and rains and dews. The ammoniated water of summer dews is the most stimulating of manures, but it is stimulating only because the fertiliser is in the right con- dition for immediate use as plant food. The same is true of liquid manures of all kinds. It is simply how TO ri'Oeoti.)elel a good potato ; that is, as well as can be done with- HOW TOimT Out cooking it, for sometimes even experts are deceived. Take a sound potato, and, paying no attention to its out- ward appearance, divide it into two pieces with your knife what is and examine the exposed surfaces. If there is so much 6, juice" that seemingly a slight pressure would water cause r i to fall off in drops, you may be sure it will be soggy after it is boiled. These are the requisite quali- ties for a good potato, which must appea• when one is cut in two :—For colour, a yellowish white ; if it is a deep yellow, the potato will not cook well; there must be a con- siderable amount of moisture, though not too much ; rub the two pieces together and a white froth will appear around the edges and upon the two surfaces ; this signifies the presence of starch, and the more starch, and consequently froth, the better the potato, while the less there is the poorer it will cook. The strength of the starchy element can be tested by releasing the hold upon one piece of the potato, and if it still clings to the other, this in itself is a very good sign.

On Wednesday, the strike at the Sunderland shipyards was virtually terminated. Mr. Justice Cave made an order on Wednesday for winding up the Universities Co-operation Association, Limited. The Earl of Dysart, has been appointed to succeed the late Earl of Gainshorough as Lord Lieutenant of the county of Rutland. The first meeting since the reformation of the Catholic synod of the arch diocese of Glasgow was held on Wednes- day. Several prominent priests received the degree of D.D. At Durham Quarter Sessions, William Walton, farmer, was sentenced to five years' penal servitude for having committed a murderoue attack on his brother with a scythe. The Vegetarian Society held its annual meeting in Man- chester, on Wednesday. It now numbers 2,000 subscribers, and last year had an income of ISM It was decided to form a children's branch. Lord Derby, presiding at a meeting in Manchester on Tuesday, in aid of the Royal Infirmary, expressed an opinion that provident dispensaries would never supplant the neces- I city for infirmaries. The church at Carlton-in-Cleveland, near Stokesley, has been entirely destroyed by fire. The parish registers were consumed. The vicar recently received a threatening letter, and the fire is believed to be the work of an incen- diary. A conference of miners representing all parts of the United Kingdom was opened on Wednesday at Birmingham. Mr. Pickard presided, in the absence, through illness, of Mr. Macdonald, M.P. The subject discussed was the adjustment of the sliding scale, it being contended that the open market affords the most direct indication. Mr. Gladstone, writing in reference to the resolutions on theland question passed at the recent meeting of Forfarshire farmers, expresses his "hope that whatever may be the urgency of public affairs elsewhere the Cabinet may during the autumn be able to give consideration to the very im- portant subject to which the resolutions refer." CONFESSION OF EmBEZZLEMENT BY A RATE COLLECTOR. —At Oldham, on Wednesday, Anthony Broderick, rate collector' was charged on his oWn confession with em- bezzling£4oo, the moneys of the corporation. The chief constable said there was no corroboration of the prisoner's statement, and, as the maiter was under investigation, a remand was necessary. A remand was granted. e,esee In Glasgow, on Tuesday, a postman named John Welsh, while delivering letters, found a small box covered with sheepskin. On kicking it, a peculiar sound was emitted. It was handed to the police, and a practical clockmaker believes it to be are infernal machine. The police are making private inquiries into the matter. A Glasgow correspondent telegraphs that the supposed infernal machine is found to constitute the mechanism of a toy ship. LOPEMENT OF A CURATE.—Great excitement has been aroused by the elopement of one of the most eloquent and favourite curates of a Shropshire parish church with a petty milliner. What makes matters worse, he is married, and apparently lived happily with his wife. A letter has been received from the curate, dated London, which says that it is no use following him, as he does not intend to desert the Young lady he has taken under his charge. On Tuesday evening a destructive fire occurred at New Riles Farm in the parish of Eastchurch, Sheppy, occupied Mr. Baker Morton. The conflagration was caused by a spark from a threshing machine falling] upon a thacthed barn. Nine stacks of corn and all the farm buildings and agricultural implements were destroyed, but by dint of the exertions the homestead was saved. The estimated damage is £3,000. The property was insured. Speaking at a temperance meeting in Chester on Tuesday, the Duke of Westminster said he hoped to see the day when cocoa-houses would be open on Sundays, so that—whether public-houses were open or shut—the public might have the benefit of these excellent institutions. He believed pub- lic opinion was rapidly coming round to the point of the adoption of Sunday-closing for England. The world is not won by denunciation. Tell a boy that he is disagreeable, and how quickly one loses influence over him. We must commend the good in people, and kindly pray over and reason about the bad. Most persons can be led, few can be driven, even children, without spoiling them. Law is essential, and obedience ; but true justice is always tempered with mercy. A total penalty of £2O 7s. was inflicted by Mr. Raffles on Tuesday upon the Liverpool, Manchester, and Birmingham Industrial Insurance Company, for neglecting to register their office as required by the Act. The company were liable to a fine of £5 a day by this omission, the aggregate amounteof the penalties to which they had subjected them- selves being, it was stated, £BOO. It was explained that the Board of Trade had instituted this prosecution in pursuance of a recommendation of a Select Committee of the House of Commons, which advised that the penalties under the Com- panies Act should be more rigidly enforced. In the present case, it was further stated, the delinquents dealt with a - poor class of clients, who paid but a very small sum per week. Their Royal Hiehnesees the Prince and Princess of Wales were present on Tuesday at the opening of a new dock at Swansea. The dock, which has been constructed at a cost of nearly £200,000, was christened the Prince of Wales Dock. The occasion was not only memorable as being the first visit of their Royal Highnesses to South Wales, but from the fact that the Prince took the opportunity of allud- ing to a letter written by Mr. Goldwin Smith,in which credit was not given to the Royal family for doing what they con- sidered right in helping on great public works. Amid great applause, the Prince ventured to express the hope that that was not the case generally. The proceedings seem to have been of a most enthusiastic character. EX-PARLIAMENTARY SPEECHES. —On Tuesday night a Liberal gathering was held at Ayr, the chief speakers at which were the Earl of Elgin and Mr. Parker, M.P. for Perth. Lord Elgin defended the foreign golicy of the Go- vernment, and said that the Irish Land Act could stand well for the work of the past session, although the Tories had said that nothing had been done. He expressed sorrow at the letter published by the Duke of Argyll on this Act. Mr. Parker characterised Sir Stafford Northcote's conduct in re- gard to the question of free trade as unw.onrothayt aonf important d states- man—Mr. Agar Robartes, M.P., speaking meeting of agriculturists at Truro, on Wednes ay, referred to the Land Bill that had bcen drafted by the Farmers' Al- liance, which, he said, contained the germs of those princi- ples, which were being advocated throughout the country .t and though it might not be passed in s present state, ye he had no doubt that in its main principle it would be adopted. THE PARUERS ALLIANCE AND THE LAND BILL.—At a meeting of the Farmers Alliance, held on Tuesday in Lon- don, there was an interesting discussion on the Landlord and Tenant Bill for England prepared by Professor Hunter. The Chairman (Mr. James Howard, M.P.) argued that, as the system of paying a tenant for improvements according to valuation had failed, the best substitute for it would be one giving to outgoing tenants the right to sell their improve- ments and their interest to the incoming tenant. Under a system of free sale every outgoing tenant would b 3 bound by his own interest to find a good successor. The provisions of the bill were explained by Professor Hunter, who said its erinciple was compensation for improvements by giving to every tenant the right to sell them in the open market for the best price he could get for them, or, in other words, to give the tenant a marketable security. In brief, the object of the bill was to secure good husbandry, to secure good tenants against bad landlords, and good landlords against bad tenants. A hope was expressed that the tenant right at present existing would be preserved, and the Chairman re- plied that a clause to effect that object had just been prepared loy the committee. -Mr. D. Grant, Mr., feared that as the bill was based on the principles of the Irish Land Act it would reawakas opposition which would be fatal to it, and that the bill in its present form would injure the farmer as much as the landlord. To this the Chairman replied that the bill was quite distinct from the Irish Land Act, and was a great improvement upon it. Mr. G. W. Latham, Sand- bad), speaking as a landlord, asked if something farther could be done by giving to farmers centinuity of tenure, which would benefit both landlord and tenant. There was an animated discussion on the proposal to abolish the law of distress, and the clauses of the bill having been considered seriatim a resolution was passed adopting the measure as amended. A deputation from the Alliance will wait upon the Premier when he returns to London—it is hoped early in November. THE NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATION.—The annual meetings of the National Liberal Federation, which are to be held on the 25th inst., at Liverpool, premise to be very successful. In the morning the council of the federation will meet in the New City Hall, when • the reports for the past year and resolntions on the English land, the franchise, and other questions will be submitted. At five o'clock a reception will be held at the Reform Club, and this will be followed by the great meeting in the evening in Hengler's Circus, which will be addressed by the President of the Board of Trade, the Rtght Hon. J. Chamberlain, M.P. On the 26th a banquet will be given at the Reform Club in honour of the l'resident of the Board of Trade. In addition to Mr. Chamberlain, the meeting will be attended by the the following members of Parliament :—Mr. R. N. Philips, Mr. T. Rowley Hill, Mr. H. H. Fowler, Mr. Edward Waugh, Mr. Jesse Collings, Mr. J. G. Mclelinnies, Mr. S. C. Evans Williams, Mr. William C. Borlase, Mr. Ashton W. Dilke, Colonel A. H. Brown, and Mr. John P. Thomasson ; Baron de Ferrieres and delegates from Liberal associations in all parts of the kingdom will also he present. The towns from which one or more delegates have been elected to the Federation Council are as follow :—Birkenhead, Leicester' Warwick, North wich, Wolverhampton, Stockport, Knighton, Cardiff, Bolton, Taunton, Burnley, Worksop, Wellington (Salop), Shipley, Bradford, Stourbridge, Slaithwaite, Hud- dersfield, Darlaston, Newcastle, Stoke-on-Trent (Stafford- shire), Hinckley, Southwark, Walsall, Ruabon, Denbigh, Denbighshire, Coalville, Oswestry, Liscard , Bbriotnehwayvlfean outh Leicestershire, Staleybridge, Derby, Dudley, Bilston, 3 Salford, Runcorn, Accrington, Llanfyllin , w Ifarboorne Sandbach, Kuutsford, Tredegar, Wrheexahhairme, Macclesfield, Mold, Manchester, Lancaster, thd.C' West Cheshire. div.head: LAND _QUESTION.
div.p: THE LAND _QUESTION.

V. It has been already shown that the custom of primogeni• ure, as carried out by settling estates, has the direct effect of keeping four-fifths ,iff England in the hands of a com- paratively few individuals, but it has also the additional effect of so increasing lawyers' bills by preventing any simple and effective system of registration of title as to amount to a positive tax on those who purchase property, and thereby practically discourages people of comparatively small or moderate means from investing in land, as the ex- pense often bears a totally unfair proportion to the purchase money.

Let us suppose a case of two people having arranged for the sale and purchase of some property, the price being fixed on. The intending purchaser instructs his solicitor, who communicates with the professional man of the owner, or vendor, as he is called. Unless the purchaser is prepared to accept the title to the property as satisfactory without investigation, and thereby take a very considerable amount of risk, a sort of history of the dealings with it, called an abstract of title, is prepared by the vendor's solicitor. The preparation of this document involves the perusal of all the title deeds for many years past, and the extracting of the purport of the contents with a view to show that the ven- dor is the only person then entitled to sell it, or, if any others are also interested in the property, how they came to be so, and that there is no other person with a claim to it or any portion of it. As this kind of work is charged for by quantity (10s. per brief sheet, on which it is finally copied), it is not the interest of the vendor's solicitor to make the abstract a short one, and they generally range from 20 to 400 brief sheets long, according to the circum- stances. The purchaser's solicitor then goes himself, or sends a couple of his clerks, to the office of the vendor's solicitor to compare this abstract with the original deeds to see that it is correct, which comparison occupies sometimes half a day, sometimes a week or more. The purchaser's solicitor then "peruses" the abstract, for which perusal he does not forget to charge, as it is really a very respon- sible and arduous duty, involving both great legal know. ledge and extreme care, and then he embodies his comments as to its insufficiency on various points in another document, which is called "Observations and requisitions on title," which he sends to the vendor's solicitor for his explanations. If these:explanations (which are called "Answers to Observa- tions and Requisitions on Title," and also often cover many pages), are not satisfactory, this most amusing game of "battledore and shuttlecock" goes on for several weeks, of course at the expense of the people who are only wishful to sell and buy. It often results in the whole title being sub- mitted to some barrister called a conveyancing counsel, who says what may be dispensed with, with safety, and he charges rather more than six and eightpence•per interview, as the clients find out. There are also frequently searches made in London or other places for what are called "registered incum- brances," again involving charges, this time by solicitors in London, or the town where the registry office is. Suppos- ing that the question of title is finally settled, a long draft of the intended conveyance is prepared at the rate of one shilling for every folio of 70 words, which is afterwards fair copied at the rate of fourpence for every 70 words, and then this last copy is sent to the other solicitor for his ap- proval, and then the game of battledore and shuttlecock begins again, of course at the expense of the clients, and finally the terms of the document are settled or agreed upon by the two solicitors, and the result is a document (en- grossed on sundry skins of parchment at so much per folio) that nine-tenths of the clients don't clearly understand when they have read it, and have to consult their solicitor occasionally to find out what it means. The expense of the whole transaction forms a considerable item in addition to the purchase money, and has a very strong tendency to dis- courage people from purchasing property who otherwise would invest therein. To save the expense of a lawyer's bill is very false economy and "penny wise and pound foolish" with a ven- geance, as the want of a few pounds spent at the right time may cause the loss of hundreds afterwards. The worst feature of all is, that after every precaution has been taken, and the solicitor employed has exercised the greatest care, there is'still uncertainty of title under our present system, for as Sir A. Hobhouse,Q.C., said in his address to the Social Science Congress at Leeds in October, 1871, "Its ex- pensive, dilatory, and vexatious character, its proneness to drift into litigation, and after all the uncertainty of the title conferred by it, have been exposed again and again." The writer has personally known cases where, after due diligence was used by both sides, twelve months have elapsed before the title could be cleared up satisfactorily, while the uncertainty of titles is aptly expressed by Mr. Frere, a well-known solicitor, who in his evidence before a Parliamentary Committee said he had known people to go on for years without the least idea that they were anything but owners in fee, and an old deed to turn up in their cellar which showed that they were only tenants in tail. In fact, the distinguishing characteristics of the sale and purchase of land in this country are delay, expense, and un- certainty. What else can we expect when the only means of proving the owner's title to property is the production of a quantity of detached deeds, which are liable to be misled, lost, destroyed, or forged. The fault does not rest with the lawyers. There are painstaking, conscientious lawyers, and many of them, too, who make their clients' interest and protection their paramount object, and often (within the writer's personal knowledge) in these complicated transfers of land have been so ashamed of the utter disproportion be- tween the charges and the value of the property, that the bill has been voluntarily reduced to such an amount as would not really reimburse the solicitor for the time involved and the money out of pocket. On the other hand, there are lawyers—well, of another sort, or, to put it mildly, "no better than they should be; and to them the present system offers inducements which they do not always withstand. Let us refer to the evidence given before a Parliamentary Committee in 1873. Mr. Frere, before mentioned, said, "The proper way to shorten deeds is not to make them the gauge of the remuneration of the per- sons who prepare them; there is no deed ever prepared which might not be expressed in one-third of the words with equal or more lucidity. We are paid upon the most vicious principle—we are paid, first of all, by the length of the docu- ments; we are paid by the quantity of time and discussion that can be thrown into the thing; and a man who under- stands his profession, and who can in half an hour put the thing so straight that there is no more trouble about it, gets paid nothing at all. Such is a solicitor's opinion. The Parliamentary Committee on Land Transfer reported in 1879 that' the vicious system of paving solicitors and conveyancers according to the length of the instrument still leaves the client at the mercy of his lawyer both in England and Ireland." Now, in America, our own Colonies, and some of the Euro- pean countries, matters are managed altogether differently. They have there Registries where all the owners of land are recorded, with a description of the propecty they own. In tpheerteyv,ehnet aoefdatlhaendpoewrenhearetehreeraen gselling a portion of his pro- Office, and at a very small expensg,taontehfetrento the ee eßamegeisdtaryy the transfer is completed and the purchaser's title regis- tered, too, the whole transaction being distinguished by cheapness, speed, and certainty, the very reverse of our own system; in fact, if the purchaser loses or destroys his title- deed, he can get another on payment of a small fee at the office. Some reader will naturally ask—Why cannot we have the same system here ? Well, various attempts have been made and Acts of Parliament passed, and registries are now in existence in London and Yorkshire, but the attempts have not been successes. To give the reasons for the various failures would take too much space and be too technical for non-professional readers. We can, however, consider, irrespective of these various " meddlings and muddlings" with. the subject, why a general registration of title cannot be carried into effect in this country so long as we have the present system of life estates. In 1878, on the motion of Mr. Osborne Morgan, a Select Committee of the House of Commons was appointed to in- quire and report "whether any and what steps ought to be taken to simplify the title to land, and to facilitate the transfer thereof, and to prevent frauds on purchasers and mortgagees of land." The committee inquired into the causes of the failure of the various Acts intended to pro- mote registration of titles, and the evidence of one of the witnesses, Mr. Follett, the registrar of the Land Titles Office Is too rich to omit here. Mr. Robert Lowe, M.P., asked. "Does not a great part of the solicitor's remuneration de- pend upon the length of the deeds which they draw, and is It not rather unreasonable that we should expect solicitors to give up profitable work for the purpose of coining to this registry office of yours?" Mr. Follett's answer was, "I think so." " Then," said Mr. Lowe, "is it not like setting up a clock and forgetting to wind it up, if solicitors have every inducement not to avail themselves of it ?" Mr. Fol- lett, in reply, told the committee of an owner who, having registered his title, required a loan, "his solicitor found it extremely difficult to get a loan, because there was no title to investigate, and therefore no costs to be made out of the transaction." The most important witness before the Committee, how- ever, was Mr. Joshua Williams, Q.C., an unequalled master of the English Law of Real Property, and his evidence leaves not the shadow of a doubt as to the obstacle which Entail constitutes to a general Registration of Title. He said, "In Englandwhen a man buys land, it is very often at the end of a successful mercantile career, and he buys a large estate with the intention of making a family. He either settles it by his will, or by deed, and then begin all the complications. So long as settlement is allowed in the way that it is allowed, I confess that I do not see that we can have in England a satisfactory registration of title." Further on he said, "You have your settlements and the interests under the settlements are sometimes mortgaged again and again in different ways, and there is so much complication in dealing with land that I do not think that the registration of titles will succeed unless you please to abolish settlement altogether." Speaking on the length of legal documents, he went on to say, "If you have a thoroughly good settlement of land, with sufficient powers, you must have a very long instrument; it is of DO use if you settle property, settling it at all, unless you have the proper powers; that is, the triumph of the conveyance, a thoroughly good settlement." Mr. Young, a leading solicitor and ex-President of the In- corporated Law Society, tbld the Committee the great diffi- culties which arise are upon settlements in this country. "If you could have simply conveyances of estates the titles would be very simple, and even by common conveyancing you might convey an estate of a large amount for a trifling cost when you have mere conveyances on the title, but when you come to have settlements introduced on the title with charges and mortgages also, then comes the difficul. ties."

Much similar evidence might be quoted were it necessary, but enough has been given to show that the best of lawyers cannot avoid big bills so long as we have not a proper Regis- tration of Titles applicable to the whole country like they have in other countries, and it is also clear that we cannot have this until the titles themselves are simplfied. The Parliamentary Committee finally reported:—" If in- deed an Act of Parliament could be passed for England and Ireland, either prohibiting the owner from tying it up or charging it except in a particular manner, or giving to the possessory proprietor the right of dealing with it as if it was his own; in other words, if the law recognised nothing but estates in fee simple, or gave to the holder of land the same power of disposition which the holder of stock now enjoys, the registration of titles would be as easy as the title itself would be simple. It seems to your Committee that to legislate for the registration of titles without as a preliminary step simplifying the titles to be registered is to begin at the wrong end.' Let those therefore who feel inclined to grumble at what they consider the serious amount of lawyers' bills on the purchase of property, remember that but for entail and life estates the work could be done as cheaply here as it is done in other countries.

In taking leave of the objectionable effects of primogeni- ture, both as a law and as a custom, it may not be inappro- priate to state the conclusions arrived at by the Hon. Geo. C. Brodrick, who has given the question his closest study, and whose recent work on "English Land and English Landlords" is a most valuable addition to the literature on the subject. His researches and investigations have led him to condemn it in the following powerful language : " From every point of view, then, we are led to an ad- verse judgment on the extreme development of primogeni- ture established in England, by the joint operation of law and custom.

"It must be condemned, politically, as aggravating the perilous dualism of town and country, as affording the very minimum of Constitutional stability to be derived from the Conservative instincts of proprietorship, and as giving a very limited body of landlords a preponderance in the State, none the less unreasonable and obnoxious because it is de- fended on the untenable ground that it is bound up with the existence of the Upper House. "It must be condemned, socially, because it helps to stereotype the caste-like organisation of English classes ' in horizontal layers' setting up in thousands of country parishes a territorial autocracy which, however benevolently exer- c'sel, keeps the farming and labouring population in an ab- wrinal state of dependence on a single landowner, often non- resident, while the rural districts have gradually been deserted by the lesser gentry, who helped to bridge over the chasm between rich and poor in ancient times. "It must be condemned, economically, because it cramps the free play of economical laws in dealing with land, mul- tiplies the difficulties and cost of transfer, and discourages a far•sighted application of capital to agriculture either by the landlord, who is usually a mere life owner, or by the tenant, who seldom holds a lease. "It must be condemned, morally, because it holds out to almost every eldest son, in what must still be regarded as the governing class, the assurance of wealth and power, whether he be worthy of it or not, and subject to no condi• . . . . . . .

Von but that of survi;ing his father. "Lastly, it must be condemned, in the interest of family government, because it fatally weakens the authority of parents over eldest sons, and introduces a degree of in- equality into the relations of children brought up together which often mars the cordiality of their intercourse in after- life."
Surely such a system cannot have long to live.
"What's the matter with little Johnny this morning ? " Sure, mam, the bye's sick ; he tumbled off wan of thim
wheel; without a ca-rriage to-it."

..... " I dote upon that girl," said Smith. "That makes the twentieth girl you have doted on within a month," remarked Fenderson. "It is about time you had sown all your wild dotes, Smith." Jumping over a fence in the middle of the night and meeting a bull dog that is a total stranger to you, is one of those exciting little incidents of life which go far to break the monotony and rob existence of a tiresome sameness. _ _

When Christ began to teach, He did not go to the con- science, and say," Convict ;" He did not go to the reveren- tial faculty and say," Adore ;" He did not go to the reason and say, " Argue, speculate." He went directly to the heart and said," Love." In all His teachings He never forgot this. It runs through all His words and acts, clinging to them and making itself prominent, as a minor chord in music makes itself heard amid the rush of contending sounds by its clear quietness, and, when the crash of the chorus has ceased, still clings to the atmosphere as if un- willing to leave it; and you feel that that clear, quiet strain has dominated by its very sweetness over all the other parts. —Murray. BE POLITE AT HOME —lf people would only keep a little of the sauvity which they waste on strangers for the home circle, how much more charming life would be ! When among our acquaintances, many of us are always agreeable and obliging, while we are glampy and glum to those who are the nearest to us. It doesn't seem worth while to con- verse around the family table. There the brief "if you please," and "I thank you" are dropped. If only our own folk are present, we are apt to drop our good breeding for the time. This is all wrong. A certain pleasant freedom from restraint makes home happier; but carelessness and crossness, and a lazy indulgence in untidy ways, will break the charm entirely, and make home a place to eat and sleep in. .

A MUCH-MARRIED Bisnor.—Bishop Thomas, who was a man of great wit and drollery, was observing at a visitation that he had been four times married; and, should his pre- sent wife die, he declared that he would take another, whom, it was his opinion, he should survive. "Perhaps, gentlemen," continued the bishop, "you do not know the art of getting quit of wives ; I will tell you how I do. I am called a good husband; and so I am, for I never contra' diet them. But do you not know that want of contradiction is fatal to Women? If you contradict them, that alone is exercise and health, the best medicine in the world for all women ; but if you constantly give them their own way, they will soon languish and pine, or become cross and lethargic, for want of exercise." NEATNESS IN WOMEN.—A woman may be handsome or remarkably attractive in various ways, but if she is not per- sonally neat she cannot hope to win admiration. Fine clothes will not conceal a slattern. A young woman with her hair in disorder and her clothes hanging about her as if suspended from a prop is always repulsive. Slattern is always written on her person from the crown of her head to the soles of her feet; and if she wins a husband be will turn out, in all probability, either an idle fool or a drunken ruffian. The bringing up of their daughters to be able to work, talk, and act like sensible young women is the special task of all mothers; and in the industrial ranks there is im- posed also the prime obligations of learning to respect household work for its own sake, and the comfort and happi- ness it will bring in the future. Housework is a drudgery, but it must be done by somebody, and had better be well than ill done.—Anon. HER MAJESTY'S REIGN.—Very remarkable changes have taken place during the forty-two years' reign of Queen Vic- toria. She has outlived by several years every bishop and every judge whom she found seated on those benches in England, Scotland, and Ireland. She has witnessed the funeral of every Premier who has served under her, except Mr. Gladstone. Not a single Cabinet Minister of her uncle and predecessor's days now survives • and of those who held inferior offices under her first and favourite Premier, Lord

Melbourne, there can be found among the living only' Lord Halifax (then Mr. Charles Wood) and Lord Howick (now Lord Grey). Of the members of the Privy Council who sat in Jane 1837, to administer to her the oaths, only four survive. She has received the homage of four Archbishops of Canterbury, of four Archbishops of York, and of five Bishops of Chichester, Lichfield, and Durham successively. She has filled each of the three Chief Jasticeships twice at least; she has received the addresses of four successive Speakers of the House of Commons; she has entrusted the Great Seal of the Kingdom to no fewer than nine different Lord Chancellors; and she has commissioned eight successive Premiers to form no fewer than thirteen Administrations. SOME FAMILIAR SAYlNGS.—Shakspere gives us more pithy sayings than any other author. From him we cull, "Count their chickens ere they are hatched,"" Make assur- ance doubly sure," "Look before you leap," "Christmas comes but once a year." Washington Irving gives us" The almighty dollar." Thomas Norton queried long ago "What will Mrs. Grundy say ?" while Goldsmith answers, "Ask me no questions, and I'll tell you no fibs." Thomas Tusser, a writer of the sixteenth century, gives us "It's an ill wind that turns no good," "Better late than never," " Look ere thou leap," and "The stone that is rolling will gather no moss." "All cry and no wool" is found in Butler's "Hudi- bras." Dryden says "None but the brave deserve the fair," "Men are but children of the larger growth," "Through thick and thin." "Of two evils I have chosen the least," and "The end must justify the means," are from Matthew Prior. We are indebted to Colley Cibber for the agreeable I intelligence that "Richard is himself again." Cowper tells us that "Variety is the spice of life!' To Milton we owe "The paradise of fools." From Bacon comes "Knowledge ikpower," and Thomas Southerne reminds us that •' Pity's akin to love." Dean Swift thought that "Bread is the staff of life." Campbell found that "Coming events cast their shadow before," and "Tie distance lends enchantment to the view." "A thing of beauty is a joy for ever," is from Keats. Franklin says "God helps those who help them- selves," and Lawrence Sterne comforts us with the thought that "God tempers the wind to the shorn lamb." ST. IiELENS CRICKET CLUB,
ANNUAL DINNER.

The sarnual dinner of the St. Helens Cricket Club was held ea Tuesday at the Fleece Hotel. Mr. Richard Pilking- ton presided, and was supported on his right by Messrs. J. Hammill, C. H. Houseman, A. C. Carr, and Martin Ham" mill; and on the left by Messrs. J. Massey, J. I.l'Srt, and W. G. Foreman. Amongst those present were Messrs. R. i Belsher, Chandley, Varley, Johnson (Borough Treasurer), Matthias Bailey, E. Robinson, Dee, Boyle, and Robertshaw.l Major Windus occupied the vice chair. The dinner was ; served up in excellent style by Mrs. Taylor. The following I is the menu :—Soups: Oxtail, spung. Joints : Roast beef, boiled fowls, tongues, roast geese, boiled legs of mutton. Sweets Blanc mange, pastry. Cheese and celery. After dinner, the CHAIRMAN proposed the toast of the Queen and Royal Family. After a song by Mr. Pentland, Mr. MARTIN HAMMILL in an eloquent and well arranged speech proposed the "Army, Navy, and Volunteers,' which was responded to by Major WINDUS. Mr. J. MASSEY, in proposing "The Town and Trade of St. Helens," said the town was well known to them all, and it was unnecessary to trouble them with a description of it. If he were to preach to them about the town of St. Helens they would be ready to tell him to shut uf, as they knew as much about it as he did, and no doubt some of them better than he did. If he told them how dirty or hew nice it was they would just say they were quite as capable of forming an opinion about the tows as himself. What was there about St. Helens they did not know? If he mentioned the institutions, many people would think the town was lacking in them. If he spoke about the public spirit of St. Helens he might exaggerate, because he for one had not a very high conception of .the public spirit of St. Helens. He did not think they were worse than other towns in regard to public institutions, nor did he think they were better; but he had the impression that they were becoming more numerous and grander in their conceptions, and more faithful in the execu- tion of their work. He thought that was an evidence of the progress of St. Helens, both materially and morally, and was to all;observers very noticeable. He thought, too, that the Cricket Club was prospering, and he only mentioned the Cricket ChM because it was in honour of that club that they were there to help it forward and keep it alive as an ;institution of St. Helens. The town was not the best, but the people he believed were certainly some of the best in the county. (Hear, hear.) He had always heard it said that strangers who had for a time visited St. Helens carried away the best impressions of the sociability of the people. That was something in their cap, however. Men of great eminence like Matthew Arnold might thinkkfit to rate them about the smoke and chemical works, but they pointed to themselves as an evidence of their industry and capability. Although they did not like the smoke they put up with it, because they knew that in the smoke there was their daily bread, and there was the way to win wealth and success in life. In an incidental conversation with their chairman that night, he was informed that trade was improving. He (Mr. Massey) hoped that St. Helens might participate in that improvement. (Cheers.) They were going on satisfactorily after the long period of depression, and they trusted the next time they met it would be with better pockets and with better faces alto- gether. They were, he was glad to say, able to congratu- late each other on their material improvement. The toast was then drunk, coupled with the name of Councillor Belsher. Mr. E. Grime sung "The village I blacksmith." Mr. BELSIIER •in responding, said he was very much otliged for the high honour conferred upon him in replying to that toast. Mr. Massey had gone the ground over so ably in speaking of the town and trade of St. Helens, and al- though he had ptofessed to know little about, he seemed to know more than he (Mr. Belsher) did. With regard to the trade, he was glad to hear from Mr. Massey, and indirectly from their chairman, who was such a high authority, that there was at last a progress in trade. Mr. Pilkington was a man connected with one of the largest firms in the kingdom, and must have a better knowledge of trade than those in humbler circumstances. (Cheers.) He was very glad ' indeed to hear that the firm had felt the improvement, be- cause when the large firms felt it the smaller calibre would do so in their turn. (Hear, hear.) They had passed through a long course of depression, but he believed that St. Helens would, as it always did, bear its part in the im- proved trade as well as it had done in the slackening of trade. ( A ppl a use.) Mr. HOUSEMAN (captain) then read the report. The results ' of matches had not been quite so good as in 1879 and 1880,1 when only three matches were lost in the two years. By the first eleven matches had been played of which six were non, four drawn, and five lost. The best averages in first peven were as follow :—Henry Varley carried away the palm, having played in 17 innines, made 279 runs, his largest core being 51 and his average 161. R. Chandley, 17 inn- ings, 243 runs, his largest score 60, and his average 146. J. 114a6m A average t l largest score 41, average 1 216 runs, largest score 35, and average IT4h6o.maLß Thomas, seven e innings,lo. n4nriunnss6, s u , largestll7 rscorens 60, , 'trey (pro.), g , average 12.16. J. Jeffryes, 12 innings, 126 runs, largest score 38, average 115. M. Hammill, innings 17, runs 99, largest score 30, average 6.3. J. W. Fidler (who was first last year; how are the mighty fallen!), inn- ings 14, runs 87, largest score 20, average 63. C. H. Houseman, six innings, 39 runs, largest score 11, average 63. W. Gerrard, innings 10, runs 54, largest score 17, average 54. Twenty other players took part in less than five matches. The chief bowlers were Heaney, 40 wickets ; M. Hammill, 31 wickets; J. W. Fidler, 20 wickets; C. H. Houseman, 17; and R. Cnandley, 14. Unfortunately an analysis of bowl- ing had not been kept'so correctly as to allow the usual de- tails being given. The first eleven had scored 1,723 runs, giving an average of 110 runs per innings. Their opponents had made 1,502 runs, the average per innings being 90. A change had been made in their professional, Reaney, who had been with the club five years, being succeeded by S. Hind, of Nottingham, a man well recommended as a cricketer, good ground man, which was very essential, and a thoroughly civil man. The Bowling Green members had played six matches, in which they had been successful on two occasions, losing four matches. The improvement shown at the end of the season augured well for future years. The " Lawn Tennis" members had not yet entered into friendly rivalry with other clubs, but in future, when they would have a ground specially provided, no doubt many interest- ing games would be played.
