Largest In- Totl. single Aver- nings. runs. scores. age. E. Robertshaw 8 178 46 222 J. A. Baron 7 117 42 1135 D. Gamble 6 91 36 151. J. Draper A. C. Carr W. Foreman J. Scott A. Fidler W. Boyle C. Thomas ..... H. Pennington 6 19 12 3.1 J. J. ELenty ..... 7 21 7 30 Mr. A. C. Carr sang an amusing song entitled " We'll all go to cricket to-day," in which the characteristics of several prominent members of the cluk were described. Mr. PILKINGTON said he had the honour of proposing the next toast himself, and when he told them what it was, they would not, perhaps, say that it was the toast of the ,evening, because their modesty would restrain them; at any rate they thought it was the toast of the evening. He gave them the toast of "The St. Helens Cricket Club." Of course, there were many present who were not members, and those cheered and clapped as they liked at the mention of the club, but the well-known modesty of the members pre-' vented them from showing any sign of emotion whatever. From what they had heard that night the members had many gifts besides cricket, and the song they had listened to was an original production of one of the members. In speaking of the it. Helens Cricket Club he spoke of something that was not born yesterday. It was a club that had a history. Of course all those sort of things in a town like their own had more or less a chequered history. Tbey were not always thoroughly successful and in a state of high water. Some- times they were in low water. When, however, they looked back on the history of the club, and contemplated its present state, he thought they roust come to the conclusion that it was one of the institutions of St. Helens that had taken root, and would—after all the various ups and downs that attended those institutions—in the main prosper and continue to prosper. He was told, and he believed it, that the club dated so far back as 1843. He was not quite sure whether it did not at one time die a natural death ; but of course, it did not do so, or they would not have been there that night. Ile remembered the club playing on a field besides Mr. Ansdell's gates ; he thought it was the St. Helens Cricket Club, but lie was sure the St. Helens Cricket Club once played on the Eccleston side of the Denton's Green-road. A long time ago he remetn- hue,' that Ile met the St. Helens Cricket Club and played against it. It occurred to him. after the statement had been read by Mr. Houseman, that upon the whole they bad done as well as they ought to have expected. They had won six matches, drawn four, and lost five, being a balance of one in their favour. They had played some indifferent clubs and some good ones, he considered the result a very fair one. They had not only kept cricket going, but also athletic ;Os biayrfeaymlveeonaeursm,rebatebrhrileoserkeewtto:aoctsshieuNe•belr:sevirlyeTgehoenoseasidme sports, and there was no doubt that if they could stru,gle as they had done_during the last Live or six years, and mld of p, the pee r th. swl dBt hope for the future of the zltsinh eaanotherclub, ci ettr was i • it taiO • that the club would not be allowed to die out or live even in

a sluggish way, but that it would be made to go on and increase in numbers and success. Of course, there were some slight things against the cricket club, but he thought they would still be able to surmount them. The grass did not grow quite as well as in some towns. He remembered when be played cricket there was very little grass, and they had a very lively time of it; the balls rolled tremendously, and when they went to other grounds, the balls did not rise but sneaked round into the wickets. (Laughter.) Besides that they had not a grand hedge and pretty trees as some clubs had, but an artificial timber fence which was the usual apology for an hedge in their neighbourhood. (Laughter). He hoped the club would meet with every suceess, because therecould be no question that cricket was a peculiar game in England, and °nod the finest in the world. There was no nation in the world equal to it in cricket: in fact there was no nation like it in anything—(laughter) ; and although they had been beaten by the Australians, and run perhaps very hard by the Americans, it could hardly be said that these people were other natiens, hut they were simply

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 22, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 22, 1881.

their own children grown up, and were trying to race their fathers as hard as they could. (Cheers). So that it would be a strange thing if the Australians were not successful sometimes. In England the cricketers had wet weather, and in Australia they had very fine, and had better oppor- tunities of playing cricket than those in England. He hoped that cricket might long be the distinguished game of Eng- land, because it needed down right good pluck, and a brave stubborn Englishman to play it. For a man to stand behind the wickets in face of swift bowling andswiftly thrown balls, and to stand with the bat, no matter how much his leg was battered, it needed down right English pluck. (Cheers). He hoped the club, with its first-rate history, would become, as it was becoming, one of the best institutions in St. Helens. He coupled the name of Mr. Houseman with the toast. (Applause). Four members of the Excelsior Glee Party—Messrs. Grime, Hosker, J. Barton, junr., and T. Grime, gave the amusing and delightful glee, "Johnny Schinoker," part of which was repeated at the request of the company. Mr. Horsnaiere, responding, said it was a pleasure to see so many friends present. He was sorry be could not con- gratulate themselves on the same amount of success which they had enjoyed in previous years. Circunotances had worked against them during the season. Last year 13 members played in the first eleven, whilst this year 30 mem- bers played. Last year 12 members of the club averaged over 12 runs and this year six memleers only averaged ten. Business, and one thing or another, had kept many away from practice; but he hoped the result of the past season would help to stir them up, so that whoever had to respond twelve months hence on behalf of the club would be able to say that they had done their duty well. (Hear, hear.) One of the drawbacks was the bad condition of the ground. It would be difficult for a club to show a better wicket, but he was sorry to say many other cricket clubs could beat them in respect to their cricket ground. They played the Cbel- ford cricket club, whose ground was simply magnificent. They played various Lancashire clubs, whose grounds were also in good order and condition; and, he must confess, he should not like some of those clubs to see their own ground. Some of the members thought of getting up a dramatic entertainment, for the purpose of putting their ground in good condition. But he thought the best way would be to raise the money by subscriptions, as £23 would put the ground in good order. If they could not keep the ground in good order they would be obliged to have sheep on the ground to keep the grass short. As to the club, the second and third elevens each won its first match. The sports this year had been better than in previous years, for then the rain was something frightful, and had been a great drawback upon their funds. This year their bowling ground members had challenged several clubs, but they had only won two out of six matches. They had also stated a lawn tennis ground, and next year they hoped to give those mem- bers a proper part of the field for their own purpose entirely. There was such a game as football; and, although they did not wish to weaken the teams of football clubs in the town, those members of the club who take an interest in football had decided some two or three months ago that on the 3rd December a match would be played at St. Helens, and another subsequently at Widnes, and that the proceeds of the first match go to the Cottage Hospital at St. Helens and the proceeds of the second to the hospital at Widnes. (Applause.) Mr. W. G. FOREMAN proposed the toast of "The directors of the Grand Stand Company." The grand stand on the field was a very fine one, and although they had not been able to pay the company off, they hoped shortly to reduce the debt very considerably. He couplied with the toast the name of Major Winans; and the toast was duly honoured. —A duett, "Love and war," was sung by Messrs. Grime and Barton. Major WlNnts, responding, said that certain gentlemen had formed themselves into a Limited Liability Company to put up a stand to be of service at the sports, and it was cal- culated that in the course of seven or eight years the money saved by the Cricket Club would be sufficient to pay off the directors. Unfortunately their calculations had not been realised, but they were not disposed to be hard, and in coming years, with favourable circumstances, the Cricket Club will no doubt wipe off the debt. (Applause.) Mr. R. W. H. THOMAS proposed 'The neighbouring clubs," which he said was a time honoured toast. In pre- vious years it was "the neighbouring cricket clubs," but the establishment of various bicycle and football clubs had caused the toast to be expanded to include them. It had always been the aim of the St. Helens Cricket Club to maintain friendly relations with all the clubs of the neigh- bourhood, and he thought they might congratulate them- selves on having done so. He would like to mention that a slight misunderstanding had arisen between themselves and the Bicycle Club during the past season. It had been the custom of the Bicycle Club to hold their sports on their ground, but it appeared they forsook their old love and endeavoured to gain the affections of the Sutton Cricket Club, upon whose ground their sports were recently held. As to the success of that venture he would not say much, but they all knew how it turned out. He noticed there were some members of the Bicycle Club present, and he trusted that the pod feeling that had existed, and to some extent existed still, would be continued. Some of the most popular matches had been played with the members of the Recreation Club, and on those occasions great enthusiasm prevailed ; and he trusted those matches would long be attended in future years. He coupled with the toast the name of Mr. Samuel Robinson. The toast having been drunk, Mr. Belsher sang "Our Jack's come home to-day," which was so pleasing to the company that there were calls for "Seventy-two," a favourite of Mr. Belsher's, which he sang in compliance with the demands. Mr. S. ROBINSON suitably responded to the toast, and in referring to the "misunderstanding," he hoped it would not be of such a nature as to mar the good feeling that had always existed between the two clubs. He was obliged to them for coupling his name as a member of the St. Helens Bicycle Club with the toast, and he thanked them on behalf of the various clubs in the neighbourhood. Mr. J. M. HAMMlLLbriefly gave the toast of "The visitors," some of whom, he said, had entertained them by their varied talents, and added much to the pleasure of the meeting. He hoped they would become members next year and eve them further encouragement. He coupled with the toast the name of Mr. E. Robinson.—Mr. W. G. Foreman here sung an amusing piece entitled "Wedding bells." Mr. ROBINSON responded, and referred to his connection with the athletic festivals in former years. Mr. DEE proposed the toast of "The ladies," and Mr. A. C. CARE briefly responded. Mr. HART proposed "The hostess," and after "Fill the shining goblet" had been sang by the glee party, a prize of two bowling green balls was presented to Mr. James Ash- croft, the gift of Mr. W. R. Ward. The Chairman suitably made the presentation Mr. MASSEY then proposed the toast of "The Chairman," and referred to Mr. Pilkington's connection with the town, as president of the Literary and Scientific Association, as a magistrate, as a member of the Council. and as a partner in one of the largest works. Without flattery he believed Mr. Pilkington had the good wishes and the approbation of everyone in the office which they all hoped lie would shortly take upon himself. (Applause.) The toast having been honoured, the MIAMIAN replied suitably. We should say that Mr. Oswald Barton accompanied the singers on the piano. The meeting then broke up.

I ST. HELENS PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY. The House again sat on Friday night, in the Waterloo. street Mission Hall, the Speaker (Dr. McNicoll) presiding. There were about forty members present, the majority of whom sat on the Opposition (the Liberal) side of the House.

The SPEAKER regretted that the attendance was so small, although it was better than on the previous sitting. Probable the violence of the weather might have prevented many from attending. He hoped they wduld attend in larger numbers than they did that night, because if they did not he feared their Debating Society would fall. The attendance contrasted very badly with that of last year, and it seemed that the fire and zeal of the parties had abated. Before reading the Ministerial statement he would submit the question as to the desirableness of keeping to that room, and also as to the desirableness of a change in the night of meeting.—After some conversation, it was decided to alter the night of meeting to Thursday. No alteration was made in the place of meeting.—The SPEAKER then read the Ministerial statement, as follows :-- Gentlemen,—ln presenting the Ministerial statement for thel second session, the Government cannot (after 18 months of Liberal rule) congratulate the House upon a satisfactory condition of either the foreign, colonial, or domestic rela- tions of the, country. Owing to the weakness and vascilla- tion of the Imperial Government the present position of affairs in the Transvaal is preeminently unsatisfactory. The cooduct of the Boer Volksraad in refusing to ratify the Con- vention, and in demanding an alteration in its terms in material particulars, is strongly reprobated by this Govern- ment, whose opinion is that the complete observance by the Boers of all the terms of the Convention should be insisted on. This Government appreciates the importance, at all times, of the Imperial Government acting in unity with the other great Powers in all matters of European concern, and in regard to the present difficulty in Egypt it is hoped that such a solution of the difficulty will be brought about as will meet with the approval of the other Powers. At the same time, this Government is aware of the paramount im- portance of British interests in that country, and would see to their proper recognition. Negoti.tions are being con- ducted for the renewal of the commercial treaty of 1860 with France, and an effort is being made to obtain conces- sions favourable to British trade, The House may rest assured that this Government would not give its assent to any treaty of a retrograde character. The condition of Ireland continues to cause grave anxiety to the country. An effort is being made by unscrupulous agitators to render the Irish Land Act of 1881 inoperative. Although this Govern- ment does not approve of many of the extreme provisions contained in such Act, its policy is to secure to those for whom the measure was passed the full benefit of its provi- sions. In the opinion of this Government, the blameable state of affairs in Ireland, complained of in the last Ministerial statement, ought not to have been allowed to exist, and ought not to be tolerated any longer ; and this Government would fearlessly use the extraordinary powers conferred on the Imperial Government for the maintenance of law and order, and the restoration of the Executive in that part of the Queen's dominions. This Government regrets that not- withstanding the economical promises and professions of the Imperial Government, the national expenditure continues to increase. At an early date the attention of the House will be called to the incidence of local taxation, with a view of relieving the agricultural interest from certain fiscal burdens which press unduly upon it. With a view of avoid- ing in future painful difficulties in Church Government, the House will shortly be asked to consider a measure to amend the Church Discipline Act of 1840, and the Public Worship Regulation Act of 1874, in the direction of providing for the removal from benefice, instead of imprisonment, of clergymen refusing to obey the law. In consequence of the want of time the Government were unable last session to introduce the measures promised in tho last ministerial statement; and at the earliest opportunity resolutions deal- ing with the most urgent and notable of those measures, namely—the extension of the franchise in Ireland, the assimilation of the county and borough franchise, and the prevention of corrupt practices at electione—will be sub- mitted to the House.—The hon. member for Carnarvon moved the adoption of the statement, and tie hon. member for Sunderland seconded the motion.—The Leader of the Opposition and the hon, member for Salford criticised the statement; the former pointing out that the small attend- ance might be due to the nature of the Queen's Speech, which the Conservative members could not support, as it was opposed to their principles. He did not think there would be any difficulty in adopting it.

ST. HELENS POLICE COURT. FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and Mr. H. S. Hall. INDECENCY.—James McDermot was charged with inde- cent conduct on the 10th instant, in a public-house at Peasley Cross.—Prisoner said he was drunk at the time, and was committed to prison for two months with hard labour. A DISORDERLY—Patrick Green, a young fellow, was summoned for being drunk and disorderly on the 30th ult. —P.C. Fielding said that about eleven o'clock on the day in question he and P.C. Boughton were conducting a prisoner to the station, when defendant came up in a state of intoxi- cation and endeavoured to release their prisoner. They were unable to get the prisoner's name until last court day, when he was recognised in the witness box.—Fined £1 and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment. MONDAY—Before Messrs. Willis and A. R. Gladstone. A VIOLENT Wommv.—Mary Brennan, a married woman, was charged with being drunk and disorderly.—P.C. Caunce said that on Saturday night the prisoner ran her husband out of the house with a knife in her hand. She was drunk.—Prisoner denied the charge of drunkenness, but ' admitted running her husband out of the house because he had scolded her about her "being so long doing her market- ing." She was not drunk.—Mr. Willis: Have you any questions to ask ? Prisoner: All the questions I have to ask is you can do what you like with me.—Mr. Willis : But the policemen say you were drunk—Prisoner (violently) : If they do they are infernal confounded liars.—Mr. Willis : Have you anything against her? Mr. Johnston: She was once here for stabbing, but the case was dismissed.—Mr. Willis : ss. and costs.—Prisoner : And you'll get it. ELIZABETH'S 35TH APPEARANCE.—BIizabeth Lawrenson was charged with being guilty of indecent behaviour in an entry on Saturday night. Prisoner, who had been convicted 34 times previously, was sent to prison for a month. Pri- soner on going down stairs anathematised the policeman who brought her up in her usual forcible manner. ROBBERY FROM A STORE Rom.—Peter Woods, Thomas Neil, and James White, boys, were charged with stealing a quantity of note paper and envelopes, and five cotton reels, the property of John Donnelley, from his store room in BickerstafTe-street.—Prisoner said the goods produced be- longed to him, and were worth £l. 33.—Prisoners were re- manded.

THE EFFECT OF A LARX.—Owen Mooney and Michael Dolan, boys, Gerard's Bridge, were charged with wilfully and maliciously damaging a door on the 6th September, dein damage to the extent of ss.—Prisoners pleaded not guilty.—Mr. B. W. Leach said ho was agent for the house 63, Victoria-street, which was the 'property of the executors of the late Elisha Lea.—Robert Forest, a lad, said he 'saw the door damaged. He was standing talking to Mooney when Michael Dolan came up, ran against Mooney in a lark, knocking him against witness, who was knocked forcibly against the door, which broke in consequence. The door was an old one, and was previously cracked all the way up.—The case was dismissed. How TO SPEND A SATURDAY EVENING.—Wm. Mort was charged with assaulting Alice Mort, his wife, on the Bth inst.—Complainant said that on the day in question she put her husband's meat before him, and whilst eating it he called her all sorts of foul names, and broke the lamp, threatening at the same time that he would set the house on fire. He then struck her twice and ran her out of the house. She had not said anything to him. He was up last April for a similar offence.—Defendant said that his wife was drunk on the occasion in question, and on placing his meat before him told him to "get that into his --," at the same time calling him a foul name. He told her to get out of the way as he did not want any bother with her. He got up to go towards her, when she broke the door open and ran out of the house, lie had not laid a finger upon her. In a short time she came in, gave him a "pick," and knocked the table and lamp over against the staircase, set- ting some furniture on fire. She was as drunk as a pig at the time.—Defendant called Elizabeth Leyland. who con- firmed the statement relating to the complainant's drunken- ness.—The case was dismissed. MESSRS. PILIIINGTCHT BROTHERS' APPRENTICES.—Jatnes Beech was summoned for not performing his duties accord- ing to the terms of his indenture.—Mr. Swift appeared to prosecute, and said the defendant was appt enticed to Messrs. Pilkington Brothers to learn the trade of glass manufacture. Ele was bound on the 6th January, 1878, as a sheet glass flattener for four years and eleven months, so that his in- denture would expire in 14 months front the present time. His standing wages were 12s. a week, and in December next they would rise to 13s. He did not ask their worships to impose any penalty, or to inflict any punishment upon the defendant; tut the defendant had neglected his work, and had failed to carry out his contract. The Act of Parlia- ment empowered their worships to make an order directing the apprentice to perform his duties, and this was what they asked in this case. This was necessary to be done in order that they might be enabled to deal more effectually with the defendant, if he continued to neglect his duties.—An order was made.--Patrick Marr, another ap- prentice of the same firm, and engaged in the same descrip- tion of employment, was summoned for not performing his duties in accordance with a justices' order served upon him on the 20th June last. Defendant was bound on the 17th April, 1877, for six years and seven months, and has now two years and a month to serve.Joha Meredith, a man- ager at the works, gave evidence in both cases.—Marr, who said he did not wish to say anything, was sent to prison for seven days.

ST. HELENS COUNTY COURT. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. Collier, judge. AN IMPORTANT LIABILITY CASE.-1110 case under the Employers' Liability Act, which was commenced a fortnight ago, and in which a labourer named Michael Galligher claimed £l5 from John Rothwell, on account of injuries received whilst in his service through the negligence of one of defendant's servants, was resumed. Plaintiff's case was heard when the action was first gone into, and the defence was now commenced. Mr. Riley appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Swift for the defendant. —ln contradiction to plain- tiff's and his witnesses' evidence' Mr. Rothwell was placed , into the box, and stated that the bricklayers built their own scaffold, and the labourers- did the same, and were respon- sible for its safety.—Mr. Wm. Harrison, builder, St. Helens, , who said he had been in business as a builder on his own I account 29 years, and had been connected with the building trade for 40 to 45 years, said the practice was for the labourers to construct their own runs.—Mr. James Fisher, who had been in the buildiug trade for 35 years, and Mr. John Whittaker for 46 years, gave similar evidence.—His Honour said that although he sympathised with the plain- tiff, he could not, according to law, give juagment in his favour. He thought plaintiff had failed to make out his case that Myerscough, the foreman, or first hand, had been negligent in the matter. He thought it was proved that it was the duty of the labourers to look after their own runs. . .
It was his duty to give judgment for the -W-iiii Costs.

AN ACCOVNTINT'S DOlNGS.—William Kirkham, auc- tioneer, &c., St. Helens, sought to recover £3 10s. from Jos. Dennett, publican, Westfield-street, and Mrs. Greenough, widow, the defendants being brother and sister.—Mr. Massey appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Swift for defendants.— From the evidence it appeared that in June last the female defendant failed in business. Kirkham was in the habit of visiting Dennett's public-house, and was asked by Dennett as to the best means of arranging the female defendant's affairs with the creditors in a private manner. The books were produced, a list of creditors made out, and according to Kirkbam's statement it was arranged that he should receive ss. 'for his trouble, provided that he successfully carried the matter through. A statement was sent to the creditors asking them to accept a composition of ss. in the pound. In answer to that, Kirkham received one reply in the affirmative, and he subsequently visited several places, and the matter was arranged. According to Kirkham's statement he then visited Dennett and asked for payment and received 30s. on account. A conversation ensued in which Kirkham agreed to accept £2 12s. Gd. on condition that the sale of Mrs. Greenough's effects be entrusted to him. Some time after, Kirkham seeing in a newspaper that another auctioneer was announced to sell the goods, at once went to Dennett and complained of the "shabby piece of business" and asked for £2 12s. to settle thelob, but this Dennett refused to give, with the observation that Kirkham got far too much when he received 30s —For the defence it was contended by Mr. Swift that Kirkham had been paid well. He did not con- clude the arrangements, and if ha had done.there was no agreement made that he should receive five guineas for his work. He had not concluded with Allanson's, of Man- chester, and he had not concluded with Drs. Twyford and Jamison, of St. Helens. He had not gone near them ; in fact, they had paid 30s. for writing a list out. Kirkham, on seeing the list, said there was not a sufficient number of ' creditors, and the amount should be increased in order to induce the creditors to accept a small composition.—Joseph Dennett said that Kirkham stated he would have to put downs guineas as a preferential claim, to which he (witness) replied, "Nonsense, you don't mean to say you are going to charge 5 guineas." Kirkham said, "I shall have to put it down as a preferential claim." In a further conversation Kirkham said, "This money will not be sufficient," meaning the creditors' amounts, "You will have to put something down for yourself." Witness replied, "But she only owes me £12." Kirkham said, "That is not enough ; you will have to go down for more than that, and put your brothers also in as creditors." Witness said, "That will not do; that is roguery ;" to which Kirkham replied, "Oh, it doesn't matter, I did it in my own case." Kirkham then put him down for over £2O, his brother Alphonsus for £43 2s. 5d., and his brother Joseph for £26 ss. 84. His sister did not owe his brothers more than £5 altogether. Witness told Kirkham that he was sure his brothers would not allow it, and he (witness) would not swear to his own. Kirkham said there would be no necessity for swearing. Kirkham also said hs would want £5 for a deed of Release to free Mrs. Greenough of any further claims by her creditors. Witness refused to give this as he considered a receipt in full would be satisfactory. Witness never gave the figures to put down against his and his brothers names. Witness had applied to several of the creditors to get their consent, and they ex- pressed their disgust that Kirkham should have been allowed- to meddle in the matter at all. He reminded Kirkham that there were creditors he had never called upon.—By Mr. Massey: I was aware that I was down and my brothers too, for fictitious claims.—His Honour said there had been some fraud on the part of the plaintiff, and from the evidence that had been given he should be obliged to nonsult him.

ST. HELENS WESLEYAN IMPROVE- MENT ASSOCIATION. • On Wednesday, in the Waterloo-street schoolroom, Mr. Green, Liverpool-road, read an essay before the members of this association entitled, "Charles Bradlaugh: is he a fit ' and proper person to represent a constituency in Parlia- ment." The Rev. W. G. Pascoe presided, and there were several lady members present. Mr. Green described the overthrow of the "gunpowder and glory Government " in a humourous style, and the circumstances which led up to Mr. Bradlaugh'-s ejection from the British House of Com- mons. In dealing with the political objections raised against Mr. Brddlaugh's right to sit in the House, he said he could find no substantial objection. The Roman Catholics, Nonconformists, and Jews were once objected to in regard to their taking the oath, but that partition had been broken down, and the State to-day was no worse for the change. It had been the means of men of wise views and liberal opinions being introduced into Parliament. As to several objections, he asked what would become of 'the House of Commons if the same objections were applied to other members. There were others as bad as Mr. Bradlaugh although they did not express themselves so candidly. Of course he could not make light of the religious objections against Mr. Bradlaugh, and he wished that every person was a firm believer in the good principles of Christianity. But because a person's opinions were antagonistic to his own he could not reasonably refuse that person the same political privileges. He thought that no one on the grounds he had named could deny Mr. Bradlaugh the right to take his posi- tion as a member ef Parliament. There was only one object that stood in the way, and that was the oath. He would say, " Remove the oath and let him take his seat."—Mr. W. B. HOUGHTON thought that Bradlaugh was as good a man as many who now sit in the House of Commons, and he con- tended there was no law to keep him out. After being elected a second time he thought it was not parliamentary, it was not English, and it was not right to pass a statute to meet the exigencies of the case, and turn him out. He did not think Bradlaugh was a tit and proper person to represent his constituency looking at the case from a moral stand- point, but as there were other members in the House quite as bad, there was no reason why he should be prevented taking his seat. (Applause.)—Mr. MAY did not think that Christianity would win heroes by attempting to stamp out free thinking. We had no right to interfere with a man's private judgment after a constituency had sent him to Par- liament. He believed that Thomas Huxley had stated many things which had done more harm than Mr. Bradlaugh. If Parliament had the power to refuse a man after that man had been elected by a constituency he did not know what might be the ultimate restilt.—Mr. ELSE gave an emphatic negative to the question.—Mr. JOHN SCALES said that the stipulations against a man sitting in Parliament were that he should not be an alien, an idiot, blnkrupt, and so on. In olden times Jews and other foreigners could not sit, but the oath had been modified so that it could be accepted conscientiously. Mr. Bradlaugh was a man of considerably ability, which could not be said with regard to a good many now sitting ir. Parliament. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. R. COOP said that Mr. Bradlaugh was a Re- publican, and in taking the oath each member had to swear allegance to the crown. Speaking against Prince Arthur's grant, Mr. Bradlaugh said "Down with the English monarchy." When a man spoke in that manner he had no right to sit in the British House of Commons. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Bradlaugh refused to take the oath, but afterwards said he would take it; therefore Mr. Bradlaugh was not so con- scientious as some of the previous speakers had represented. As to some members not being as good as Mr. Bradlaugh be would like to know who were not. (A voice: "Ireland Blackburn," laughter, and "Major-General Fielden " renewed laughter.) As to Mr. Bradlaugh being honest and candid his sale aim bad been to make himself popular— (hear, bear),—and to spread Republicanism throughout the country.—Mr. JAMES MMDLEHUEST said If there were no better men in Parliament than Mr. Bradlaugh, the sooner they were out the better. He held that ours was a state that recognised religion, and a man who had not religion more or less at heart,ought not to sit as a mmuleer of Parlia- ment. He would not dictate the particular form of that religion, but he ought to have a religion and act accordieg to that religion.—Mr. J. G. Coos said that some test, lime was required, should be made on the hustings and not in the House of Commons. (Hear, hear.) And as the Lard. lieutenant of the county had returned Mr. Bradlaugh as a member of Parliament, the House of Commons exceeded their duty in refusing him to take his seat. The question of opinions did not govern an assembly like the House of Com- mons, and he was not the only Republican there by many. —Mr.HEIVITT thought the discussion had been taken on a wrong basis. Ills opinion as that it was a thoroughly legal question and Mr.Bradlaugh's personal character had nothing to do with it. If lie were to decide the question on personal merits he should most certainly say that Mr. Bradlaugh was not a fit and proper person to represent any constituency. The very fact that Bradlaugh could associate himself with any man who could write a book on a question which was very demoralising, as bad been the case, and advocate such principles was not fit for civilised society let alone the House of Commons. (Cheers.)—Me. GREEerlhaying replied, the meeting was brought to a close.

div.head: PRESOOI SCI-TOOL BOARD.
div.p: PRESOOI SCI-TOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Monday, at the Board-room, Derby-street, Mr. J. Johnson Brown presiding. Tho other members present were Messrs. John NVycherley and T. P. Hewitt, with Mr. Henry Cross (clerk), and Mr. Lloyd (school ~ttendance officer). THE OFFICE OF PUPIL TEACIIER IN THE BOYS' SCHOOL. The CLERK read the following letter, dated Huyton Quarry, September 26, from Mr. R. Atherton :—" I received yours of the 20th inst. in reference to 'My son not being suit- able for a pupil teacher in the boys' school. I regret this, but am glad that his conduct and attainments are spoken of so very highly by the Board. now is it that he has not re- ceived any salary ? I regret to have to mention this, but I think he is fully entitled to be paid for the five weeks he has been teaching in your schools."—The CLERK stated that the boy had been remunerated for his services. THE ATTENDANCE AT THE SCHOOLS. Miss Duke, mistress of the girls' school, reported that the average attendance at her school this month was 68 as com- pared with 70 in the corresponding month of last year.— The CHAIRMAN observed that he expected the attendance would have been much worse.—The Mistress of the infant school (Miss McGregor) said the average attendance for this month was 53 as against 101 in the corresponding month of last year.—ln answer to Mr. Hewitt, Miss McGregor said the average attendance in the previous month was 57.—1 n reply to the Chairman, the Mistress stated that, judging from the attendance at her school, she did not think the fever was abating in the town.—Miss Duke said the attendance at the girls' sehoal was worse that morning. She thought a great many were absent more from fear of the fever than anything else.—Mr. Wycherley remarked that if (nal& one child out lof a family of five children was suffering from fever, the others were prevented from attending school. It did not follow that all the children who were absent from school were ill, and he had no doubt a good many, who could attend, took advantage, and stayed away from school.—The CHAIRMAN : It will be a bad year for the School Board.— Mr. Hawrrx : We can claim some portion of the grant-- The CLERIC observed that the Act of Parliament mentioned something to that effect.—Mr. LroirrFoor, master of the boys' school, reported that the average attendance this month was MO as compared with 121 in the corresponding month of last year. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE OFFICER'S REPORT. The School Attendance Officer (Mr. W. Lloyd reported that since the last meeting he had visited the several schools and served notices upon the parents ot 13 children to appear befdre the committee. He had also visited the parents of 173 children whe have been absent, or irregular in their at- tendance.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Whiston, on Thursday, Mr. S. Marsh presiding. There were also. present the Rev. T. Chambers, Messrs. Fidler, Fisher, Birchall, Penketb, Paris, Rowe, Gilbody, Gerrard, Sadler, Eatock, Leatherbarrow, Ranson, Syder, and Tyrer, with Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk.

div.head: THB HIJAIIDLANS AND SSRS. WEEKS AND HrGHES.
div.p: THB HIJAIIDLANS AND SSRS. WEEKS AND HrGHES.

The CLERK stated that Mr. Weeks, of the firm of Messrs. Weeks and Hughes, was in attendance, and would like to see the Guardians.—After some discussion, it was resolved to admit Mr. Weeks, when the Chairman informed him that he understood he wished to make some explanation to the Guardia Weeks said it was he who required an explanation. His firm had been appointed architects, and he had never heard of the resolution appointing them being rescinded. When the schools came on for considera- tion the Guardians decided that they would not spend the money just yet, but that eventually it would have to be spent, and nothing was said about rescinding their appointment as architects. Now, however, he saw from the newspapers that another architect had been called in. He did not think that his firm ought to have been treated in that manner, and before they were so treated some expenditure ought to have been made to them. He should like to know why they were treated in that manner. —Mr. EAroct remarked that one thing was that Messrs. Weeks and Hughes had an office here at the time they were appointed, but they had not one now.—Mr. WEEKS said they had an office at the present time on the Eccleston estate.—. The Rev. T. (*AMBERS said he was under the impression that Messrs. Weeks and Hughes were appointed architects for the building of the new schools, and pot as architects for the Union, and therefore when the schools were abandoned the contract between the Board and the architects was at an end. If the new schools were ever to be built, that would be the time for the architects to assert their claim, and he should be prepared then to admit it and vote for their ap- pointment. It was quite a different thing when the chapel was built. He preferred local talent, as he would have done if he had been on the Board when Messrs. Weeks and Hughes were appointed for the schools. In Lancashire, nay, in Bt. Helens and Liverpool there were architects, sufficiently qualified to build schools without going to Tunbridge Wells, and he should have voted for the appointment of local archi- tects, notwithstanding the high opinion he had of the capabilities of Messrs. Weeks and Hughes. He considered that when he offered that the firm should be offered a douceur of 150 guineas for the plans they had proposed, seeing that it was only manual labour, they would be properly compensated. The plans from the first were to elaborate for the Board. At first they wells £16,000, and then they came down to £12,000, and then they were reduced to £B,OOO, and that was brought about by the firm misinterpretating the orders of that Board Evidently, it appeared to have been the desire of the firm to make as large a job as they possibly could. He had no wish to say anything in disparagement of Messrs. Weeks and Hughes, but he thought the 150 guineas, proposed as their solatiuim quite sufficient, especially as they admitted that they had an office over here, and did not come from Tunbridge Wells to do the business of the Board. (Hear hear.)—The CHAIRMAN said the question was really in a nut-shell. They had received a letter from the solicitors of Messrs. Weeks and Hughes stating that they would accept so much money in final discharge, and theldifference between the sum they wanted and the sum offered by the Guardians was 25 guineas. The question was, would the Guardians stick to their original offer of 150 guineas, or would they pay 25 guineas more.—Mr. HALL asked who gave Messrs. Weeks and Hughes to understand that they were to get out plans amounting to .£l6,ooo.—The CLERK observed that at the meeting of the Building Committee the highest sum named was £B,ooo.—Mr. WEEKS said Mr. Carlile gave him at the first meeting the number of 500 children and then it came down to 250 child,en. He supposed Mr. Carlile was acting under the cam- mittee's instructions.—Mr. EATOCK said that was not so. Mr. Carlile was simply acting on his own authority.—Mr. FIDLER asked Mr. Weeks if a cheque for 175 guineas was sent to their solicitors, the firm would consider themselves as architects to the union.—Mr. WEEKS answered in the negative, and added that that would settle the whole thing. —After Mr. Weeks had retired, a discussion took place, and it was ultimately decided that Messrs. Tyrer and Hall should wait on Mr. Weeks at once, and see if some arrange- ment could be come to. The result of the interview was that Mr. Weeks offered to accept £175 instead of 175 guineas, in full discharge of all claims they had upon the Board.—Mr. RANSON moved, and Mr. JACKSON seconded, that the original resolution that only 150 guineas be given to Messrs. Weeks and Hughes, be adhered to.—As an amendment, Mr. TYRER proposed, and Mr. HALL seconded, that £175 be paid to Messrs. Weeks and Hughes, and this I was agreed to by ten votes against eight.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF ST. HELENS RELIEVING OFFICERS.
div.p: THE APPOINTMENT OF ST. HELENS RELIEVING OFFICERS.

The CLERK read a communication from the Local Government Board stating that they had no objection to the appointments of Messsrs. W. Bullock and F. A. Harrison as relieving officers for the Sutton and Eccleston districts 1 respectively.

div.head: PROPOSED INCREASE OF DR. HALL'S SALLEE.
div.p: THE PROPOSED INCREASE OF DR. HALL'S SALLEE.
A letter was read from the Local Government Board agreeing to the proposal to increase the salary of Dr. Hall, the medical officer from £55 to £BO per annum.
THE ALLEGED DEFICIENCY IN THE STOCK OF FRESH MEAT OF THE LATE WORKHOUSE MASTER.

Tbe CLERK read the following letter, from the Local Government Board i--44.1 am directed by the Local Govern. ment Board to transmit to the guardians of the Pres- cot Union the enclosed extract from a report made to the board by Mr. W. Floyd, assistant district auditor, respecting his audit of the accounts for the half-year ended at Michael- mas, 1880, of Mr. L. R. Davies, late master of the work- house of that union. The board understand that there was no deficiency in the stock of meat at the termination of the half-year at Michaelmas, 1880, and they request therefore to be informed whether the guardians can explain by what means the apparent deficiency of 2,222 lb. of Meat in June had ceased to exist when the accounts for the half-year were closed." The following is a copy of the extract en- closed :—" I was informed by a deputation from the guar- dians that Mr. Davies had been called upon to resign in con- sequence of the fallowing circumstances :—`on the 21st day of June, 1880, it appeared from the provisions receipt and consumption book that the very large amount of 2,624 lb. of fresh beef was in stock, and the guardians examined it and found 4031 lb. only, thus showing 2,222 lb. unaccounted for.' No satisfactory explanation was given and the guar- dians requested me to investigate the matter. Os the face of the books it appeared that the dietary table had been strictly observed, and by the end of the half-year the books duly balanced, and I can only account for the extraordinary discrepancy in June by the supposition either that meat had been taken or sold out of the house, that the dietary had not been strictly carried oat, or that there had been!' most unusual excess in waste. I called upon Mr. Davies to attend the audit, and the only explanation be could give was that the pauper inmates must have had the difference in excess of the dietary table. There was nothing on the face of the books to account for it in any other way, and not being satisfied with the explanation, I thought it desirable to call upon Mr. Davies to make a declaration as to the genuineness of the entries in his books and as to the correct- ness of his accounts, which he accordingly made."—The CLERK observed that be did not think the Board could do anything more in the matter.—SeveraL members observed that the Local Government Board knew quite as much of the affair as the Board did.—lt was understood that Mr. Hartley would write to the Local Government Board to that effect.

div.head: SCARLET FEVER EPIDEMIC AT PRESCOT.
div.p: THE SCARLET FEVER EPIDEMIC AT PRESCOT.

The CLERK read a letter from the Prescot Local Board stating that the Board were taking steps to provide a tem- porary hospital to check the scarlet fever epidemic, -and asking for the tom of six beds, which would be returned pro- perly:disinfected or paid for if not returned. The Clerk said on receiving the letter he did not wait for the._ meeting of the G uardians, but wrote to Mr. Cross saying they could have the beds.

. A DEBT OF HONOUR. The CLxurt read the following letter from Messrs. Swift and Son :—"St Helens, 19th October. Densett's balance of La 13s. 11. d. Sir,—Will you kindly bring this metter under the notice of the Guardians once more and send us cheque for the amount, or inform us whether it is of any use for us to wait any longer. We cannot believe that the Guardians will repudiate a just debt, or that they will allow the Statute of Limitation to be pleaded in their name in order to deprive Mr. Dennett of his rights as a tradesman, or to defeat a claim for the price of goods sold to the Guar- dians, and which they themselves admit is at least a debt of honour, and one which ought to be paid. ExCept for the statute we should have no difficulty in getting a judgment." —The CLERK said he had met Mr. Swift at Prescot on the previous Tuesday, and Mr. Swift had told him he Would take out a summons if the money was net paid. He. (Mr. Hartley) told him that if he did he would plead the statute. Hr. Hartley further observed that if Mr. Swift would wait till they got an interest fund they would pay the money. He had offered to collect the money, but subscriptions did not come in very rapidly. ALARMING INCREASE OF VAGRANTS PASSING TROUOR TTIE

WORKHOUSE. Mr. HALL called attention to the large lucre Ise in the number of vagrants passing through the Workhouse. 1'374, 4,463 tramps passed through the house 5,103; in 1879, 3,813; in 1880, 5,314; and in 18, 'i.728, showing an increase during the last twelve Month. 1.414. He thought it was quite clear that this matter req.iiird the earnest attention of the Board. It was clear that the present system was ineffective, and that a better system should at once be adopted, with a view of reducing the number of vagrants going through the house. The vagrants were too well treated, and they passed the word bne to another what sort of place the workhouse was. He moved that in view of vagrancy being largely on the increase in that union, it was desirable to appoint a small committee to inquire into and report upon the subject, such committee to have power to visit vagrant wards in the count recently erected, to. enable them to inform the Guardians of the best known means adopted for reducing this class of pauperism.—Mr FIDLER seconded the motion. It was most astounding to consider that in seven years the vagrants had increased by 2,265.—The CLERK stated that the subject of vagrancy was one which was discussed at the recent Poor-law Conference, and it was approved there of having one uniform system of dealing with tramps. A gentleman from the Wigan Union showed that they had reduced their tramps from 6,000 in 1878 to 3,000 in 1881, and they had adopted the "corn mill" system.—After some further conversation a com- mittee, consisting of Messrs. Hall, Fidler, Paris, Fryer, and Leatherbarrow, was appointed.

div.head: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.

LIBRARY COMMITTEE. The monthly 1, eet'ng of the Library Committee was held on Wednesday, Mr. H. R. Lacey presiding. There were also present, Councillors Brook and Hanson; Messrs. N. Lacey, A. Sinclair, and Dromgoole, with Mr. Craik (deputy. town clerk).

div.head: LIBRARLLN'S REPORT.
div.p: LIBRARLLN'S REPORT.

The LIBRARIAN reported that 6.770 books were borrowed from the Lending Library during the month 18th September to 14th October, 1881, out of which 76 were handed out for reading in the reading-room. He also reported that there were 2,513 members in the lending department. The 6,770 books were made up as follows: History, 235; biography, 236; travels, 250; natural history, 135; sciences, 265; theology, 164; poetry, 132; fiction, 4,982; political economy. 17; fine arts, 43; general literature, 377; total, 6,770; as compared with 8,117 last mouth. The Sunday attendance had been as follows :-18th September, weather fine, 66; 25th September, weather very fine, 62; 2nd October, weather very fine, 83; 9th October, weather showery, 101; total Sunday attendance, 312.

div.head: LADIES' Room.
div.p: THE LADIES' Room.

The CalmatAN said that a recommendation was laid before the Parliamentary Committee that a door be made into the ladies' room, in order to avoid the necessity of going through the boys' room, but the committee bad declined to make a door.—lt was stated that the matter was not set forth in the first instance, and that it did not appear on the plans.—Mr. DROMGOOLR said the plans at the time were very incomplete, lie thought it was necessary that they should have a door there.—Mr. N. LA-CRY: It MSS spoken of from the first.—Mr. Snicr.ern: We were very much surprised to hear the committee's refusal.—Mr. IlexsoNT : It is because of the alterations, a bill having come in for the work done in the Library which amounted to over £400; and the matter was deferred until to-day.—The CHAIRMAN: It is a case of necessity, and it will have te be done in time.

It is for yordto say whether you will discuss them now or refer them to the treat meeting of the committee, which will be a new .com2nittee.—The matter was referred to neat meeting.

PAVING, HIGHWAY AND SEWERING COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting of this committee was held on Wednesday, Mderman Johnson presiding. There were also present Alderman Harrison (Mayor), Councillors McKechnie, Belabor, T. Cook, Walker, Foster, Baxter, with Mr. Brewis (town clerk,) Mr. Craik (deputy town clerk), Mr. Johnson (borough treasurer) and Mr. Hart (borough engineer). MR.. MELLING'S SEWER. Mr. CRAIK, deputy town clerk, said that sometime age, the Corporation charged Mr. Melling of the Eccleston Corn ' Mills £BO 18s. 7d. for putting in a sewer, and it was after- wards resolved that the Corporation take payment on ac- count £4B 4s 3d, and:that that he the cost of making an ordi- nary sized sewer. Mr. Melling had placed the matter in the hands of Mr. Oppenheim' solicitor, from whom a letter had been received saying that the original sewer had cost Mr. Melling £6O, and Mr. Melling was under the laftression at the time that it should be utilised for the purposes of sewer- ing the street and not tu be called upon again to contribute to the expenses of sewering the whole street. Mr. Melling considered it a great hardship that he should be called upon to pay for another sewer, but was wishful to avoid litigation, and offered the sum of 125. Mr. Ross, who was surveyor when the original sewer was put in, had in- formed Mr. Melling that he (the surveyor) would not con- struct a sewer; and that if Mr. Melling contsructed one, it would ultimately be utilised and an allowance made. The sewer was carried all the way from Mr. Melling's own mill down Boundary-read.—The CHAIRMAN : Mr. Ross had no business to inform Mr. Melling what he did.—Mr. HART: No doubt he had to carry it a long length, perhaps a hundred yards further than he would have done if the street had been sewered.—The CHAIRMAN did not think they could make any abatement of the £4B 4s. 3d. He moved a resolution to that effect.—Mr. Mcßacaxne seconded the motion.—Mr. CRAIK said the resolution was that the Corporation would take £4B 4s. 3d. on account, but by some misunderstanding had sent in a bill with the altered figures as an apportion- ment.—The Towsr CLERK said that under the circumstances he thought the Corporation weuld have some difficulty ins getting the £4B 4s. 3d.—The CHAIRMAN: We must Insist upon it. He has only been served in the same way as many others.—lt was decided that no abatement be made.

THE OBSTREPEROUS TRAMWAY CONTRACTOR. Mr. HART said that he had had lately some trouble with the tramway contractor who had gone in direct opposition to the instructions of both himself and Mr. Beloe, the Tram- way Company's engineer. The contractor had opened out 245 yards instead of W, not a fourth of which was paved, although he (Mr. Hart) informed him that the length should not be opened out, before the other portion was paved. Mr. Speight (the contractor) said "Oh, never mind the Corpora- tion; get on with the work." He (Mr. Hart) afterwards sent for a gang of men and got some carts and steam roller and rolled down the road again. He (Mr. Hart) called upon Mr. Hammel], the secretary to the company, and Mr. Hammell informed him that the company could do nothing at all with the contractor. He also wrote to Mr. Beloe, who replied that the contractor ,had broken up the road contrary to in- structions. The contractor was perfectly beyond all reason and control.

°EJECTING TO PAY FOR SEWERS. Letters were read from Richard Grimshaw,. Maley, and Burrows objecting to pay the amount charged against therm for sewering Peckers Hill Lane. It was decided that the Town Clerk reply to the letters, referring the respective writers to the 151st clause of the St. Helens Improvement Act, 1869.

Mr. HART suggested the cleaning out, de., of the culvert of the brook beneath the Blackbrook branch railway, and the Hardshaw brook works: and he stated that this could be done for £lOO, and most probably for a less sum.—lt was resolved that the work be executed, and that the chairman and deputy chairmas of the committee be authorised to give instructions in the matter.

THE ROAD TO POCKET NOOK PROM BALL-STREET. Mr. HART called attention to the dangerous state of the road from Hall-street to Pocket Nook. Anyone driving ort the road in the .1 Lrk would be in great danger, from the want of a wall to proteet it on the right side from St. Helens. The matter had been brought before the railway company, and ha (Mr. Hart) wished for instructions to press forward the matter.—Several members of the committee ex- pressed their opinion that a wall was . necessary for tya protection of the public.—Mr. Hart was instructed to write .to Mr. Worthington, of the Railway Company.

div.head: VOTE OF THANES
div.p: VOTE OF THANES

The MAYOR proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman and Deputy Chairman for their services during the year. They had attended regularly to their work which included a great many things relating to sewers, erection of houses, and building land, and he thought they deserved their most cordial thank'.-Mr. WALKER seconded the motion, and said

1 RUNCORN COUNTY COITRT.—A sitting of this court took place on Tuesday, before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge. The cases were not of public interest. RUNCORN MERSEY MISSIONS.—On Sunday morning, the Rev. T. Patrick, chaplain of the Mersey Missions to Seamen, preached a sermon at the Parish Church, on behalf of these missions, and the collection realised .£9 2s. 9d. WESLEYAN FOREIGN Mostous.—On Sunday, two sermons were preached in the Victoria-road Wesleyan Chapel, Widnes, by the Rev. J. Agar Beet, of Warrington, on behalf of these missions. RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.—The members and friends of this society intend holding a soiroe in the Public Hall, on Wednesday evening. Tickets may be obtained of Mr. Rogerson. LECTURE BY Mn. HACK, OF RUNCORN.—On Wednesday eyening, the Rev. George Hack delivered a lecture in con- nection with the Wesleyan Methodist Improvement Class, the subject being " The tentmaker of Tarsus." NEW PULPIT FOR ST. AMBROSE'S CHURCH, WIDNES.—A special sermon was preached on Wednesday evening at St. Ambrose Church, Widnes, by the Rev. Dyson Rycroft, vicar of Christ Church, Kensington, Liverpool, on the occa- sion of the opening of a beautiful new pulpit. Ruxcoux TRINITY DAY SCHOOLS.—On Thursday evening, a children's concert will be held in the Public Hall, Runcorn, in aid of the fund for enlarging Holy Trinity Schools. On the same occasion the prizes will be dis- tributed by Mr. Clarke Aspinall, J.P., of Liverpool, who is well known as a popular and entertaining speaker. WIGAN MUNICIPAL MATTERS AND Mn. MAWSON, OF RUNCORN.—Our Runcorn readers will be pleased to hear that Mr. J. Y. Mawson, formerly of Runcorn, has been chosen as the Conservative candidate for All Saints' Ward at the forthcoming municipal contest at Wigan. Mr. Wat- son is a gentleman gifted with considerable tact, and be has taken a good position in the borough of Wigan. FIRE AT A RUNCORN BOOT SHOP.—Shortly after six o'clock on Tuesday morning, a man named Peter Stubbs, found that a fire had broken out on the premises of Mr Thomas Whinyates, boot and shoe dealer, Church-street. He ran to the police station, and Inspector Hollingsworth and several officers rushed to the place, after ringing the fire bell. Immediately afterwards a :number of the fire brigade, under Superintendent Wright, reached the street with the hose and reel, and commenced to play on the flames. Considerable assistance was rendered by the police, the neighbours, and Mr. Samael Yarwood in extinguishing the flames, and carry- ing considerable of the stock into Mr. Coventry's woollen, draper's shop, on the opposite side of the street. The damage which is pretty extensive, is covered by insurance.

KNUTSFOILD SESSIONS.—RIINCOEN SEMI/NOM—Mir - ing the week, Knutsford Quarter Ssseions have taken place, and the following are the sentences on the prisoners from this district :—Joseph Rowlands and William Millington who at the April sessions were sentenced to four months' hard labour for felony, and had been in gaol another six weeks awaiting trial, were indicted for stealing a cheese, the property of Mr. Samuel Tomlinson, grocer' Lowlands-road, Runcorn. The jury had to be locked up before they were able to come to a decision in the case. They acquitted Row- lands and found guilty Millington, who was sentenced to one month's imprisonment.—John Roylance, Thomas Massey, Stephen Hough, and George Bettley, who were committed for trial a few days ago on a charge of stealing a new nal e, of considerable value, the property of the Bridgewater Navi- gation Company, were each sentenced to three months' iin- prisonment.—Mary Hitchen and Alice Gilbert,who had been committed from Frodsham on a charge of stealing a hand- kerchief, a skirt, two pieces of ribbon, a petticoat, and four napkins, the property of Thomas Gerrard, of Barrow, were acquitted.

Four/ MEN RESCUED PROM DROWNING BY A RUNCORN SCHOONER.—On Saturday the schooner The Saint, of Run- corn, arrived at the mouth of the Tyne in tow of a tug. The storm, however, was so violent that the tow rope slipped and the vessel was left to herself. There was no canvass set, and a leeshore only a mile anay. The jibboom was partly rigged in, and the decks were lumbered with haw- sers and fenders which had been got out preparatory to docking the ship. A gale of wind was blowing, and as soon as the elements permitted sail was made towards Bridling- ton. In the midst of the confusion the vessel hove in sight of a cobble with four Shield pilots on board. The boat was full of water, and the poor men were well-nigh exhausted with their long struggle with tile storm ' • in fact the boat was on the point of sinking when the Saint came in sight. Captain Veal SO manceuvred his vessel that he succeeded in Picking up the men from the boat and landing them at Brid- lington quay, where he ran for shelter. The captain and crew are to be highly commended for their pluck. With the exception of a few ropes and other portable things about the deck which were 1 ost, and a split staysail, the Saint has not sustained much damage. Sr. BEDE'S CATHOLIC CIIAPEL, APPLETON.—Pno- POSED NEW Scaocms.—The first of a series of entertain- nients, which it is proposed to give during the present winter, was held on Monday in connection with St. Bede's Catholic Chapel, Appleton. The chief object is to provide a fund for the new schools, which are now urgently re- quired. The present accommodation at the St. Bede's Catholic schools is inadequate, and the provision of greater conveniences has become a necessity. Tile Rev. Father Finigan presided, and at the commencement of the enter- tainment said that the present series had been commenced with a two-fold object, to furnish an agreeable entertain- ment to his people during the winter months (and keeping this end in view the prices of admission were low) and to provide fuuds, from whatever profit there might be after expenses were paid, for the new school, which all knew must be soon built in the parish. He might mention with ngard to this question that that day he entered in the log-book of his schools Her Majesty's Inspector's report, with which he was very much pleased, and on the result of which their congratulations were justly due to the scholars and teachers. —The programme was a varied one, and embraced the trio, the duet, the ballad, the humourous song, and the humour- ous sketch. The principal vocalists were Madame Mills, Mr. J. Morrison, Mr. Jolley, and Mr. Josef Canter. The last-named, a vocalist whose name is well-known to Liver- pool audiences, and who is one of the favourite artistes at the Hope Hall concerts, was on the programme for four songs, viz.: "Uncle Jack" (a humourous piece), "Tom the Tinker," "The Three Maidens of Lee," and "Sleep Gentle r Lady," a finale in which, he was assisted by Madame Mills, Mr. Morrison, and Mr. lelley. Mr. Cantor sang the pieces in question in his best manner, and his efforts to please were evidently appreciated by, the audience. Madame Mills' "Rose Softly Blooming ' was well received, and Messrs. Morton and Telley's duet, "Excelsior," was rendered with taste and spirit. Mr. J. Morrison's rendering of Molloy's pathethic ballad, "Vanished Years," and the "Children's Home," were marked by that, taste and correctness for which this gentleman's singing is so distinguished. The other pieces were " Tbe Slave," wHich was well rendered by Mr. Tellev ; "Zitti," a trio; "Beloved again," by Madame Mills; "A. Word at Parting," and "The Stirrup Cup," the last-named being spiritedly given by Mr. Telley. The con- cert was well attended, there being at least 300 persons present.

RtrNonni; 2ND V. CREWE BRITANNIA 2&n.—This match was played on the ground of the former. The ground, owing to the heavy rain, was very wet and dirty. At 3-50 Mason, the Runcorn captain, decided to play with the wind ba no idn rkefgookl- , ftahre C , three wilco captain,noorn fo r kwi acrkaead two f fa n. a g eTd h toe ballwor kn oit t UP near to the Crewe territory, where a line was formed, and nc‘Pcoronf. Sherlock,rhe ball wa nbdo wr aans ibne ha ni ndd ateheen rf aodr wtha red fis ,r tg ottry pfoosrs eßssui He was entrusted with the kick at goal, which he improved upon. The ball being brought out the Crewe captain sent the ball up to 'he Runcorn goal, which Pownall returned, when Mason (who had been playing remarkably well), after some fast play, ran in. The kick at goal was not improved upon, the wind being against it. Scrimmages were formed near to the Crewe twenty-five, and Roach (whose play was greatly admired) secured the ball, and being unable to get through the Crewe men, very wisely passed to Mason, who replied by registering the third try for Runcorn. The kick at goal was not improved upon, and half-time being now called, five minutes were allowed for recruiting themselves. Time being called, Mason put the leather again in motion, which was well returned by Roberts. A 'scrimmage was formed, and the Crewe forwards worked it up well, and dribbled it into the Runcorn goal. Ball was in the act of registering a try, when Pownall ran it up and forced him to kick it in touch. The ball was soon brought back near to to the Crewe twenty-five, when the ball fell into the hands of Pownall, who gained ground, and when collated was able to pass to Walkey, and he, aided with other players, forced his way through, but the ball fell, and Mason drib- bled it well up and was able to register another try for Run- corn. This being Mason's third t7l, he was loudly cheered by the large attendance of spectators present. Sherlock was entrusted with the kick at goal, but the ball being rather badly placed and the wind dead against him he was unabl e to amend it. Page seeing that the Crewe men did not touch it down, immediately replied to the invitation and scored another try for Runcorn, and Sherlock, with all his steady and courageous play, was unable.to improve upon it. The ball being brought out, Page, with the aid of NValkey, Sher- lock, and Roach, ran in again and secured the fifth try for Runcorn, but it could not be amended. "No side" being now called, and after a most pleasant game, Runcorn proved the victors by one goal, five tries, and six touches down, to Crewe one touchdown and one touch in goal. We cannot speak too highly of Mason, Sherlock, Roach, and Walkey, Pownall, Page, and Roberts did good service. For Crewe, Gregory, Dutton, Ball, and Roberts played well. The fol- lowing were the teams :—Runcorn: Full-back, Wainwright; three-quarter backs, Walkey and W. Pownall; half-backs. Roach and Sherlock ; forwards Riley, Roberts, Dennisson, Dunbavand, Page, Kirkham, Gittens, Burrows, Dutton, and Mason (captain). Crewe : Full-back, Roberts; three-quarter backs, Riley and Gregory (captain); half-backs, Dutton and T. Bebbington ; forwards, A. Bebbington, Betney, Groves, Wareham, Williams, Marlow, Ball, Whinyateo, and Half- Penn.

SERVICE or SoNa AT WIDNES.—On Tuesday evening, a service of song, entitled " Pilgrim's Progress," was given at Oakland-street Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, Widnes. Mr. B. Dutton presided, and the connective readings were given by Messrs. T. Whitby and R. Keyworth. A collection was made on behalf of the trust funds.

A WIDNES PaEsmrrarrorr.—A few days ago, the workmen employed by Messrs. Mort, Liddell and Co., of Widnes, presented a testimonial of a purse of gold to Mr. John Hallett, jun., on his leaving the firm, by whom he has been employed about seven years. Mr. Macllmaine, manager at the works, made the presentation.

BAND OF HOPE MEETING AT WIDNES.—On Tuesday evening, a Band of Hope meeting took place in the Albert- road Wesleyan Sunday school, Widnes, under the presidency of Mr. T. A. Carver. The proceedings consisted of recita- tions and songs. Miss Corkhill and Mr. Hughes.were amongst the vocalists. THE REV. T. Annowsmiu, OF RuNcortx.—The Rev. T. Arrowsmith, of Runcorn, who has for the past three years been studying at the Didsbury branch of the Wesleyan Methodist Theological Institution, has been appointed third minister of the Chester circuit. RUNCORN NEWTOWN MISSION ANNIVERSARY SEE. TlCES.—These sermons were preached on Sunday, in the morning by the Rev. G. T. Simpson, curate of Runcorn, in the afternoon by the Rev. Canon Barclay, and in the even- ing by the Rev. T. Monton Arroson, late curate of Barnolds- wick, near Leeds. The collections were on behalf of the Sunday and day schools.

Iltrxccurg CALVINISTIC METIIODISTS.—The anniver- sary sermons of the Sabbath school in coanection with this place of worship were preached on Sunday last by the Rev. John Jones, of Brecon, to large congregations. In the after- noon the choir and children gave a service of song entitled "The Creation," when the connective readings were given by the Rev. J. Jones, and the singing was conducted by Mr. J. Warburton. Mr. J. Clough presided at the organ. The collections amounted to £l5. PROPERTY SALE AT WIDNES.—OR Monday last, ten dwelling-houses and a dwelling-house and shop, in Davis- street, West Bank, Widnes, were put up for sale by auction, by Mr. B. Dutton, at the Central Hotel. There was a fair attendance and some good business-like bids were made, but the highest £7OO was not so high as the reserve price, and consequently the property was withdrawn. Mr. S. Owens, of Widnes, was the agent concerned for the property owners.

Rurroomr GOOD TEMPLADISM. —The members of the Hope of Runcorn Good Templars, and Widnes Haste to the Rescue Lodges, met together on Monday evening, at the coffee rooms of Mr. Arthur Riley, Bridge-street, Runcorn. A. capital tea was provided, and the evening was afterwards passed in a social manner, under the presidency of Bro. Wat • son, who was supported by Bros. W. Hoxworth, J. W. Jones, J. Mcßride, and J. Jones. A very pleasing entertainment was gone through.

ACCIDICNTS A.T WlDNES.—During thn terrible storm on the 14th inst., John Jones, labourer, Water-street, whilst working at Messrs. Hutchinson's Chemical Works, Widnes, was knocked down by a plank falling upon him, and rendered insensible. He was taken to the hospital, and at- tended by Mr. Pattison, assistant to Dr. Cooper. He is stated to be progressing favourably.—On Saturday, a young.. Irian named Thomas Walker, of Widnes, whilst having a little practical fun with his brother, fell and hurt his Itmee so seriously that he had to be removed to the hospital, where he was attended by Dr. McLennan.

HALTON 1111TT.711. IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—OR Mon- day evening Mr. D. Bisbrown, of Runcorn, read a paper to the members of the Society on " Divine Providence." There was alarge attendance: The essayist related many instances of God's providential care for his creatures. He argued from the scriptures that God was, continually caring for all men, and interposing on the behalf of those who faithfully trusted in Him. There was no discussion, • and the paper giving general satisfac:ion, Messrs. A. E. Davies, J. Looker, R. Hughes, T. Miller, S. Barrow, and the Rev. J. Bateman (president) made a few remarks, most of them giving in- stances illustrative of " Divine Providence." WIDNES WASPS V. OUGRTRINGTON ROVERS.—The first match between these clubs took place on Saturday last at Widnes. The Rovers' kick off was well returned by Mar- tindale, and up to the call of " time " no decisive point had been scored. The score standing Wasps, 4 touchdowns, 2 touches in goal, to 3 touchdowns, and 1 dead ball. It would be hard to single out the best players as both teams worked hard for victory, but perhaps Martindale and 11. Wright, J. Pountain (back), J. Ghorst, and Kiddie (forward), shone best for the Wasps, as did Clark, Kirk, and Shaw for the Rovers. Teams :—Wasps : Martindale (full-back), J. Wright, Harding, and Wareing (three-quarter backs), H. Wright and Pountain (half backs), Kiddie, Shaw, Ghorst, Mather, Davies, Ankers, Gregory, Woods, and Whitfield (forwards). THE BISHOP OF LIVERPOOL'S PRIMARY VISIPATION. The Bishop of Liverpool commenced his primary visitation in that capon Wednesday. In the course of his charge, be reviewed the state of the diocese, and showed by a recital of facts and figures that the spiritual requirements of the population demanded a large increase both of ordained ministers and churches. Alluding to the dangers to which the Church of England is at present exposed, he remarked that there was no proof that the Liberation Society's agita- tion had been successful. On the contrary he believed the Church was even stronger now than when that movement commenced. The public mind was evidently not prepared for the state of things which disestablishment would bring about if conducted to its logical consequences. The chief internal danger arose from the existence of a hotly of Church- I men that seemed determined to unprotestantise the Church and to reintroduce principles and practices which our fore- fathers deliberately rsjected three centuries ago. Scores of clergymen had adopted the practice of administering the Lord's Supper with usages which to the vast majority of thinking men seemed intended to bring back into the Church that most dangerous of all Romish doctrines the sacrifice of the Mass. Worst of all, they were aided and countenanced by hundreds of clergymen who never dreamt of breaking the law themselves, but who seemed to regard those law- breaking brethren as martyrs. If that did not constitute a most dangerous state of things, he knew not what was danger to a church. Without some change it would be the ruin of the Church of England. He was of opinion that the theory of those who would refer all ecclesiastics causes to clerical judges would never work. Ecclesiastics as a rule were unfit to be judges. There appeared to be no alter- native but to refuse to depart from the old paths and usages about the Lord's Supper with which our forefatheral bad been content for 300 years. His sentence was that they ought so to stand firm, and abide the consequences, whether secession, disestablishment, or disruption. HARVEST THANKSGIVING AT RUNCORN PARISI/ Caunca.—This annual service took plac3 on the evening of the 14th inst., when there were exhibited the usual artistic and elaborate decorations for which the church is noted. Appropriate harvest texts were seen above the north, south, and west entrances of the nave and on the east wall of the chancel, wrought in wheat ears and tastefully gemmed with flowers, of which material the capital letters were entirely composed. Suspended from the capitals of the pillars, which were wreathed with greenery, were shields of various grounds, heraldically quartered and emblazoned with various ecclesiastical devices, formed of corn and flowers judiciously intermingled. A fringe of oats, looking like lacework in gold, was carried round the prayer desk and pul- pit, each panel of which exhibited a separate device in flowers, fruit, and corn. The communion table had a special frontal of blue with orphreys of plaited straw ; and in the place where the sacred monogram is usual seen was a radia- ting star of barley with a centre of scarlet geraniums. An arcade ran along the east wall, the arches of which were formed of wheat and oats, with an emblem in each panel composed of similar material. ,On the communion table was a magnificent floral cross flanked on either side by sheaves, from the fascis of which hung bunches of grapes ; these, as well as the other material used in the decoration of the church, having been presented by members of the con- gregation. Effectively, however, as these had been used, we heard complaints from several of the fair decorators of the scarcity of material, which, it is only fair to say, they attri- buted to the unusually late pert )d at which the service was held, and to the inclement weather, which has made such havoc of the gardens. Certainly, the general appearance of the church did not suggest any lack either of material or workmanship; for whilst the general effect was very strik- ing, every letter, emblem, and device was most carefully wrought, and would bear the minutest inspection. At half- past seven o'clock the choir, augmented by a contingent of girls, in white, from the Sunday School, entered the church, singing the usual processional hymn, "Come, ye thankful people, come." Prayers were said by the Rev. J. J. Bryant, M.A. ; the first lesson was read by the Rev. G. T. Simpson, and the second by the Rev. T. Manton Armson. The ser- mon was preached by the Rev. H. Victor Macdona, M.A., vicar of Cheadle Hulme, from Exodus xxiii. 16, "The feast of harvest." The anthem, effectively sung, was Goss's, " I will mangnify thee, 0 Lord, my King., ' Mr. Johnson pre- sided at the organ. The preacher's text was, "While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, land cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease." HOLY CROSS CHURCH, ST. HELENS.—On Thursday even ing a harvest thanksgiving service was conducted in the Holy Cross Church. An appropriate sermon was eloquently preached Sy the Rev. A. Dignam, S.J. Weber's jubilee cantata was sung by the choir. A collection was made* in aid of the proposed alteration in the choir.
