EMMANUEL CHITECH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, WARRINGTON.—The first paper of the season in connection with this society was read by the Rev. Mr. Cartwright on Thursday evening last, the subject being "The life of the late President Garfield, having special reference to his character as a young man." A brief discussion followed, and a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the essayist for his very able and instructive paper. , THE SUDDEN DEATHS AT WARRINGTON.—Verdicts o "died from natural causes" were returned at the inquests held before Mr. C. E. Driffield, at the General Woolfe Inn, Church-street, on Saturday, on the bodies of Giles Ashworth (36), 5, Battersbv-lane ; the infant son of Richard Mason, Howley-lane; and Mary Elizabeth Percival, infant daughter of a forgo labourer, residing in a court off Church-street, who died suddenly under circumstances reported last week.

SIGNOR Bosco.— This gentleman's 'Great American Enterprise" Company has attracted large audiences at the Public Hall, Warrington, this week. The entertainment was of a very enjoyable character, its variedness being very at- tractive. The rapid changes of costume by Mr. Harry Stewart, the great American electric change artiste and vocalist, were loudly applauded and he was recalled. The ventriloquial performance of Professor H. Miller, was an excellent and laughable one; while Banvard's diorama, overland route to India, was very effectively shown by the lime light. A number of portraits of celebrities of the day were also thrown on the screen. Some conjuring tricks were performed by Signor Bosco. The dialogue "A nightmare," was very good, and Mr. Joe Mortimer and Miss Annie Clarise took their respective parts most creditably. That ever fresh entertainment Punch and Judy," was greeted with roars of laughter and thoroughly enjoyed. Un- doubte ly a great attraction is the gifts which Signor Bosco distributes, and some of which, to jndge from the list, were valuable. Next week Signor Bosco will visit Widnes.

A YEAR'S CRIME IN PRESTON. —Mr. J. Oglethorpe, chief constable of Preston, has issued his annual report, in which he says that during the year ending the 29th Septem- ber there were two cases of murder, two of manslaughter, six of shooting, wounding, or stabbing, and one of rape. The number of indictable offences, including the above more serious crimes, was 269, being an increase of eight on the previous year. There were 166 persons apprehended, and of this number 123 were committed for trial, 55 of the 166 being known thieves. The number of persons proceeded against summarily before the magistrates shows a decrease of 198 on the previous year. The population of the borough being now 96,514, the number of persons proceeded against for drunkenness has been one to every 108 inhabitants. The number of cases of felony was 401, as compared with 402 ' last year. The value of property stolen was £1,171 123. 11d., of which £686 ss. 10d.has been recovered.

ELOPEMENT WITH A. YOUNG WIFE. CAP. JI3.E ON ! THE LIVERPOOL LANDING STAGE—The ways and means resorted to for the purpose of overcoming the difficulties I that proverbially beset the path of lovers are as varied as I they frequently are amusing, and the manner in which a young wife endeavoured last week to free herself from being "an old man's darling "by eloping with a fascinating young farmer of her acquaintance suggests a somewhat novel, though in this case, unsuccessful, course of procedure. The young lady in question is said to be possessed of consider- able personal attractions, and resided with her husband— very much her senior—on a farm near Hollingwerth Lake, where he acted as bailiff for an Oldham gentleman. There also lived in the neighbourhood a young farmer, with whom ' an intimate acquaintance had existed for some time. Re- cently the three came to the conclusion that they would sell up all their belongings and try their fortunes in the "Far West." Matters were all arranged, the auctioneer had been busy with his hammer, and a start was made towards the end of last week for Manchester, en route for Liverpool and ' America. So far apparently all went harmoniously, but in Manchester the young farmer and the wife gave the (Ad I gentleman the "slip," while he was at the height of con- viviality taking leave of old acquaintances. This is said to ' have been the inteniion throughout, but at all events the enamoured couple came on to Liverpool, took tickets for New York by the Cunard steamship Parthia, and intended to leave for America on Saturday. In the afternoon of that day, however, just as they were going on board the Cunard , tender, the husband arrived, and to the amusement of not a few people who were on the landing-stage, he protested against the treatment he had received, and gave the now unhappy couple into the custody of the Liverpool police. In the eyes of the law, however, they had not transgressed, so they were soon afterwards ' terwards liberated. The old gentle- man's troubles or the young wife's conduct did not end there, for the latter emphatically declined to abandon her intention, or to return to her late home by the lake. WARRINGTON CRICKET AND BOWLING CUM—The annual dinner of this club was held at the Lion Hotel, on Saturday evening, and was well attended by members and friends. Mr. W. Sharp, the president, occupied the chair at the after proceedings. Tha toast of "The Queen and mem- bers of the Royal family" having been duly honoured, Mr. Robert Davies proposed "The Army, Navy, and Reserve Forces," to which Mr. Thomas Hutchinson responded. The Chairman, in proposing "Success to the Warrington Cricket and Bowling Club." said the club was one of the oldest institutions in Warrington. He referred to the removal of the club to the new ground, which, he said, if it was not the most beautiful in England, was certainly one of the best, and admirably suited for its purpose. On the occasion of that change the Bowling Club was added, and he was sure the bowling ground was, without exception, the finest in England. They had lately added lawn tennis, and the new green had become so small that they were obliged to take in additional land. Some of the older cricketers thought it was a mistake to have bowling and lawn tennis on the same ground as cricket, but the results this year went to show that the addition of these two games had been an advantage to the Cricket Club. Their numbers had never been so great as they were now, and the cricketing power had not been so strong for many years. Mr. H. Fairclough, in responding for the cricketers, said the club started with a debt of £5OO or £6OO. Last year the treasurer announced that they had some funds in hand. They had won nine matches, drawn five, and lost three during the season, which was a greater success than ever they had before. The batting averages also were more favourable, and the bowling had not been exceeded by any club in Lancashire. Mr. T. Morris, who responded on behalf of the bowling club, said he should go to the bowling green twice a week if they had a better way , to it,*the present one not being very pleasant when the water was high. If they would only put their shoulders to the wheel he thought they could obtain a better entrance. Mr. Tucker responded on behalf of the lawn tennis players, and said they had only played two games this year, and bad won one. Other toasts followed.

div.head: POOR-LAW CONFERENCE.
div.p: THE POOR-LAW CONFERENCE.

The CLERK said the gentlemen who were appointed to attend the recent Poor-law Conference were the chairman, Mr. Mackie, and Mr. Winstanley. It turned out that Mr. Mackie was unwell at the time, and could not attend. He had received the following letter from Mr. Bleckly "Warrington, 17th September, 1881.—My dear sir,—l saw Mr. Hibbert a few days ago, and he urged me to attend the I next Poor-law Conference. I told him it was doubtful whether I should be at home at .the time, but I should be glad if you would let me know when it will be held. I think he said the place of meeting is Rochdale. Can you refer to the last Local Government report, and tell me the average cost of lunatics throughout the country? So far as I recollect it is 9s. 7d." He consulted with the Chairman and Mr. Winstanley, and they were very pleased that Mr. Bleckly should be invited to take the place of Mr. Mackie. Mr. Bleckly, however, was ca,lled away to Plymouth, to attend the meeting of the Chambers of Commerce. The Chairman was also indisposed, and Mr. Blackburst, the senior vice-chairman, took his place. There was a very large attendance, and the subjects discussed were of a most interesting charac:er, particularly the subject of vagrancy. A long and important discussion took place upon that sub- ject, and he was pleased to state that Mr. Winstanley spoke upon the question in a way that called forth general appro- bation. The next conference was fixed to take place at Lancaster, in October, next year.

Major C. ARTWRIGIiT observed that the deputation was appolidoil by the Board, but it was not the one that went. Mr. W INbTANLEY said he agreed with Major Cartwright that the deputation was not as official as might have been sent from the Boat d. For example they might have sent Major Cartwrigllt—[Major CARTWIZIGRT: He would not go.]—and had he atlorded as much amusement to the con- ference as he did at the meetings a the Board he would hits been a most valuable addition. (Laughter.) He was ' pleased to tell the Board the conference was a most interest- ing, one, and the question of that fluctuating population which roamed about, and preyed upon, the country was very fully discussed, and would, he believed, lead to such an alteration in the law as would enable Boards of Guardians, if they thought tit, to detain such persons and make them work for a dsy or two. By that means would be broken up the charm that seemed to attach to the vagrant life. Several other subjects were brought under the notice of the con- ference, and from the tetiour of the remarks made by the Chairman it was quite clear that the Government intended to deal with the question of the administration of relief very shortly. He thought it was very likely that next spring it might be necessary for a deputation to go to London with other Boards.

div.head: BOARD AND THE COUNTY CALLS.
div.p: THE BOARD AND THE COUNTY CALLS.

The CLERK read the following letter:—" County Palatine of Lancaster, October 11.—Dear Sir,—l am informed by Mr. ' Meekly that you consider the time given to the overseers to collect the rates is insufficient. 7I would gladly do any- thingtin my power to meet their wishes by an extension of the time. The rates are assessed at the annual sessions, and levied by order of quarter sessions, and 50 days, the time allowed for payment, was no doubt fixed after due considera- tion. I have consulted with the Clerk of the Peace on the subject, and find that there are considerable difficulties in materially lengthening the time allowed; but if on further consideration, it is found that an extension is practicable I shall be only too glad to give the overseers the benefit of it. Although the time fixed in the precept is 50 days, pro- ceedings cannot be taken until the succeeding annual session, which varies from 70 to 90 days. I will ask the Clerk of the Peace to forward the precept in future at the earliest pos- sible date, so that the interval may always by as large as possible. Truly yours, HENRY ALLISON. J. C. Sutton, Esq."—He replied as follows:—" My suggestion is, that, ' when practicable, notice of ptobable material increase of county rates should be given. This Union lies within two counties, and estimates of future expenditure made one month before March 30th and before September 30th. They are based on averages, and though reasonable provision is made for contingences, it is undesirable to seek large re- serves. Credit is given to each parish for the balance in favour. Now it may of course be that the sums required by the counties may exceed by several AS by one thousand pounds those paid in the corresponding half of the previous year; and cannot the increase be sufficiently foreseen as to justify an intimation prior to the periods named of the probate ad- vance? lam obliged by your consultation with Mr. Hulton, and if my suggestion is practicable, its adoption, would, I think, be convenient to Union clerks generally. Jam aware of the remidits available to us, but as overseers levy rates approximative with the calls half yearly made upon them it is desirable to avoid supplemental calls, I think the time between service of precept and date of payment satisfac- tory." He had received no reply. Beyond the very large and elaborate system of accounts contained in the book which came annually or half yearly, he had received a clas- sified summary of the county expenditure. They had sent I a few copies and any gentleman who felt interested in 0,3 question could have one. Mr. DARI3YSHIRE said he would like a copy. Ho sup- t posed there was nothing in it to show the ratepayers there ' would be no further increase in the county rates. ! The CLERK : No, sir; but I referred to that in my letter. Mr. HAIZBYSIIIIIE did not know that. He thought when there was an increase of £l,OOO in a half year in a Union like this—or a portion of the Union that is in LancAhire— the Board ought to have some notice of it beforehand to that they could provide for payment.
The CHAIRMAN said that was the very suggestion the Clerk had made, and they had intimated their willingness to comply with it as far as they possibly could.

div.head: EPILEP lIC LUNATICS.
div.p: EPILEP lIC LUNATICS.

Mr. WINSTANLEY said within the last month or two a difficulty had arisen in getting lunatics into the asylums be- cause they had been subject to fits. Patients had been re- fused at Prestwich, Whittington, and Rainhill ; and only last week Mr. Caldwell took a patient to Itainbill but the authorities refused to admit her because she had been sub- ject to fits. He had to remain there more than 20 minutes begging and praying before they would take her in. He wished to know what provision was made for cases of this sort. There was no provision for them at the workhouse, and he did not think there was at any other workhouse ex- cept Bolton, and if the county authorities refused to accept them who was to take them ?
The CHAIRMAN: Mr. Clerk, did you ever here of that before?

The CLERK said provision was being made very exten- sively at Whittington for this class of patients. He was going there shortly and would mention the matter. Mr. WissveimEr : Then you had better get the letter which Mr. Caldwell received a week ago, in which they said they won't receive these patients.
The CLERK: The onlyditlieulty is that they are wanting room for them.

div.head: LIABILITY OF SOLDIERS.
div.p: LIABILITY OF SOLDIERS.

Major CARTWRIGHT referred to the recommendation of the House Committee that proceedings be taken against a soldier with his regiment at Fleetwood for the maintenance of the illegitimate child of Mary Taylor. The CLERK said if the wife of a soldier was chargeable, a portion of the soldier's pay would be set aside for her maintenance, but no proceeding could be taken in respect of an illegitimate child.
Mafo'r CARTV7RIGHT : Now, Mr. Clerk, you know very well. (Laughter.) The REV. Joror YONGE asked if soldiers were exempt 4n such cases.
The CLERK said that any proceeding against a soldier would have no practical result. Mr. WiNisrAwr.wy: It is useless to spend money on pro- ceedings of no.use to us.
THE maort ON REMOVAL CASES.

Major Canzvatinur drew attention to the number of re- moval cases in the House. :le said at the Barracks there were 74 deserted children, and he was pretty certain a number of the deserters could be apprehended. They had a case brought from Scotland which was very success- ful, and there were so many deserted children he thought some steps ought to be taken in regard to them. It was evi- dent the Board would want a vast amount of money to lay out at Padgate very shortly, if the removal cases were not attended to and apprehensions were not made. A man was sent to gaol a month or five weeks ago. Previous to his commit tal he was in good employment and could maintain his family as he was earning from 30s. to 50s. a week. But he was sent for a month, and the children still remained in the House, as the wife was undergoing three months' im- prisonment. The man had had sufficient time allowed him since he came out of prison to come to the House for his children and look after them, bat he had not done so. He knew the man was in employment, and that he refused last Saturday week a constant place of work that would have brought him in 30s. to 50s. weekly. There was no excuse for the man because his wife was in gaol, and he ought to have come to the Board and made some arrangemeat in re- gard to his children staying at or leaving the House. It was these cases he complained of.
The CHAIRMAN: I believe that case trill come before the Board in the ordinary way.this morning... . ....

. . Major CARTWRIGIIT said he knew that, but it vvas not satisfactory. What he wanted to know from the Board was —and he had put it several times—whose duty was it to see that these cases were properly attended to? Mr. WINSTANLEY : Hear, hear. That is what we all want to know.

Major CARTWRIGHT: That is all I want to know, and I want, as chairman of the committee, to have support of the Board. These cases are continually brought before the House Committee, and we have to make remarks such as these—" This committee requests that Ann Kelly, William Watson, and Patrick Helligan be removed at once." "The committee requests that Thomas Higgins be removed at once." I have been looking at the Removal Book, and have been thflugh the house this morning, and I see the Clerk I has pet opposite one name—"sick." Now, be is not sick. He is fit to be removed, and if you don't remove him now, while he is sufficiently well to be removed, you will have him here nobody knoivs how long. The CLERK is an Irish case, and he is admitted as a sick man, and, being sick' is irremovable to Ireland. Major CARTWRIGHT: You have written him down as sick ?
The CLERK : Yes. Major CARTWRIGHT : Weß, VOU should not do that he is

r not sick. When we put it down in the report book we r expected it would be attended to. At the request of the Clerk, Major Cartwright read the names again, and , The CLERK said Watson was born in Warrington, and was settled here. He was not removable.

Major Clarrwatoirr said the man had turned round; some one had put him up to it. The man had got a com- fortable place, and he had turned round. The CLETUS: His statement was clear, and he in no way contradicted himself. It is a mistake to have too comfort- able a place here for him. Higgins and Helligan were both sick.

Major CiRTWRIGHT hoped the Board wouH bear with him, because these were complaints that ought to be attended to. Some time ago the Board passed a resolution that no person should be in arrear for more than a fortnight. The CLFrac: When Mr. Burrows was here you passed such a resolution.

Major CARTWEIGHT : We have passed a resolution since Mr. Shearer was appointed, Mr. Clerk; it is on the books. He mentioned the case of a flat captain named Hillidge, who was sued for the maintenance of his children, and said he only resided at Widnes, and yet he was allowed to fall into arrear to the amount of £4 18s. 6d.

—Mr. WINSTANLEY asked if Mr. Shearer was about. It was only right be should hear these statements. Major CARTWILIGHT said when a man served a month's imprisonment the Clerk advised they could not then recover • the arrears.

--Tile-a-sax: If you consider a man is sent to prison be- cause he does not pay something, it is pretty good evidence that he can't pay. Major CARTWRIGHT said that was not what he was aim- ing at. 'II the Board allowed a man to get into arrears to the extent of Ll, and summoned him at once, they got the money, but if they allowed him to get into arrear to the extent of .65, he went to prison because he could not pay. This man was arrested and the £4 ISs. 6d. wiped off, and that was what he complained of. Ile wanted to know whether it was the duty of Mr. Shearer or Mr. Harbonrne to I look after these cases. Mr. SHEARER, who had been called into the room, said, in reply to Major Cartwright, that the man Hillidge did not owe £4 18s. 6d. He was summoned for £1 14s. 6d., and that sum included the costs of a previous hearing. Major CARTWRIGHT was proceeding to question Mr. Shearer, and then to refer to a previous discussion with the Clerk when . .

Mr. DARBYSHIRE (interrupting) said he did not think it necessary to go into the matter. It was not before the Board. He thought the Chairman was rather too easy in such matters in not stopping the discussion, because it really was not a question for the Board to go into. It was not for the Board to enquire who had the best or the worst memory on a matter that did not concern them.

Mr. Wptsramatir : I think that is a question for you to consider, Mr. Chairman, because you are liable to a fine for permitting gambling. (Laughter.) Major CARTWRIGHT If Mr. Winstanley put it in that light, he knows as well as I do that he is putting it in a manner that he ought not to do. I have no doubt he has been in the habit of being in the ring at Newton, or some- where there where they make wagers. The CLERK said there were a considerable number of gentlemen who were present at the time, who were quite impartial and heard all that took place, and when those gentlemen together concluded that he made a wager and the Major won the wager he would pay it. He did not want to refer to anything be saw in the newspaper except to say that there was not a single word of it, as far as he was con- cerned, that was true. The editor, and the gentlemen who appeared there on behalf of that paper, were aot in the smallest degree responsible for what appeared in the paper on the subject. Beyond that he was not going to notice the matter or say a word on the subject. He went away not in the course of that discussion at all—business was over— but it was pretty nearly at the end of Mr. Caldwell's case he was obliged to go away. He knew perfectly well had he chosen to ask for information where Co obtain it, but made no such enquiry. Upon his return from the County Ses- sions to the room, he was told by the Major he had seen the case entered in the books upon which he replied "Well I cannot put my recollection against what you found in the books." The CHAIRMAN: I did not hear that said.

Major CARTWRIGHT : I never heard it. The CLERK said the Chairman would not hear it for his (the Clerk's) seat being occupied by his assistant he sat by the Major and conversed with him upon it. It was then he was so informed, and Mr. Gornall, a gentleman whose word would be accepted by every person, sat next to them. The communication to the paper put it that on his return he said certain things. Now on the contrary he welled tot only until his own seat was at liberty, but elin he took it other business was preceeded with, and it was after the other busi- ness he stated that he bad remembered that Major Cart- wric,ht sat on the Warrington Bench at the time and he stated what conversation he had with the Major on his return to the room.
Mr. DAIII3YST,UP.E again ashed what the Boatd had to do with the matter. ,

Major CAIITNN FI6TIT : It is a very important matter. If you don't study your character I do mine. Mr. DAnnrsurnE (warmly): I don't want you to domi- neer over me. Ido study my character rkulte as much as you study your character. Yon.have no right to ask me if 1 study my character. I believe it will turn out that you I were both wrong. It was tried at both places, and why I should we waste our time here?

i Major CARTWRIOITT: Mr. Darbyshire, all I want is fair play. I have not had fair play, and I am surpriied at you attempting, at all events, to stifle anything I have to say. The CHSIRMAN: Mr. Clerk, I just want to ask one ques- tion in iefe-ence to the report which appeared in the news- papers. Da you say there is not a word of truth in it? The CLERIC said there was not as far as he was concerned. In the first place there was a statement—"At this point the Clerk- left." He heard the whole of the discussion which arose when Mr, Caldwell's business came on, and which oc- cupied a column in the newspapers, but the inference was thrown out that he went to look over some musty docu- ments, and it was otherwise untrue. Major CARTWRIGHT : I have nothing to do with the report. The CLERK : I am sure you would not be capable of say- ing to any person what is represented to have been said. Major CARTWRIGHT : I have had no hand in anything of the sort.

Mr. WOOLFALL : Mr. Sutton does not believe you have. Mr. WINSTANLEY joined with Mr. Derbyshire in saying the whole matter was intolerant. What did it matter if the case took place at Warrington or Darman:try What had it to do with the Board? He protested against these pro- ceedings._

MajOr CLUTWRIGHT: I have no doubt you do• The CLERK, who had to appear in some cases at the sessions house, and who, during the discussion, stood by the door ready to leave, said that he must really go, unless the Board wished him to remain.

The Rev. Ram YONGE : I move that we proceed to the next business. With all respect to Major Cartwright and the edification he intended to give us, I do not know we have to do with it. I have been trying to find out what ,we have to do with it, but I can't see what we have to do with it.

THE CHAIRMAN was bound to say the matter was not relevant, and was not quite what the Board was bound to listen te. But it was a matter which rested with the Beard whether they were desirous of showing Major Cartwright courtesy by hearing what he had got to say upon a discus- sion that took place at the last meeting in which a statement was denied.

The Rev. J. YONGR personally had no wish to show Major Cartwright any discourtesy, but [said if the matter was to be gone into Mr. Sutton should remain. At present he had not been edified by what the Major had said. Major CARTWRIGHT said he wanted to show in the book before him he was right. The CLERK said the Major was quite right for there was the book to show it. The question of where the case was heard was altogether secondery, and immaterial to the real point before the Board, which was, were there not collateral circumstances attending the case quoted by the Major, which were atsent from the case considered by the Board. Major CARTWRIGIIT : lam satisfied if you admit that it was tried before me. The CLERK: Certainly I do, Major, I believe Mr. Darby. shire is also correct that the case in the first instance came before the magistrates at Daresbury. The woman got no remedy, and came before the Warrington magistrates, and they in the first instance dismissed the case, but afterwards made the order. (The Clerk then left the room.) The question of removals was then reverted to, and The CHAIRMAN said there was only one officer to attend to the matter, and he thought that was the Clerk. He did not think the clerk would for one moment attempt to deny it. If the Board remembered there was a suggestion which came from the clerk that the Local Government should be applied to, to say whose duty it was to take action after the Board had made an order for the prosecution of any one for neglect. He thought it was quite an understood thing that there should be no more discussion. But the question had cropped up again, and the Board seemed to he as much at sea u ever they were.

A long and desultory discussion then took place on the subject of the letter received from the Chief Constable, and after Mr. Hirbourne, Mr. Shearer, the porter and porteress had been questioned on the subject, the matter was dropped without anything definite having been come to. Upon the 'clerk's return, the medical officer's books were examined, and it appeared in them that the persons named by the com- mittee for removal to Ireland, were under medical treatment lit was decided to take no steps.

div.head: STATE OF THE HOUSE.
div.p: STATE OF THE HOUSE.

The MASTER reported 503 inmates as against 454 in the corresponding week of last year. During the week 184 vagrants, 151 men, 24 woman, and 9 children were relieved. The Master, on behalf of the children, was desirous of thanking Mrs. Woods for a quantity of toys, &c., she sent them, and whtch pleased them very much.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

Mobel Wilberforce, Indicted for perjury, was again:brought up at the Central Criminal Court, the hearing of evidence for the prosecution being resumed. Prisoner protested several times against the evidence. A photograph being pro- duced she admitted it to be a genuine likeness of herself and it was proved that at the trial she had stated she knew nothing of tais photograph. Several witnesses were examined to prove that in 1864 prisoner, under the name of Amy Normanly, was in Manchester with two children. Several other witnesses stated positively that in 1870 prisoner was in Liverpool, as Mrs. Trenefide. The case was adjourned. A telegram was received at the Admiralty yesterday after noon from the Earl of Clanwilliam, reporting the arrival of the detached squadron at Yokohama yesterday. There are at present six fishing boats missing from Yar- mouth since the late gale—four loggers with crews of ten each, and two smacks with crews of six each. Great fears are entertained for their safety.

At Limerick City Quarter Sessions, yesterday, the County Court Judge said the calendar was a light one, but no index of the state of the city. The conduct of the police during the late disturbance he characterised as highly meritorious.

John Shey, dealer, was arrested at Tralee, yesterday morning, on a charge of intimidating a number of men who came into the town to join the Royal Constabulary. Fri. Boner will be brought up at the next Pttty Sessions. Three furnace chargers, principals in the recent strike movement amongst the Cleveland blast furnace men, were Yesterday brought before the Middlesborough magistrates for leaving work without notice and were fined £lO each and costs,

At Cork Corporation yesterday a land league member proposed a resolution condemning the Government's action in having arrested Mr. Parnell and others. Some of the Home Rulers, Liberal, and Conservative members of the Cuporation protested strongly against the resolution in. the face of the no rent proclamation, and the matter was abandoned.

div.head: STORNI AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: THE STORNI AT ST. HELENS.

On Friday morning a storm of unusual fury visited St. Helens, and raged for the greater part of the day accom- panied by showers of rain. The wind was extremely strong and did a great deal of damage. Slates from the roofs of houses and bricks and chimney stacks fell into the streets, to the great danger of the pedestrians who were muoh exer- cised as to their safety. The centre of the road was greatly used by those who did not wish to run the risk of being in- jured by contact a ith missiles which now and then felt from the tops of the houses. This was not contested to a few par- ticular streets, as most of the streets ia the town bore indi- cations of the injurious effects of the storm upon property. The new schools on Cowley Hill, which are yet unopened, being unprotected, and in a position which gives the elements good play, received some injury, some portion of the roofing being carried several yards away. The Holy Cross Church was also damaged, the cross at the east end, and some carved masonry being thrown to the ground. The chimney of the sacristy fell through the roof of an addition which is being made tel the church. The damage done to this chapel is estimated at about £l5O. la the neighbour- hood of Boundary-road on the outskirts of the town several windows were blown in, wooden railing torn up, and cen- siderable damage done. In Hardshaw-street a chimney was greatly damaged, and as contributions of bricks, dm., were being deposited on the pavement bplow, it was deemed neces- sary to protect the passengers by placing obstructions across the parapet. Sergeant-Major Tyson's apartments at the Volunteer Hall were damaged by a chimney stack falling through the roof, and a portion of the rcof of the Engineer Hall was carried away. Two cld uninhabited houses at Gerard's Bridge fell into ruins, and in the same locality the occupants of some cottages (which were much swayed by the wind) left their abodes in alarm and subsequently re- moved part of their furniture. At St. Ann's and Thatto Heath damage was done to windows, and at Rainford also much damage was committed; notably to the house of Mr. Westhead, the window of which was completely wrecked.

FATAL ACCIDENTS: The most painful effects of the storm was witnessed at Sutton National Schools. While the children were in the school, the bell rope, which hung over a class of children in the gallery was seen to vibrate from the force of the wind. This, together with the noise of the wind and the rain out- side, attracted the attention of the children. Soon after, about eleven o'clock, there was a loud crasb, a portion of the roof having fallen into the gallery, which was greatly smashed. Miss Rosebotham, one of the teachers, exhibited much courage, and attended to the children, masy of whom she extricated from painful positions. Mr. Flews being out at the time, and becoming aware of what had occurred, hastened tO the place and assisted in getting the children out and pacifying them. One child named Harriet Bradbury was found lying in a hole underneath the broken gallery, covered by a large stone which in its fell had broken through the gallery. She was dead. This stone was the half of the arch which surmounted the bell. Another pf the ibelfry stones fell on the wall of the play grouild and broke it down About twenty feet of the play ground wall was blown in. Several children were injured, their names being Frank Capper, Thomas Woods, Paul Barrow, John Hayes, Josiah Marsh, and Ellen Challoner, the two last-named being i very seriously hurt, and now lie n a precarious condition. The inquest on the body of the child Harriet Bradbury was held on Monday, at the Glassmaker's Arms, Sutton, before Mr. Driffield, coroner.

James news, headmaster of the schools, slid he was in the boys' school when the accident occurred, which was about 11 o'clock. The first lie heard was the boys scream- .ing ; he could not say that he heard the crash. The boys were rushing for the door, which could not be opened for the pressure. It was the same in the girls' r6om ; and with difficulty the doors were opened and the children let out. He then went to the infants' room, and found that such a rush had been made to the door that the children were lying on each other. When they were cleared he found that the room was filled with dust, through which he could see Miss Rosebotham on thegallery:pulling a child out from the ruins. As soon as she pt this child out 'witness asked her if she thought they were all out, and said she was sure they were. When the room was clear he examined the coping stone which had fallen, but could see no trace of anyone, and the infant school was left. Five or six children were 'wounded, and they were carried home. About half an hour after- wards the mother of the child, Jane Bradbury, came and said her child had not come home. Houses in the neighbour- hood were searched, but the missing child could not be found, and Mr. 'Westhead again examined the stone, which was a large one and weighed Id cwt. The debris was moved from round the stone, and witness put his hand under ond felt the child's head. The stone was removed, and the child taken out, but it was quite dead. From the knees to the head every bone must have been broken. The bell and one large stone fell inside, and the others outside. They would fall 25 feet or 30 feet. It was an extraordinary gale which was the cause of it, and six or ..even feet of the play ground wall was blown down at the same time. The wall was 14 inches thick.—By the Coroner : Witness had been there 14 years, but bad no suspicion the belfry was unsafe. The schools were erected in 1862. The bell fell once but nothing was done to the belfry. He had never heard any suggestion that the belfry was unsafe before the accident. The stones were not " clamped " together. He thought .it had gone over bodily. If he had heard complaints about it, he would have laid it before the committee and relieved himself of the responsibility.—The Coroner: Had you no suspicion that morning? No, sir.—The Coroner: The streets were not safe that morning.—A Juryman: The brickwork of the belfry was not sufficient to hold the stone.
Jane Bradbury, Robin's-lane said the body she had seen was that of her child who was four years of age.

Margaret Annie Pye, 13 years of age. pupil teacher in the 1 infants' school, said she was on the gallery teaching a class when the accident occurred. She beard the wind howling and saw the bell rope shake, and all at once the roof fell in. She caught hold of two children, and shouted to the others to run away. She had no suspicion of awe' danger. She drew back as (Illicitly as she could, and clasped the two children in her arms, and went out as quickly as she could. A Juryman remarked that the witness seemed to have haft a very narrow escape herself. Hannah Rosebotham, assistant mistress in the infants' school, stated that she was at the end of the echoed furthest from the gallery when the accident happened. She beard a crash and at first could see nothing for the dust and timber flying aboue. All the children were ,creaming and rushing out of the school. She went to the gallery and got three or four children out of the rubbish. There were seven or eight hurt. She did not see deceased. She did not see the stone fall. There had never been the slightest alarm before.
In answer to the Coroner, the Rev. Mr. Vaßamey said he had never heal d that the belfry or any part of the schools was insecure.
The Coroner, in summing up, said they could only attribute the occurrence to the extraordinary severity of the gale. _ _
The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

THE BIRTH AND DEATH-RATE OF WARRINGTON.—Week ending 15th October. The mean temperature was 45.6 Fehr, and therefore 11 F higher than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 60.1 F was recorded on the 11th instant, and the minimum temperature 28 F on the 9th and 15th insts. The rainfall measured 243 inches. The general direction of the wind was north-east. During the the week, which was the 42nd of the current year, 34 births and 11 deaths were registered. The death-rate from all causes was equal io 136 per 1,000, against 173, the average of the previous four weeks, and against 16.9 the correspond- ing week of last year. The deaths included 1 from croup and 2 from typhoid fever. The death-rate, therefore, from zymotic diseases was equal to 37 per 1,000, against 14.6 the average rate of the four previous weeks, and against 3.9 of the corresponding week of 1880. Three deaths were referred to acute lung disease, and one to pulmonary consumption. Eleven cases of infectious disease were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament, viz., 10 cases of scarlet fever and 1 of typhoid fever„—JonN 11. GIoRNALS. Medical Officer of Health.

TETE CONGREGATIONALISTS AND TOTE VYRNWY SERVICES. —An important decision was given on Tuesday on Tuesday by the united meting of the North Wales Congregational Union having charge of the mission work in Montgomery. shire among the Liverpool Corporation water scheme work- men. It will be remembered that the Church of England and the Congregationists each applied for building sites, which the Corporation agreed to grant, adding a gift of £5O yearly towards sustaining each mission. While gratefully acknowledging this kindness and accepting the lease, the Congregationalists unanimously felt they could not consis- tently accept the money, and respectfully declined the game. a decision which will give general satisfaction among the Nonconformists.

Such an assertion was easily made, and from its generalness it was not easily replied to; but it must b . remembered that the results were not often such as cc .1d be easily seen by travellers or scientists. The direct results lay too deep for the observation or estimation of such men, who said the I work had been begun at the wrong end, as the Kaffirs and Zulus required to be taught agriculture and other such matters. He thought it was only fair to say that these men had never tried their own schemes, or if they had the success had been of so doubtful a character as to make them look uninviting. The world was a very large one, and he for one would be quite willing to assign a place for a trial of these philantrophic plans. Twenty years of thoughtful observa- tion went to prove that the natives of South Africa would graft too easily upon the many abominable vices of civilisa- tion. They leaned to be drunkards much more than to be tem- perate. A Kaffir would purchase a gun at any price, while he would scorn the idea of a plough, a wheelbarrow, or a spade. What would become of the natives if the missionary did not go before the civilizer ? The good effects Of the Gospel could not be exaggerated. The natives had begun to adopt many of the blessings and proprieties of civilisation through the influence of the Gospel. They now wore clothing which had been manufactured in Manct)ester and Bradford. He could tales them to a mission where a beautiful chapel had been erected almost entirely by native workmen, and paid for by native subscriptions, and it was worth no less than £4,000. A native preacher occupied the pulpit, and a native musician performed on the organ. They would see thousands of people clad in European garments, and carrying on the seine industries as in England. And 50 years ago these same people were naked savages with no better employment than war, mid this civilisation had all been accomplished within the memory of men who were still working on the station. He mentioned that one case as only one of many which had come under his own observation. The abomin- able practice of killing some of the counsellors on the death of a chief had been abolished, and many other good results had been attained through the preaching of the truth. He wished to prove that the natives would yield to the mission- ary when they found it galling to submit to English warriors. Able governors had gone out, like Evelyn Wood and others, but the natives had dealt treacherously with them, and confounded them in diplomacy. This all went to prove that the power of truth, as it was in Christ Jesus, was a better means of civilising South Africa than all the legions of warriors which might be sent out to that country. —The custom4ry vote of thanks having been passed, the proceedings terminated. div.head: EXPENDITURE.
div.p: THE EXPENDITURE.

The CLEER7presented the statement of the accounts of the Board for the year which showed that the receipts amounted to £6lO 19s. 94., including grants horn the Committee of Council on Education, £69 13s. 91.; payments made to the treasurer by the rating authorities, £5OO (at 20. in the £) ; and school fees, £6l 14s. 54. The principal items of ex- penditure were :—By balance on the 29th September, 1880, £79 lOs 24.; election expenses, £8 ss. ; salaries of officers of the Board, £167 is. 44.; repayment of principal of loans' £24 lie. 4d. ; interest on loans, £26 18s. lid.; legal and othcr expenses, £79 17s. 101 ; salaries of teachers, £97 Os. 24.; fuel and light, and repairs to buildings and furniture, £37 4s. ; expenses of maintenaCe of industrial schools, £23 ss. 7d. The total expenditure was £573 lie. 3d. The balance in the hands of the treasurer on the 29th September, this year, was £63 17s. 74. The net expen- diture was £503 17s. 6d.—During a conversation upon the balance sheet, the CLERK said there appeared to have been an increase in the rateable value during the year. It was now £48,000, and it used to be £35,000.—Mr. NORMAN moved that the accounts should be passed and signed by the chairman. The statement was very satisfactory indeed.—Mr. BRISCOE seconded the proposition, which was passed. PAYMENT OF SCHOOL FEES TO INDIGENT PARENTS.

The CLERK read the letter which he had written to the Runcorn Board of Guardians on this subject, and their reply, which has already appeared in The Examiner.—Mr. NORMAN remarked that the Guardians seemed to think that their enquiry officer' Mr. Wright, was in a better position than Mr. Bowyer to decide which were proper cases in which school fees should be paid, but, for his own part, he did not see that this was necessarily the case.—The CHAIR- MAN; Would the Guardians consider that where the in- ability to pay the fees was caused by drunkenness, they were justified in paying the fees.—Mr. NORMAN thought the G uardians had really no option but to pay the fees in such cases, as the unnatural parents did not seem to care whether the education of their children was attended to or not.—The CHAIRMAN: It is a very difficult question.—Mr. BRISCOE remarked that the cause of the letter being sent to the Guardians was owing to the statements made by different parents to the committee of the School Board, to the effect that when they applied to Mr. Wright for payment of fees they were told they must attend at Dutton workhouse, which .was several miles away. They said that Mr. Wright de- clined to listen to their applications, and told them they must attend at Dutton.—Mr. NORMAN was of opinion that it was a very hard case to send the parents to Dutton.—The CLERK pointed out that it was somewhat of a hardship that guardians from other townships than Runcorn should, in reality, decide as to the payment of money which did not come out of the common fund of the Union, but out of the money paid by Runcorn.—The CHAIRMAN said it ap- peared that some of the families referred to had a sufficient income with which to pay the fees for their children attend- ing school, but they spent it in drink. Under such circum- stances it seemed hard that the ratepayers of the town should be called upon to pay the fees.—Mr. Nor/mAN said that at the meeting of Guardians on the previous day, an application came before them for the payment of school fees from a person living in Halton-road, who was actually in re- ceipt of between 245. and 25s per week. Such requests were abominable, and the particular one referred to was, of course, refused.—Mr. PRITCHARD observed that about 28 parents attended the last meeting of the School Board Attendance Committee, and out of these a considerable number were really not able to pay the school fees. In many of the cases the children were not attending school, the fees having been stopped, and for this no satisfactory reason could be given.—The CHAIRMAN: We are as wishful as the Guardians that the fees should not be paid in casesrhere they ought not to be ; but if we hay° to pay them in instances where the parents spend their money in drink, it is very hard upon the ratepayers.—Mr. NORMAN : If you summon a man, and he is sent to prison, you have to keep the family, and that is a very awkward affair. (Laughter.) —lt was decided that the parent applying for the payment of his children's school fees should take a note to Mr. Wright, the relieving officer, stating that the Attendance Committee considered his a proper case for assistance, and that a list of all such cases should be given to Mr. Norman in order that he might lay them before the Guardians. Mr. Norman promised to do his best to remedy the complaints at present made, and it was resolved to leave any action in the matter over for the present, in order to see how the new plan worked.
ATTENDANCE RETURNS.

l'he returns of Mr. Bowyer, attendance officer, for Sep- tember, showed that the total number in attendance at private adventure schools, under ninepence per week, was 6. At the Attendance Committee meeting on the 31st August, he reported 57 parents for the irregular and non-attendance of their children at school. Twenty-nine parents appeared before the committee in answer to the notices. In 16 cases the parents were ordered to be served with final notices. Three applications were made for half time and granted; and the school fees of six children attending the Board school were also ordered to be remitted until Chrsitmas.— The CHAIRMAN remarked that several other School Boards, with the operations of which he was acquainted, were con- siderably more strict with parents in the matter of their children's attendance than theßuncorn Board were. As her Majesty's Inspector stated that the attendance made by the children in this town was less than he found to be the case anywhere else, he (the speaker) was of opinion they would be quite justified in exercising more strictness on this matter.—Mr. Pnrrcnenn : If we had accommodation it would be advisable to do so, but I do not think that con- sidering our circumstances, there is much room for us doing so,—The CHAIRMAN considered that it was quite evident in I the cases they hadenquired into that morning, the children were not kept away because it was found impossible for them to be provided with accommodation at; the schools. In many of the instances under their consideration, it was perfectly clear that the children had attended properly enough at the beginning of the various weeks, but after- wards remained away.—The CLERK : There is a very long list, and most of the parents whose names are upon it have had notices served upon them to attend.—Mr. BOWYER : Yes, and many of them have been fined.—Some further dis- cussioe ensued, and the general feeling appeared to be that they had been too lenient in dealing with parents in the past, and stricter measures must be taken in the future.— The CLERK said that it was provided by the Summary Jurisdiction Act that if a parent refused to pay a fise the Authority might distrain, but they did se upon the responsibility of the Board, and it frequently happened that there was an outlay of about 203. in recovering a fine of ss. (Laughter.—Mr. BOWYER : But if they have no goods, you can ask for a commitment to Knutsford.—The CLERK: That involves another outlay, and you must also may the fine.—The CHAIRMAN: And how about the children P—The CLERK: Why, they are worse off than they were before! (Laughter,)—The CHAIRMAN was inclined-to believe that if the Board would only spend a little more money they would be enabled to improve the at- tendance, and thus carry out the object of the Elementary Education Act.—The CLERK The Summary Jurisdiction Act has worked very badly in large towns, but if it became known what the real provisions of the measure are, we should get on very badly. However, as a rule, we do not deal with the cream of the working classes.—The Cllant- MAN : The law is made for evil doers! (Laughter.)—lt was resolved that summonses should be issued in 25 of the cases which had been before the Board. ' GIVING A WIDE BF.RTII TO TRINITY SCHOOL. It was reported by the CLERK that Mr. Bowyer had been told by an inhabitant named ealkeld that his child bad been refused admission to Trinity school.—The CHAIRMAN: I do not see that we can do anything with the matter. All that we have to do with is the fact that the child has not ttended school.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.

MAGISTRATES NVANTED.—These sessions were hAd on Wednesday, in the Borough Court, and, as has been the case for months, business was much delayed for want of a second magistrate. Mr. John Rylands made his appearance on the Bench at 10-30, and adjudicated on the cases which were within his jurisdiction. Complainants and defendants in other cases, however, after a weary waiting of 45 minutes, were told the court would be adjourned for an hour. This irksome delay is of almost fortnightly occurrence, and calls for a remedy. At 11-10 a man named Keating was placed in the prisoners' dock to answer a charge of committinea breach of the peace, and, as it was by no means his first appearance at the court, he evidently knew the mode in which the business was conducted, for when asked why he did not come at 10-30, he replied, "I thought I'd be time enough." ~At Newton there is invariably a full and punc- tual Bench, but they live at such a distance from Warrirg- ton that it would be unreasonable to expect them to attend Warrrington Sessions. Clearly, therefore. the' only remedy is to increase the number of magistrates, by placing on the Commission of the Peace gentlemen residing in Warrington or its immediate neighbourhood, and who have sufficient time at their disposal to fulfil the duties. Something ought, at least, to be done. Before Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P., and Mr. John Rylands. DANGEROUS PLAYTHINGS.—Frederidk Massey (9) and Charles Allen (12) were charged with haying, on the 26th September, at Great Sankey, stolen 24 fog signals, of the value of as., the property of the Cheshire Lines Committee. —Defendants pleaded guilty.—lnspector Yates said the fog signals were stolen from a platelayer's cabin about 1501 yards from the-Sankey canal. The company had been much troubled by cabins being broken open and thefts committed, but they had no desire that the boys should be severely dealt with, as they were of such tender age. The night after this theft was committed, another cabin was broken open.= In answer to Mr. Peter Rylands, Mr. Yates said it was gener- ally fog signals that were stolen. They had been placed on the rails in one or two cases.—Mr. John Rylands: For the fun of nearing them go off 2—Mr. Yates: Yes. They are dangerous thing's for boys to play with.—Mr. P. Rylands: Very.—Defendants were fined 2s. ed., and Bs. ed. costs each. NUISANCES.-.—SIX persons were summoned by Mr. Far- rington, the nuisance inspector, at the instance of the Rural Sanitary Authority, for neglecting to cleanse their ashpits. —Benjamin Holding was , fined 58. and costs, the case against Michael Curtis was dismissed, and the rest were adjourned.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: STATE OF IRELAND.

- A National Conference of Miners, which opened on Wed- nesday, was resumed at Birmingham on Thursday. Mr. B. Pickard, in the alaence of Mr. Macdonald, M.P., president of the National Association of Miners, presided, and dele- gates attended representing 326,000. A letter was read from Mr. Macdonald, in which he said that the question of framing a modal sliding scale had engaged his attention ' very earnestly since the last meeting. He had turned his attention to it over and over again, until he had finished with the conviction that he could not fulfil the obligations that he had entered into. Were all things equal, he could have seen no trouble in framing a scale for all. When, however, be found fifty different circumstances in as man,- differentlocalities that had to be considered in framing such a se%le, the hope of success passed away. He bad come to the conclusion that, though there were a few lines which would apply to nearly all, yet matters of detail must be left Ito individual districts. As far as the mining population was concerned, arbitration and conciliation had fated, and ito his mind the sliding scale as a principle was the. best whith they had secured to give peace and justice to both , parties. The Bishop of Liverpool delivered the concluding por- tion of his primary visitation charge at the Wigan Parish Church on Thursday. Speaking on matters of general in- terest to Churchmen, this Lordship referred to the Burials Act, which he advised his clergy to accept loyally, en- deavouring to allow it to work with as little friction and confusion as possible. Whilst deeply grateful to the re- visers of the new Testament, he did not join in the chorus of unmixed praise with which the publication of the revised version had been received. The work was chiefly valuable as affording the highest proo of the soundness of their doctrinal system of Christiay. Pending the report of the Royal Commission appointed to consider the workings of the present Ecclesiastical Courts of First Instance and Final Appeal, he would express no opinion, but warned Churchmen against expecting too much, for the Comthission would not exceed its poWers. .
• WARRINGTON CEMETERT.—Returns of interments in the Warrington Cemetery during the week ending yesterday : Adults, 2; children, 8; total 10.

ARREST OF LAND LEAGUE LEADERS. ALARMING RIOTS. Mr. Parnell' s name has been removed from the Commis- sion of Peace for County Wicklow. : It is announced that all the Land League communications are to be addressed to Mr. A. O'Connor, or to the secretary of the League at the ,Holyhead Hotel. The Chief League, of the Dublin metropolitan police has issued a notice that the police have been instructed to prevent and disperse assemblies of disorderly persons in the streets of the city. An outrage was committed on Saturday on a party of men and boys who had been working a threshing machine for a Queen's County farmer who is "boycotted.' No fewer than six of them were shot—five of them in the head. The Lord-Lieutenant returned to Ireland on Tuesday, and attended a meeting of the Privy Council, at which it was resolved to issue a proclamation warning the people of the city of Dublin not to collect in the streets at night, as the police had been instructed to disperse all assemblages. MB. Fonsma ,VNDER Psomarros.—The Chief Secretary for Ireland was escorted from his residence in the Phoenix Park to Dublin Castle, on Tuesday, by an escort of mounted police. This is the first occasion since he came to Ireland on which he has been so protected. LIMERIM—In view of further apprehended disturbances the resident magistrate in charge of the military and police forces in the city, on Tuesday afternoon issued orders direct- ing that all public-houses should be closed from five o'clock in the evening until the morning. Another regiment and 1200 extra constabulary arrived in the city. It is estimated that £l,OOO will not cover the cost of the I glass broken in Dublin during the three days. Amongst the sufferers were the Dublin Mail and the Irish Times offices, and the Express was only saved by the prompt action of the police. Upwards of fifty cases have been treated at the hospitals during a like period, most of them being baton wounds and kicks received by members of the police. The Central News states that the authorities have taken steps to ascertain whether the Land League of Great Britain and that of Ireland are not to all intents and purposes one and the same body. It is understood that if it can be shown they are allied, proceediegs will be instituted against the leaders of the movement for conspiracy, in which event the Irish members of the League would be liable to be tried In England. Two suspects, named James Power and Dennis M'Carthy, of Middleton, county Cork, who were arrested on Monday, arrived under a police escort, on Tuesday, and were lodged in Cork gaol. M'Carthy is a draper's assistant. The in- vestigation at the police barracks on Monday evening, re- sulted in a number of young men being returned for trial to the assizes on a charge of having been engaged in the riot- ing on Sunday night. Mr. Parnell, M.P., Mr. Dillon, M.P., and Mr. William O'Brien, editor of United Ireland, were visited at Kilmain- ham, on Monday. Each prisoner is entitled to see only two persons, whom they may choose each day, in addition to a legal adviser or a medical attendant. The governor of the prison has a deal to do in answering all the enquiries that are made by would-be visitors of "suspects ;" but the discharges the monotonous duty with untiring civility. As usual large numbers of persons had to go away disappointed. The Government have followed up the arrest of Mr. Parnell, M.P., Mr. Sexton, M.P., and Mr. Quinn, the Land League assistant secretary, by the apprehension under the Coercion Act of Mr. O'Kelly, M.P., the re-arrest of Mr. John Dillon. M.P., and the taking into custody under the powers of the Act of several other more or less prominent members' of the League. Mr. Biggar, M.P.' becoming alarmed lest he might be inclnded in the list, fled the country; Mr. Healy, on his way to Ireland, was implored by his friends to remain in England; and Mr. O'Connor, M.P., against whom a warrant was out, succeeding in eluding the detectives, andl got away, for England, by a steamer from Belfast. The, Government's action has been followed by a series of riots' in Dublin, Limerick, and elsewhere, and the excitement i throughout the country continues. Mr. E. D. Gray, M.P., made a serious charge against the Government in his speech at Monday's meeting of the Dublin City Council. Referrieg to the conduct of the 1 police in their affrays with city mobs., he said he "believed honestly and in his soul that the police were acting under girders from the Government for the purpose of provoking a collision between the people and the police in order, and he said it deliberately, to give the Government an opportunity of shedding blood." Mr. Gray was warned by other members of the Council of the fearful crime he was imputing to Her Majesty's Government, but he repeated that he made the statement deliberately and could not withdraw it, though he was fully aware that upon what he had said he might be clapped into prison. Wednesday morning's papers, how- ever, published a letter from Mr. Gray, in which he said that after Mr. Forster's statement that he had good grounds for the directions given to the police, :he (Mr. Gray) "felt himself bound as a gentleman to accept the statement and to withdraw his accusation against the Government. 'Considerable reinforcements of troops leave been ordered to llreland. A newspaper correspondent interviewirMr. Biggar and Miss Anna Parnell at Holyhead, on Wednesday. Mr. Biggar said it was impossible to say what the Land •League in- tended to do in the way of any new policy. He believed the existing state of affairs was chiefly owing to the speeches of Mr. Gladstone, which were ef a bunkum character, and lintended to inflame the prejudices of the English people with reference to the real merits of the case in Ireland. Mr. Gladstone had no doubt been more or less misled by sycophants or flatterers. Miss Parnell said she intended returning on Thursday to Dublin, where the Ladies' Land League was chiefly engaged in attending to the wants of the prisoner " suspects " and others, who owed their imprison- ment to the straining of law. The Government was doing its best to manufacture an excuse for proclaiming martial law. The police bad 'paraded the streets of Dublin on Saturday and Sunday to attract crowds, and then the people were attacked and dispersed. She held that the Castle authorities were responsible for what had occurred, as there was no reason to suppose that there would have been any crowd if the police had not attracted the people in the first Instance. Extensive precautions against possible outbreaks have been taken, and a flying column is ready for immediate movement. There are now in Dublin over 5,000 troops, with 1,000 horses, and 16 guns. The whole of the troops are confined to barracks in readiness for instant action. Her Majesty's ship Penelope, with a full complement of Marines, was under orders to leave Harwich on Thursday morning for Kingston harbour. On Saturday afternoon the streets of Dublin were thronged by excited crowds, cheering for Mr.. Parnell. Mr. Biggar, M.P., walked along the streets, and was greeted by the people most enthusiastically. The police were on duty, both on horse and foot, in Sackville-street, endeavouring to quell the demonstration. Late at night a conflict occurred, and the police charged the crowd, inflict- ing, in some cases, severe injuries. The crowds were I eventually dispersed, after the police had been 12 hours on duty. A meeting in London was held by the Democratic Federation on Saturday evening, at which the action of the Government in regard to the Land League wail denounced,, and it was decided to hold a mass meeting next Sunday. I The Limerick branch of the Land League on Saturdayl passed resolutions denouncing the arrests, and a similar resolution was passed by the Cork Land League. Mr. John R. Heffernan, of the Cork Land League, who was lately released from Limerick Gaol, was re-arrested on Saturday evening. Wednesday's news from Ireland was more reassuring. All was quiet in Dublin. The general subject of conversation was the extensive damage inflicted on places of business by the mob on Tuesday night. The damage done to laneo win- dows and shop fronts is estimated at more than £l,OOO Several young men were fined by the magistrates for stone throwing, and three others were remanded, but admitted to bail, on the charge of wrecking the shop of Mr. Fitzpatrick, in Sackville-street, and stealing a number of watches and gold chains. The Land League have sent by post to every branch throughout the country copies of the manifesto, and placards for publication containing only the words "No rents," signed by the chief executive officials, all of whom are in, prison. It is thought that the Government will everywhere prohibit the posting of the placards. A pro- Iposal made at a "Land Convention" at Cavan, on Tuesday, , that the fanners should pay no rent till the leaders of the c League were liberated was warmly opposed by several priests as being ill-advised, and was !ejected by a large majority. It may be hoped from this indication that the advice that the people should have nothing to do with the Land Act will not be generally followed. The Chairman of County Waterford (Mr. G. Waters, Q.C.) in his charge to the Grand Jury on Tuesday, in which he showed the ab- surdity of expecting innumerable totally dissimilar cases to be settled by a few test actions, said he was Riad to learn that 600 farmers in Limerick were applying to the court to have fair rents fixed. Two or three additional arrests under the Protection Act were made on Wednesday. Some further areeets were made in Ireland on :ffi-onday, but no more members of Parliament have been taken into custody. All the suspected arrested on Monday are local leaders of Land League Branches. In no case was there any attempt at resistance. The Land Leegue office in Dublin is still in charge of a few clerks. It is understood that the principal work of the League will now be carried on at Liverpool under the direction of Mr. Healy, M.P., Mr. Arthur Connor, M.P., ffir. Biggar, M.P., and Dr. Commies, M.P. The same military precautions at Deblin which have been observed since the arrest of Mr. Parnell are bing con- tinued. Mr.. Sexton, M.P., is reported to be in a very low state of health, and he has been allowed to occupy a separate room at Kilmainham Gaol. Mr. Dillon. is reported by his relatives to be in a worse state of health than that which caused the Executive to release him some weeks since. In consequence of the collision of the crowds with the police on Saturday and Sunday nights, a resolutlon was agreed to at a meeting of the Dubiln Town Council on Monday, to the effect that the guardians of the peace had exceeded their duty. Subsequently a deputation from the Corporation waited upon the Chief Secretary for Irelatnde in order to represent their disaPProval of the conduct of had police. Mr. Forster, in reply, said many policoemen h , if they been injured in the collisions with the mobs, e had got possession of certain par w ts of t ct,r information 7w.ed have done great damage. which they had, were boThuned tPoOttliceteilesntbheezedeo to call the did and, and, if they had not done so, it would have be military, when the Consequences would have been more serious. If the necessity Woe, the police. wo, he said, act in the same manner again. The rioting continues a Limerick. A meeting which was to have been held in Limerick on protest against the arrest of Mr. remelt and his Sunday, to b colleagues, was prohibited a proclamation. It had been
