div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

At the fortnightly meeting of this Board, on Tuesday, \ 1 there were present the Rev. Canon Barclay (in the chair),l I the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner; Messrs. W. Handley, T. Norman, J. Challoner, C. Rigby, G. Whitlow, W. Fisher, G. S. Hazlehurst. Jas. Darbyshire, J. Stokes, J. Weir, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk.) 'WORKHOUSE HOSPITAL EXTENSION. On the motion of Mr. :NORMAN seconded by Mr. HANDLEY, the following resolution was carried :—" That the tender of he Royal Exchange Assurance Company to advance the sum of £2,400 required for the extension of the workhouse hospital. in accordance with plans approved by the Guardians and Loca 1 Government, on security of the rates of the Runcorn Union, at Li per cent. per annum, interest. repayable by forty equal half yearly instalments of principal and interest combined, be, and is, hereby a 0... ...

tepted." THE SCHOOLMASTER AS A SCRIBE: EXTRAORDINARY CORRESPONDENCE. The DEPUTY CLERK read the following letter from the schoolmaster:—" Runcorn Workhouse, 15th October, 1881. To the Guardians.of the Runcorn Union,—Gentlemen,—ln obedience to vour resolution of the 4th instant, I respectfully beg to submit the following the first part of his letter, Mr. Coke writes the children are frequently late.' With regard to this statement I have to say that if it had been made two months back I should not then have questioned its accuracy, and I feel bound to confess that about that time the children were frequently late. But a little more than six weeks ago, the chaplain conveyed to me a gentle pro- test on the subject of nay irregular attendance at church, and I at once resolved that he should not have cause to do so aga.in. So from that time forth, I always started from the workhouse in what I con,idered good time (9 50), arriving at Aston church for three consecutive Sundays shortly be- fore divine service ciumenced However, on the fourth Sunday I left the Workhouse at the usual time (9-50), but on reaching the church found that I was three minutes late (Aston time); but exactly 10-30 by my watch (workhouse time)—our entrance thereby disturbing Mr. Cole and his familg, and the congregation while repeating the general confession. After the service was enaed Mr. Coke stopped me on tile road and asked me if 1 could not leave the work- house a little earlier. I told him I thought 'perhaps I could.' He then said you're always late;' and I, instead of wishing him 'good morning,' as I ought to have done, coolly asserted that such was not the case.' Mr. Coke then informed me that he should report my conduct to the Guardians. He also went on to say something abont mismanagement at the workhouse, and a few other things which I cannot reeollect, his voice at the same time rising in tones most loud and ungenteel ; but beyond contradicting his statement that the children were always late, I said nothing. I will speak now on the ap- parently unwelcome note which I addressed to Mr. Coke, and which was the cause of him troubling you with a second complaint. When Mr. Coke beckoned to me in the road, intimating thereby that he desired a word with me, I thought most likely he was going to compliment me on the appearance of the children (as strangers often do), and perhaps give me a trifle to expend in sweets for them. But when he introduced a very different subject I was quite 'taken aback '—thrown on my beam ends, so to speak. In fact, I felt so angry and confused that I really could not find words to express my feelings, so the next day I thought I would make amends to myself by calling in the aid of my pen; and it seems I succeeded only too well. Let me tell you, gentlemen, it was not the simple fact of his inter- ference which irritated me so much as the authoritative, not to say bullying, manner in which Mr. Coke conducted him- self. The latter portion of his 'remonstrance' was, I am sure, d;stinctly audible to any one within a radius of fifty yards, and I think you will agree with me, gentlemen, when I say that this style of remonstrance ' does not become any one who, by his outward appearance and bearing, seems desirous of being considered genteel. I ask you to note also, gentlemen, that Mr. Coke conducted himself in this manner in the presence of the children, which fact, I think is rather surprising in a man of Mr. Coke's years and experience. Any stranger being an ear-witness of the alter- cation between us would doubtless think that I was in his employ, or even more nearly attached to him ; but I feel thankful that I am accountable to more reasonable gentle- men. In the last paragraph I read : Had I the least idea he would have resented any remonstrance in the manner he did at the time,' I cull imagine what Mr. Coke means by this, unless it is that my meekness surprised him, for I assure you, gentlemen, I took it like a lamb.' Mr. Coke knew well what line of conduct to adopt in order to get his grievance righted, and why could not he follow it up with- out making himself so publicly officious at my expense? I have here endeavoured, gentlemen, to give you the plain, unvarnished facts of the case. I cannot conclude without saying I feel sorry that through some remissness on my part you have been troubled with this unpleasant correspon- dence.—l remain, gentlemen, your obedient servant, THOS. HARDIE."—Mr. NORMAN asked if they considered that an apology.—The DEPUTY CLERK: He was asked for an ex- planation, 1 think.—Mr. RIGBY : I think, Mr. Clerk, the Guardians decided to have both of them present.—The CLERK : Ga, no.—The DEPUTY CLERK said Mr. Coke made a complaint ln writing, and it was decided that the schoolmaster should write a reply.— CHALLONER thought the schoolmaster had made a good explanation, and that the matter should drop.—Mr. RIGBY : Oh, the letter is a " topper " that the schoolnfaster sent. It's a "clinker," the best letter I ever read in my life. 1 wish I coull write one like it. (Laughter.)—The DEPUTY CLERK : Would you write about the rents ?—(Laugh- ter).—The CLERK said there was no doubt the children were in the habit of being late.—Mr. HAZLEHURST : Do we want it to go all round the neighbourhood 7—Mr. RIGBY : Yes, I think it is a good " clinker."—Mr. HAZLEHURST thought they had had toe much about the workhouse in the papers.—Mr. Daurasninn remarked that there was no doubt the children had been frequently late, and he thought one of the schoolmaster's first duties should be to teach the --- He the.,,ht Mr. Hardie's letter waschildren punctuaio.y. _ . a deal stronger than there was any dahöii for.—Mr. AIGB, said they did not know what Mr. Coke had said to the schoolmaster, and only having their evidence by letter, there was very little to decide upon. If the Board were to decide upon the matter let them have the parties before them.— The CHAIRMAN : The question is whether you are satisfied with Mr. Hardie's explanation as contained in the letter to- day.—Mr. RIGBY :I am satisfied.—Mr. NORMAN : I have never heard the original letter read,—Mr.llazt.Enunsv again asked if the Board wanted the matter to go all round the country, like previous discussions. The CHAIRMAN I pointed out that there were two courses open to Mr. Hazlehurst He could make a motion that thel;"..t.t.`-': t't; l'eJi read, or ask the reoor% nut to publish it.—Mr. HAZLEHURST thought they had bean in the papers sufficiently. They were made the laughing stock of the community not long ago, and lie proposed that the Board should not be made a laughing stock twain. He moved that the letter be not read,—Mr. FISHER seconded the motion.—Mr. WHITLOW moved that the letter be read. He thought the Board should have nothing private either as regarded correspondence or anything else. —Mr. HAZLEHURsT : The letter is not addressed to the Guardians 7—The DEPUTY CLERK said it was sent by Mr. Coke to the Guardians asking them to take it into considera- ' tion.—A MEMBER : The Guardians have not heard it.—Mr. HAZLEIIURST : Well, of course, it is in their discretion whether they hear it or not. He suggested that if the lefter was ',pled round the tahle it would suffice.—The 'CLERK : I:lo,and to itsVO the letter read,—Me, I RIGBY : I thin there is nothing detrimental to the Board I in the letter. It's a" clinking " good letter.—Mr. Hazle- burst's motion was then put and lost.—The DEPUTY CLERK then read the letter as fellows :—" Runcorn Union Work- house, Preston Brook, 20th Sept., 1881. Sir,-1 have a few words to say to you on the subject of your very I officious interference with me immediately after Divine Service at Aston Church yesterday. First with regard to my conduct in coming late to church, if I am, answerable for the same to anyone, and of that I make no question, it is not to you more than to the humblest member of the congregation then present; and I look upon your meddlesome conduct as a gross piece of impudence wholly unbecoming any person who by his outward appearance and bearing seems desirous of being considered " genteel." Again, why did you not, as in former instance, repeat your complaint to the Churchwardens, and not vent your religious spleen on me, who did not in the least desire the honour of a more familiar acquaintance than I already had of you through your connection with Aston Church? And lastly, the manner in which you publicly harangued and exalted yourself (in your own large opinion perhaps) in the eyes of th 3 Workhouse children, justifies me in offering you the following piece of advice :—When you lay your threatened complaint before the Guardians be careful to observe that it is couched in terms becoming a Christian and a gentle- man: let not your righteous indignation betray you (as it did on Sunday last) into any unseemly expressions of anger, for the Guardians of the Runcorn Union will not be bullied into noticing any complaint, even if it comes from such a great man as Mr. Coke, of, " Aston Lodge." I am, Sir, yours truly, THOMAS HARDIE —To Mr. Coke, Aston Lodge, A ston. The CHAIRMAN: I think Mr. Coke was perfectly justified in sending the letter to the uardians. —A MEMBER: Why?— The CHAIRMAN: I think it is a very impertinent letter. I think he had no right to conch a letter in those terms to anyone.—Mr. CHALLONER did not approve of the letter, but said perhaps, the schoolmaster got a little overheated. —Mr. HANDLEY : This was written in cold blood the next day. I think Mr. Hardie ought to make an apology to Mr. Coke for writing that letter, apart horn the comolaint.—Mr. RIGBY : e ought to know what Mr. Coke said to him.— Mr. HANDLEY : I do not think anything could je-tify such language as contained there.—The CLERK: It •e 'I have a very prejudical effect upon Mr. Hardie if it cam. ,efore the authorities.—Mr.ileNintEi : Is a young man wb indulges in such language fit to teach the children here ?—Mr. NOR- MAN thought Mr. Coke or anyone else had a right to ask the schoolmaster to have the children in church before the ser- vice commenced. He did not know what Mr. Coke said to Mr. Hardie, but whatever he said he thought the school- master should have taken notice of it. TheCHAI it was the language in which the letter was couched that said tlla he did not like. It was quite right to say it was a pity Mr. Coke humiliated him before the children, but it was not right to put it in the way he had.—Mr. WHITLOW did not think the man would have written a letter like this without he had been insulted previously.—'Mr. RIGBY: No doubt. We must have them here.—The CLERK then read the following letter from Mr. Coke to the Guardians :—" 25th September 1881. Aston Lodge, Preston Brook. Gentlemen,--Permit me to bring to your notice a point of irregularity in the management of the tUnion which I think calls for your

_ interference. The school children attending the Aston Church are frequently late, coming in during the confession, and disturbing the congregation. It occurred to me that the Churchwardens and the clergyman might take notice of such disturbance, and adopt means to obviate it, but seeing that the habit, of late, has become almost general, I spoke to the young man in charge of the school to-day; he coolly asserted that it was not the case that the school Ina often late, whereas I, who attend the church regularly, am under the impression that the children are brought in as often after the commencement of the service as before. At any rate they were late to-day. If, however, the schoolmaster is under the impression that no irregularity exists, I should advise the Guardians to call for a report from the Church- wardens of the church whenever the congregation is dis-. turbed by the school which may have the effect of ensuring punctuality.—I am gentlemen, faithfully yours, H. COKE —Mr. CITALLONER though the matter had gone far enough. —The CLERK said it would do Mr. Hardie a seNice if the Board got him to make an apology.—Mr.RlGßY: For what? —The CLERK: Having written that letter. There is nothing could justify the letter.—Mr. RIGBY said no doubt the schoolmaster had received great provocation, and very in- sinuating remarks, Of he would not have written such a letter:—The Rev. J. W. N. TANNER proposed that Mr. Hardie be called upon to make an apology to Mr. Coke. Mr. Nonarmit seconded. -- Mr. RIGBY pro- posed that he be not called upon to make an apology. He did not :see what Mr. Hardie had to apologise for. He had written the letter there was no doubt—(laughter)—but doubtless he had received great pro- vocation. He thought they ought to have both the gentle- men before them and then the Board could investigate the case thoroughly.—The CLERK : Hardie admits the clergy- man has spoken to 12i:11,-U:1e CHAIRMAN thought if the churchwardens neglected their duty it was very good of Mr. Coke to mention the matter.—The CLERK thought he as churchwarden had neglected his duty in not calling Mr. Hardie's attention to the matter.—After a little further dis- cussion, the Rev. J. W. N. TANNER altered his proposition to the effect that Mr. Hardie be recommended to make an apology, and Mr. Hardie having been called into the room, the CHAIRMAN said he was directed by tha Board to say in the first place Mr. Hardie was wrong in taking the children late to church from time to time, and that should not occur again. In his church they did not allow anyone to go in after the confession began ; but whether in church or chapel they objected to the service being disturbed. Without entering into the conversation that took place, the Guar- dians thought the tone of Mr. Hardie's letter was very unbecoming indeed, and for his own sake, in case he wanted a testimonial, they recommended,him to make an apology.— Mr. HARDIE said the tone of the letter was certainly un- becoming, but when he wrote it he did not feel very calm. What he said he thought was quite right, but it was the way in which he had said it that the Board wished him to apologise for 7—The CHAIRMAN : Yes, that is what we object to.—Mr. HARDIE said he would adopt the Board's suggestion, and promised them the children should not be late again.

TIM COST OF INMATES. Mr. HANDLEY laid a fiaancial statement before the Board which showed that the total expenditure during the quarter had been £915 16s. 7d. There was one thing which he thought spoke well for the management of the House. Dur- ing the past four quarters the average expenditure had been £465 66. 11d. per quarter; or, to put it more closely, the cost of each pauper for food and clothing, had only been 3id. per day. He did not think they could be called an extravagant Union. (Hear hear, and laughter.)

div.head: PRESCOT POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: PRESCOT POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

TCESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Pilkington and Colonel Blackburne, M.P. DRUNKENNESS ON LICENSED PREMISES.—A man named Tierney was charged with being drunk on the licensed pre- mises of Robert Charles, Market-place, Prescot, on the 24th nd refusing to quit. Defendant was further charged with Sept.,'being drunk in the Market-hall, Prescot, on the let Oct. A fine of ss. and costs was inflicted in each case. TRANSFERS OF LICENCES.—The following transfers were granted :—Licensed victuallers: Queen's Arms, Huyton, from John Pearson to Thomas Edwards; Crown Hotel, Kemble-street, Prescot, from James Plant to Richard Web- ster; Star Inn, Widnes, from Isabella Jones to John Gould ; Eagle and Child Hotel, Warrington-road, Prescot, from Paul Hunt to Mark Kellett. Beersellers : Beerhouse at Sewell- street, Prescot, from Catherine Connor to William Bram- hall ; beerhouse at Kemble-street, Prescot, from Jonn Birchall Barrow to James Plant; beerhouse at Upton, Widnes, from Samuel Jackson to Robert Baldwin; beer- house at Farnworth, from James Wood to William Twist. Temporary authorities: Frank Richards, to sell at a beer- house, Liverpool-road, Huyton, till the next transfer day; Patrick McLoughlin, to sell at a beerhouse at Acres-street, Prescot; and Thomas McKeon, to sell at the beerhouse lately kept by Patrick McLoughlin. POOR RELATIONS.—Four brothers named Edward,Thomas, Joseph, and Hugh Bonney were summoned to show cause why they should not contribute towards the maintenance of their mother, who had become chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot Union.—Mr. Hartley. clerk to the Guardians of the Prescot Union, stated that be had been in- structed to ask their worships to make are order upon each of the defendants for the payment of Is. per week towards the support of their mother, who was 73 years of age and a cripple. She had six sons, two of whom had paid Is. per week for some time towards :heir mother's support, but the other four were not willing to give anything, although they were is full work,—Defendants were each ordered to pay is. per week. NEGLECTING TO MAINTAIN HIS WlFE—Thomas Ather- ton, of St. Helens, was charged with neglecting to maintain his wife, Emma Atherton, who had become chargeable to the Prescot Union,—From the evidence for the complainant it appeared that the parties had been married for 28 years, and eight years ago, Mrs. Atherton left her husband on ac- count of his Immorality (as she alleged), and it was then agreed that he should pay her 4s. 6d. per week, so that she might live apart, as he had shown a preference to cohabit ssl.th a woman nannA Lee, whom lee had, previous to his marriage, courted, and who at IlSe time named was a widow. The Guardians had paid Mrs. Atherton 4s. 6d. per week up to the present time, and defendant bad kept up the payments till May last, when he discontinued them and refused to pay any more. About that time,or shortly after,Lee died, and he then sought out and invited his wife to live with him at his home. She declined, and the woman and her husband appeared before the guudians. when the latter determined to continue I the relief and to asft the magistrates to confirm their order. It was elicited in cross-examination of the witnesses that , while before tbeguardians defendant again offered his wife I a share of his home, but that she refused.—For the defence, Mr. Swift submitted that the question in this case was not whether the parties ever agreed to live separate, but whether at the time the summons was applied for a month ago or at the present time • this woman was a woman who legally required relief without her husband, and he contended that she was not. He pointed out that from July last when defendant offered' his wife his home, she ceased to be a married woman requir- ing relief from her husband. That court was not a divorce court, and whatever misconduct there might have been on the part of the husband, the wife did not seem to have set her- self against it very much, but whatever it was it was all over and gone. It was not for a wife to come into a court of that kind and complain of that form of misconduct on the part of her husband. There was another court open in another quarter to which she ought to have had recourse.—The magistrates, after some deliberation, considered there was no cause existing why the woman should not go back and live with her husband, and they accordingly dismissed the case. 11 PITCH AND Toss.—Peter Ashcroft, John Glenuon, and Michael Melia, were charged with playing pitch and toss on some waste land off St. Helens-road, on Sunday afternoon, the 25th September.—Melia was further charged with com- mitting a similar offence on a later occasion.—Glennan Was fined ss.'aed Costs, Ashcroft 7s. 6d. and costs, and Melia, who had been ten times previously convicted, was fined 20s. and costs for each offence.—For similar offences Thomas Aldred, Henry Abrams, John Saggerson, and Richard Travis, were each fined ss. and costs. YOUTHFUL THIEVES.—John Saggerson and William Old- field, two boys, were charged with having, on the 12th instant, stolen two pairs of drawers from the shop of Mr. John Aldred Brown, draper, Marltrebidace, Prescot. The articles were stated to be worth 3s. led. Prisoners were further charged with stealing 61 lbs. of black puddings, value 35., from the shop of Mr. John Hockenhall, butcher Eccleston-street, on the night of the following date.—Both prisoners pleaded guilty, and were ordered to pay ss. in each

case. THE EDUCATION ACTS,—For neglecting to send their children to school,the following were fined the usual penalty of 6d. and costs :—John Cunningham and Nicholas Law- renson, Prescot; James Vincent, Mary Wall, and Henry Catton, Huyton ; Michael Shields, Whiston ; and Peter Leonard, Rainhill. THATCHED COTTAGES ON RAINHILL-BOAD OHO BRED To' BE CLOSED. —Dorothy Thomas, widow, was summoned at the instance of the Prescot Union Rural Sanitary Authority for allowing a nuisance to exist on her premises at Rainbill- road, Whiston, which was injurious to health.—Mr. S. H. Hartley stated that proceedings were taken in August last, and after hearing the case the magistrates agreed that de- fendant should have a month in which to leave her cottage. A man named Mutch was also summoned for permitting a nuisance on premises adjoining those occupied by the present defendant. He was allowed a fortnight in which to leave, and he had since gone, and the house had been bricked up and the doors and windows fastened. He was instructed to ask for an order to close the premises, which were not fit for habitation. The cottages had belonged to a man named Parkinson, who was sent to Lancaster Lunatic Asylum in 1831, where he remained till 1874, when he died. During his incarceration in tl4e Asylum the rents of the cottages were collected and applied towards his mainten- ance, but since his death no rent had been collected, as no owner to the property could be found. No money bad been spent in repairing the property, consequently it bad fallen into a very dilapidated state—in fact, into an utter wreck.— Dr. Hall, medical officer of health, said the cottages in his Opinion were unfit for habitation. The walls were thoroughly dilapidated and the thatch was old, damp and unhestthy, and the premises had evidently been in a filthy condition for many years. There were no drains attached to the nreimses, no water supply, and no proper privy accommodation.—The magistrates made an ordar for the ' premises to be closed.—Mr. Hartley said the Aufhoritv simply wanted to get the people out for the benefit of the health of the district. They did not want any penalties or
costs inflicted.

_ got somewhat mutt., _ pression that" Mr. Gladstone said we were within measurable distance of civil war. He believed the remark was made many years ago (in 1868) when the Irish Church Debate was such as led him to say that the nation was within mea- surable distance of civil war. There were many illustrations trotted out and piled upon Mr. Gladstone. Probably the last speaker considered he gave the Liberals a hit front the shoulder when he said they made use of the Irish to get into office; but lie (the speaker) did not think the Irish had truer friends than the Liberals. Speaking about the agita- tors as the leading demagogues, he said if it had not been for these men the Liberals would perhaps not have bad any trouble whatever with the Irish people. He supported the action of Mr. Parnell last session, and spoke of him in eulogistic terms as a hero; but he must say he had been deceived in that man. Perhaps there was no one stronger in his opposition to the coercion acts of the present Govern- -1 ment than himself at the time referred to, but now he was a most firm believer of coercion. The Land Act, he had no doubt, would prove a remedy and bring about a wonderful change in that country. The whole subject bad been very fairly expounded by the member for Walsall, and if they received no more criticism than had already been given, they would be able to do some work this session. He hoped the Opposition would turn up in large numbers so that they would be able to carry on the work in a splendid manner.—The member for Cheltenham said the honourable gentleman who last addressed the klOtThe was Conte on the Opposition sicte as he made so many mistakes. He was congratulating himself on the Liberal outlook, but he could not look to Ireland for it. Whatever difficulties presented themselves during time Liberal term of office were always put down as a relic of the Conservative Government. The Conservative party impressed upon Mr. Gladstone and his followers, the necessity of renewing the Peace Preserva- tion Act, but what did Mr. Gladstone say? He said there was no necessity for such a course. Ireland had made vast strides in commercial prosperity, and it was quite unneces- sary to renew such a measure, as that country was in such a peaceful condition. Again what did Mr. Gladstone do during &thilathiar. narnrizian He raised Irish expectations - „ - by promises; he was in an irresponsible positional that time, 1 and he made certain statements which he could not keep, and the result was that the people are disappointed; they felt sore; they had been deceived and were now on the point lof open rebellion. The Government were trying to crush open measures, and the Irish would undoubtedly hold secret meetings.—After a somewhat lengthy speech from the member for Chelsea, in winch he supported the action of the Government, the debate was adjourned on the motion of the Leader of the Opposition. The House then went into COM- mittee for the purpose of appointing a deputy speaker and chairman of committees.

THE HIGH-STREET BUTCHER. AND Hts CUSTOMER.— Julia Powell, a woman about 45 years of age, was charged with stealing 211bs. of mutton, the property of Mr. George Slater, butcher, High-street—Mrs. Slater said that between one and two o'clock, on Saturday afternoon, the prisoner visited the shop, and from what was said to her by another woman she followed Powell across the' street, and found a breast of mutton in her apron. Prisoner bought one pound of pieces whilst she was at the shop.—Mary Ellison, wife of Thomas Ellison, Grosvenor-street, said she was in the shop and saw the prisoner put a large shoulder of mutton into her apron, and she said to her" Now, Mrs., don't take what does not belong to you "•' on which she put the larger piece down and placed the smaller one in her apron.—P.C. Clarke proved apprehending the prisoner, who had no money upon her.—Prisoner admitted that she took the mutton, but said she did not do so with the intention of stealing it.—Superin- tendent Williamson said the woman was drunk at the time. —Prisoner was committed to gaol for one month with hard labour.—On leaving the court Mrs. Ellison was threatened by a relative of the thief, and on the fact being reported to the maelstrates by Superintendent Williamson, the magis- trates ordered a warrant to be issued for the apprehension of the man. ToEsnAv,—Before Mr, William Usukes (chairman) and Mr. TiloMaS. THREATENING WITNESSES.—A WARNING.—WiIIiam An- trobus was brought up on a warrant, charged with threaten- ing a respectable woman named Mary Ellison, who gave im- portant evidence in the case of a theft from a butcher's shop, heard at Monday's Court. We understand that Antro- bus is related to the woman who was convicted for that offence.—Complainant stated that on leaving the court on Monday, defendant, who was standing near the door, used very insulting language to her, and expressed the pleasure it would afford him to give her a good beating. She im- mediately returned into the building and told Superin- tendent Williamson what had happened, and he laid the matter before the magistrates, who ordered that a warrant be issued for the prisoner's arrest. On that worthy hearing the course which events had taken, he decamped, but P.C. Hibbert was sent after him, and succeeded in lodging him in the cells after a rather long chase.—The Chairman gave Antrobus a severe leeture for his conduct, and reminded him that the offence of which he had -been guilty was one of a Most Serious nature. He would be leniently dealt with on this occasion, and only be ordered to find one surety in £lO and two in £5 to Jceep the peace, or, in default, be com- mitted to gaol 14 days.—Antrobus could not find the sureties, ad he waS sent to prison. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Thomas, ALLEGED ROBBERY BY A SWEDE. A SWediSit sailor, named Emanuel Johnson, WAS charged with stealing several articles of wearing apparel, the property of Marcus are Glade and other seamen employed on a vessel named the Agnus --,rt left on board

Wyllie, of Irvine, Scalaild. Prisoner had been lett, the board the schooner in the absence of the other men and on their return the things were missed, but they had not since been found.—The evidence being of so unconclusi t e a noture, the prisoner was set at liberty. YrTEßD&Y.—Before Messrs. John Thomas and Jain Brundrit. GROSS CASE OF CRUELTY TO A HORSE BY A WARRINGTON MAN.—James Dollard, a Warrington salt hawker, was charged with cruelly ill-treating a horse by working it in an unfit state.—Sergeant Morris stated that about a quarter past four on the morning of the 19th instant he saw the prisoner in charge of a brown horse cob, attached to a cart loaded with salt, in Bridge-street, Runcorn. On examining the animal, he found that two of its knees were broken, and on one of them was a wound about the size of a ss. piece, from which blood and matter were oozing freely. There was also an old wound on the oil side of the horse, which was in so poor a condition as to present an appear- ance very similar to that of a skeleton, lie took the animal out of the cart and put it in Mr. Yarwood's stables.—ln- spector harper, of the R.5.P.C.A.., said he looked at the horse at Mr. Yarwood's, and it was in-so weak a condition that it could not stand up owing to, continuous work 'and starvation. He had it killed.—The prisoner was fined £3 and costs; or, in default, two months imprisonment. He • was not able to pay the money, and was sent to gaol.

WIN SFORD. THE GALE AT WINSFORD.—It is not Often that such a , display of natural force is manifested in Winsford and its neighbourhood as on Friday last. For hours preceding and succeeding the day the elemental struggle for equilibrium was going on, but the main force was exerted ou the day named, when nothing could withstand its fury, unless it was most stable. The trees might be seen pulled up by the roots. Chimney pots, copings, and even chimneys, and slates often, were very seriously damaging the roofs upon which they fell. St. David's Church will cost, it is said, ' £2O or to repair its damages, and many houses also sustained much damage.

THE TRADES UNION PARLIAMENT- ARY COiIMITTEE AND THE FAIR TRADE DELEGATES. The Trades Union Parliamentary Committee have issued to the trade of the United Kingdom a few words of explana- tion and advice relating to certain events which transpired at the recent Con greskin London. The committee state tha no lengthened statement is necessary to show that in the past the Congresses have been constituted as nearly as pos- sible of bond fide representatives of genuine trade societies— inviting only those who, while not of their own order, had rendered special service and assistance at times when their help was of great value—and quoting a couple of standing orders referring to the constitution:of the Congress and ex- planations thereon. After this:the circular goes on to say : —" Shortly before our last Congress the committee received information from various provincial centres that influences were at work by which it was hoped to foist upon Congress as genuine delegates, under standing order 3, men who were in the pay of outside organisations which wete not in any sense of the word trades unions or trades councils. The bodies chiefly concerned in this movement were the Anti- Sugar Bounty Association and a society calling itself the Fair Trade League, or some such name. The leading spirits of this latter movement convened a Conference in London on the last three days of the week preceding our Congress week. A great many delegates from the country attended this Conference, and used the names of their society in con- nection therewith, though not delegated by them to attend. IThe terms offered by the Fair Trade League to these so- called delegates were—all railway fares paid, 15s. per day expenses, and luncheon on the Saturday.' Reviewing the position of the Fair Trade elelegates, it is stated that the society of sailors, which Mr. Lind (one ef those expelled) and Captain Bedford Pim claimed to represent, had during the year 1880 an income of £lB6 6s. 6d., while working ex- penses alone absorbed £260 17s. Having given a descrip- tion_of the proceedings which led up to the expulsion of the delegates, the Parliamentary Committee state that they have repeatedly declined, financial assistance wi,en made by parties not directly connected with the working classes, and conclude as follows : "We therefore, appeal most earnestly to the Trade Unions and the Trades Councils of the United Kingdom, whether they be individually large or small, not to barter away their great position and influence in the affairs of the nation to wily and well paid agents of vested interests. Individually they care nothing for you except as a unit of the millions; but they are most desirous of obtaining the influence of your representative assembly to assist in maintaining and more firmly establishing ancient monopolies under the guise of giving you some plausible but spurious help. Above all, be careful how you allow volunteer delegates to profess to represent you unless you are sure of their intentions and can guarantee their good faith, otherwise we shall become in- db ectly the tools of the Armits and Bedford Pines, or any political adventurers of our time, and shall lose all the influence we possess in the council of the nation, and which we require for our special social interests. Your record of work accomplished for the good of the labouring classes is one of which you may well be proud. Your past policy has been one of independent action. We ask you to maintain this policy. Do not ally yourself with those whose interest is not your interest; refuse to permit speculators to trade upon your name and position. Far be it from our intention to counsel you against taking part in advocating your respective political views; to do so is amongst the highest duties of citizenship. All we advise is that your trade organisations should not be let out to the hire of bubble- movement makers. In „conclusion, we congratulate the trades of the United Kingdrom upon their strength of charac- ter in resisting the proposals of the classes referred to. Suc- cess has only followed them in a very few quarters. We trust that their future attempts will prove as fruitless as their efforts have been in the past. We thank the trades at the recent Congress for their firmness of purpose in the diffi- cult situation in which they were placed, and fervently hope that such a display of strength will not again be required of them."

RELIGIOUS TRACT SOCIETY'S MEET- ING AT ST. lIELENS. On Friday evening, a meeting in connection with the Religious Tract Society was held in the Assembly Room, Brook-street. There was a poor attendance, amongst those present being the Revs. R. R. Moore (chairman), R. J. Ward, W. M. Walmsley, J. Brown, Sarvent, W. C. Tayler, and Green. The Rev. R. R. MOOLLE, of Ravenhead, said that the society had rendered great service to various denominations in St. Helens, and he hoped that in future it would become better known. He was quite sure that the libraries had been replenished from time to time by free grants from the society. In his own case he had three grants of books to their library at Ravenhead within the space of three year He thought that showed that the society was ever ready to help those who were helping themselves. The society did not give the books free, but said," If you can give so much, say £3, we will give you £5 worth of b mks." They had sent him volumes he had not paid for, saying, "We will give you these ; they will interest Sunday school teachers and others." He had been looking through the report for the last year, and it appeared the society was very busy both at home and abroad. It was not satisfied with small things; it had a large income, and did a very loge work. Its work was similar to that of the British and Foreign Bible Society, only that the Bible Society provided tb,! scriptures, whilst the Tract Society provided an explan Ilion of those scrip- tures. In this country we were inundated with literature, some of a very foolish, and some of a ry vicious character, and it was the duty and the object of juch societies as the Tract Society to counteract the evi tendencies of such literature amongst a class which 40 y. are ago did not read at all. We had in our midst an it: 1 =crab's number of penny papers, and some of them sc. of a very debasing character. That society endeavou: 1 to present God's Truth in an attractive manner, so :Ls to counteract the wretched printed matter that was set broadcast over the land. The society's work extended to India, and according to the report there was a great deal of scepticism amongst the Hindoos. They had found their own religion afforded them no comfort in the day of sorrow, and no strength in the day of temptation, and made them no better; great difficulty therefore was being experienced in inducing them to accept the true religion. Mr. BUTCHER, deputation from the Tract Society, said that the operations of the society were not crippled by the want of °palings, but by the want of means to carry them on. The object was to provide a literature lor the churches, and to issue tracts amongst every class of the people. The society was 82 years old, and what had the Lord enabled it to do? The past 80 years had been marvellous years of progress. The Religious Tract Society commenced its operations 20 years after the Sunday school had commenced its work. A member of Parliament once said, "It was a very important thing to teach to read. 'out it was quite as imp.ortant to find the right stuff to read." Eighty years ago books were few and poor. Mr. Butcher here produced a newspaper printed in 1800, and which he had discovered amongst some old papers of his grandfather's. It was a paper of 16 columns, and the price of it was sixpence. He mentioned that to show the great difference there was be- tween that day and the present as regards the facilities to becoming acquainted with literature. To show the progress the society had made since its foundation, he mentioned that in the first year 200,000 tracts were issued, and over £2OO turned over. In the year ending March, 1881, the issues were 81,000,000, and the amount turned over £195,000. It was plain to see that it was a great trading society, but it was not a proprietary society. The shares belonged to the churches of all denominations. There was not a church that might apply but would receive some aid from the society, and he advised secretaries of Sunday school libraries not to let their libraries by any means suffer for the want of books.

The CLERK said he had settled all the claims made against the Authority out of the money due to the con- tractors, and he had paid them the balance. He had also paid £4O to the Daresbury Highway Board for injury to the road from Tom Payne's Bridge to Wilderspool.—Mr. WrnT LOW said although the money had been paid to the High- way Board the road had not been repaired.—Mr. RIGBY said the road was in an abominable state, and asked who was responsible.—The GIBE% The Surveyor I suppose.—Mr. WHITLOW said, the road was in a very bad state;and a child, if taken down there, would " stut " ever afterwards. DIEDICXL OFFICER'S REPORT.

The DEPUTY CLERK read the Medical Officer's quarterly report which stated the registrar's returns showed that during the quarter ending September 30t1e there had been 125 births and 67 deaths in the three districts of the Authority. Of the births 65 were males and 63 females, birth-rate 66; and of the deaths 35 were males and 32 females, death-rate 3.4. 22 were under 5 years, 16 of these being under one year; and 45 were 5 years and upwards. The Medical Officer called attention to the marked decrease in the num- ber of deaths.

DANGEROUS PROPERTY. Mr. FARRINGTON reported that certain cottages at Five Crosses, belonging to the Marquis of Cholmondeley, were so dilapidated that they were unfit for habitation. The walls were in an unsafe condition, and the Medical Officer's report stated that the buildings were in a generally dangerous con- dition.—Mr. CHALLONER said he would at once take pro- ceedings against the owner to compel him to improve the premises.—The CLERK: Would you summon thc Marquis? —Mr. CIIALLONER said of course he would, and stand no ceremon with him, either. He would act with him in the same way as he would deal with any other man. The pre- mises were in a shameful state, and he believed it was true that snow had been in the bedrooms to the depth of two inches where the people were sleeping. It was scandalous, and he would stand no ceremony with such a man.—The Inspector was instructed to take proceedings against the Marquis of Cholmondeley to obtain an order for prohibition.

LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE SAVINGS.—A return just issued gives the number of depositors and amounts to their credit in the Post Office Savings Banks: in each county in England and Wales. In Lancashire there were 131,907 depositors, with credit for £1,634,348, against 120,986 de- positorf and £1,336,005 in 1873. In the county of Cheshire there were 34,567 depositors, with credit for £513,200, against 28,289 depositors and £356,653 in 1873. TERMINATION OF TEE GOLRORNE COLLIERS' STRIKE.— I Messrs. Evans and Company's men, who last week struck against an alteration in the price for getting coal, have for the present amicably settled the question. A deputation waited upon Mr. Glover, who visited the Golborne colliery on Monday morning. The men were informed that the employers were not disposed to alter the original pro- posal, viz., the round coal to be separated from the small at the following rates :—*Seven feet seam, round coal, Is. Id.; ditto small ditto, 101 Four feet seam, round coal, Is. 2d.; ditto smfil ditto, 101. With this the deputation returned and intimated the result of the interview to the re- mainder of the men who, after consulting together at the Royal Oak, consented to commence at these terms on the following Wednesday morning. Four "pieces "Were to be chosen as a test, the men agreeing'to try the new scheme for a week, the firm again undertaking to revise the terms if the trial proved against the earnings of the hands.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held on 'Monday Mr. Pennington presiding. There were-also present Messrs, Howat, Stozldey, J. Birehall, and Hy. Webster.
THE HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.

The Medical Officer reported :—I am pleased to report that the health of the district continues most satisfactory. I am unaware of any disease of an infectious type. Number of deaths 3, one beisg upwards of 60 years, the remaining being both inquest cases. Number of births :—Males 10, females 11; total 21.

FINANCE. At a meeting of this committee, on the 13th October, ac- counts amounting to £25 188. 7d were recommended to the Board for approval. The statement showed a balance in bank, after paving all cheques signed last meeting, of £444 17s; collected and paid into bank since last meeting £2O 7s. 6d.; leaving a balance in the bank of £439 65.; cash in clerk's hands £3o.—The minutes were confirmed.

THE BAILING OF THE BROOK INMOSBRO-LANE. At a Meeting of the General Purposes Committee, on October 1401,1881, it was moved by Mr. Barton, seconded by Mr. John Birchall, that the offer of Mr. Howat be ac- cepted, namely, "That he will give rails to rail off the brook in Mosbro'-lane for a length of 327 yards, oi,posite Mr. Stockley, and ditto for 210 yards opposite Mr. C. Barnes, the Board to find the men to make the stump holes; and this to be on condition that the Board will put in 244nch pipes , for thp 210 yards opposite Mr. Barnes, and the Boyd to have the brook under their control. The pipes to be put in at some convenient time.—The Chairman : Is it within our jurisdiction 7—Mr. Howat: Yes.—The Chairman : But is it our road ?—Mr. Howat: Yes; the road is not 30 feet wide —Mr. J. Birchall : There was once a horse killed there. The roads are two of the most dangerous places in the township.—Mr. Stockley :It is the most dangerous place for miles round.—Mr. Howat It has always belonged to the township.—Mr. Stockley :In the past year it has cost the township a good deal of money in looking after the wall.—Mr. Birchall: To keep the wall from falling into the brook.—Mr. Howat: It is no interest at all to Lord Derby; it will do for him as it is.—The Chairman: I was only wanting to know how we stand— Mr. Howat subsequently said that he did not want anything at all to do with it. People might think that he was work- ing for the benefit cf Lord Derby, but that was not the case. —On the motion of Mr. Stocki ey. the matter was adjourned for farther consideration as to the cost,
THE WARRINGTON TRAGEDY.

THE PRISONER BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. On Thursday, at the Borough Police Court, Edward Scholtze, was brought before Captain Litton and Councillor Fairclough, charged with having, on the sth of September, attempted to murder his wife Cecilia Scholtze. It is now seven weeks since the tragedy was enacted. Scholtze during' that time has been an inmate of the Infirmary, suffering 11 from his self-inflicted wounds, which at one time were con- sidered fatal. Under the care of Dr. Richmond and the nurses, he has, however, recovered, though he is yet very weak and thin. The wife's wounds were not dangerous, and she was discharged from the Infirmary three weeks ago. ' Scholtze is an Austrian and his wife a Dane, having settled I in Warrington 14 years ago. They have had eleven children, I six of whom are now living. The circumstances of the case are fully reported belo : Mrs. Scholtze, who was much agitated, said I am the wife of the prisonur, who is a glass engraver, and resides at 29. Hoyle-street. I have been married to the prisoner 20 years. Since Christmas he has been very strange, and for two months before the offence now charged against him he had several times threatened me. On one occasion he said he would shoot me to get me out of the road. On the 4th Sep- tember last we went to bed together a little after 10 o'clock. I He was restless during the night, and about two o'clock I I wakened and saw him smoking his pipe. The lamp was 1 burning. He said, "Cecilia, cannot you go to sleep T'' I said "No, I don't feel very well." I suppose I then went to sleep, for I don't remember any more until the morning when I awoke and felt blood running down my face. There was a lump on the side of my head, and I stretched forth my band but could not feel my husband. I called out " Ernest, 1 have got a lump on my head and father is not in bed." We had had no quarrel. He was better than usual that day and we were very comfortable. I recognise the hammer produced ; it is the prisoner's. It was under his pillow on the night of the 4th September. He had the hammer lying under him several nights. He never said he would do anything with it. Prisoner : It is a false statement. I will speak the truth. It is not right before God in Heaven. Mr. White (magistrates' clerk) : Do you want to ask any question ? Prisoner : Well, for the missus that is one false state- ment, that from Christmas I have been raving in my head and I was queer. Mr. White: She says you were changed in your manner since Christmas. Prisoner: Certainly; a man will change when he has a bad woman. Witness : I have not been a bad woman to you and never were.

„ Prisoner : Have I threatened to shoot you ? Witness : Didn't you put the revolver three times to my face and call out ; and didn't little Christiana begin to cry and say ” Mother, mother ;" and didn't that take effect and you directed it at your own head ? Prisoner : Had I got the revolver loaded at the time ? Witness: Yes, you always carried it loaded. I would not tell an untruth. Prisoner : I never did. Witness said prisoner had on one occasion pointed a revolver at her in the street saying he would shoot her. Captain Litton : Have you any idea why he slept with that hammer under his pillow ? Witness : No, he never said. Captain Litton, pointing to a rope with a heavy weight at one end, asked what it was. Witness: He carried that in his pocket. He called it a life preserver. Mr. Hunt: Did he carry it regularly in his pocket ? Yes. Captain Litton Was he in the habit of going out at night? No in the day time. Why did he carry this, then? I don't know, sir. flow long has he had this revolver? He brought it back from America in 1880. Ernest Scholtze said: I am son of the prisoner, and work at Bewsey Forge. My father is a glass engraver, and worked for Mr. Bolton up to a short time after last Christmas. He has been queer in his head since Christmas. He used to be haggling. About three weeks before September sth he threatened to shoot my mother. He did not say why he would shoot her. About half-past three on Monday, the sth September, icy mother awoke me. She came to my bed- room door. She said she was very bad, and told me to waken my brother Edward. I got up and awoke my brother, who was asleep on the sofa downstairs. I and my brother went into the parlour, where my father was lying bleeding from his throat. There was a lamp burning. I went up- stairs to see my mother. She was in bed, and bleeding•Aout the temples. I then knocked up the next door neighbour, and my brother fetched a doctor. My father and mother were removed to the Infirmary. I did not notice any ham- mer in my mother's bedroom. I know the hammer pro- duced; I have generally seen it in the parlour. I saw it on the sth in the parlour, lying by the side of my father. Captain Litton : Was the blood on the hammer when von found it, as there is now? Yes. Edward Scholtze, son of the prisoner, was next examined. He said: I was wakened about a quarter to four by my brother Ernest. I got up, dressed me, and went upstairs. When I got upstairs there was no light, and I went downstairs to find a candle. I again went upstairs :Led found my mother in my brother's bed, and at her request I took her to her own bed. She was bleeding badly from the head. I went into the parlour, and on the floor, with his head under the bench of his machine, my father lay, bleeding from his throat. Dr. Richmond shortly afterwards came, and my father and mother were removed to the Infirmary. I know the hammer produced; it is my father's. I have heard icy father threaten icy mother. About three weeks before the offence I was sent for from my work. I went, and my mother told me my father was very bad to her. He told me three times he would go upstairs and throw my mother out of bed. I stopped him twice, and then I went to speak to my mother, and he followed. He caught hold of her, and I pulled him away. He then seized the bed, and pulled it half way off. Seizing me by the throat, he attempted to push me away. About a fortnight before he attempted to murdee my mother, he threatened to shoot her and put us two out of the road. He meant me and my mother. Prisoner: It is a lie. Speak the truth. Witness (continuing): I have heard my father repeatedly say that my mother went carrying on with other men. Prisoner said that when Edward was fetched from his work it was his mother who commenced the row because be would not let her go to town. Witness : You never let her go up town so when she wanted. You told her after you came from the workhouse that you would lead a better life, and you asked her to go to bed with you and she slept with you three nights. Prisoner: You say you kept me from striking her. Witness: You said you would throw her out of bed. Prisoner : You are my own son and tell lies against me ! Witness : It is not a lie ; it is the truth. Isabella Morris deposed: I am the wife of Richard Morris, and live at 6, Albert-street, off Pitt-street, Warrington. On Friday afternoon, the 2nd September, prisoner came to my house and asked if his wife was there' and I said "No." "I have met her in the rabbit run," said he "and when she saw me she turned back in the town." Prisoner then sat down and said "I sha'n't say any more to her, but the next thing that you hear tell of I shall kill her and myself and all. r Prisoner: Speak the truth ; you are a liar. You are as bad as my wife. Witness (continuing): I told him not to talk like that. I don't know why he kept saying all this. I don't think he had any cause for it at all. He was jealous and frequently came and told us of all sorts of men and so on, but I knew it was all wrong. He was very peculiar in his manner when he came. I don't think be was in his proper senses. Prisoner: You say that I said I would kill myself and my wife? Yes. Prisoner: You are a liar; you speak untruth—greatest untruth. In answer to a further question, witness said she thought , prisoner could not be right when he talked same as he did. Prisoner: Have I ever used any bad language in your ' house ? Yes. Prisoner: No, I never did. No bad language whatever. Did you give my wife idea in head and fetch doctor? You are a bad woman. Dr. Richmond, resident surgeon, Warrington Infirmary, said: On the morning of the sth September, about four o'clock, I was sent for to Scholtz's house. I was informed there was an attempted murder and suicide there. I took a nurse and went down. In the front room on the ground floor I found the prisoner lying on his back, with a fright- ful gash in his throat, and apparently dead. The floor was covered with blood, and the hammer produced was some- where near the fireplace. I did what I could for him, and then went up to the wife. I found her in the front upstairs room, very faint and weak from loss of blood, and suffering from several—l think six—severe contused wounds in the scalp, such as could have been inflicted by the horse- men I dressed her wounds, and on going down stairs I was shown the razor produced. I had both patients removed to the Infirmary, where Scholtze has been until this morning. His wife was discharged about 011.6% weeks ago. She has since been weak and sickly. He has been very quiet and good since he has been in the Infirmary. On the morning of the sth end a few days afterwards I despaired of his life. He has once or twice spoken to me about her. He has ac- cused her of wasting his money and making his home wretched, of selling his furniture, and of infidelity. He seems to be suffering from some delusion as to her conduct. Inspector Singleton deposed: On Wednesday tire 31st August, about eight o'clock in the evening I received a letter from the Chief Constable referring to priseeer, and from certain instructions that he gave use I went with the Relieving Officer to the prisoner's house. 'The door was opened by the prisoner. I asked him if te would kindly show me the revolver which he had, and he said "Yes come upstairs." I went upstairs, and in a box I found the re- volver produced, loaded in four chambers' and a quantity of damp rope. He withdrew the cartridges from the revolver. We then took prisoner to "Dr. Spink's surgery, where the doctor and he conversed, for about half an hour. At his own request I afterwards took him to the Workhouse where he stayed until Friday. On Monday morning, the sth Sep- tember, about ten minutes past four, I was in the police office when prisoner's son Edward came and said that hie father had nearly killed his mother and cut his own throat, and that he believed his father was dead. I told him to at once get a doctor and I ran to the house accompanied by P.S. Johnson. On entering the house, I went into the first room on the ground floor, and found the prisoner lying on his back with a frightful gash in his

throat, and bleeding. I thought he was dead at first. I got a wet towel, and put it over the wound to stop the bleeding ; and then tied a handkerchief round his neck. Shortly after he put up his right hand, and got hold of 114 n , saying," It all through a bad woman, a bad wife." He repeated it se v e r a l time. I saw on the floor near his right hand the razor pro' duced, covered with blood. On the left hand side was the hammer produced, also covered with blood. I went urtaire and found his wife bleeding from several wounds ou the head. She was in bed, and I put some wet cloths on her head. At that time Dr. Richmond came, and they were t removed to the Infirmary, where he has remained in care 0 the doctor and in charge of a constable up to this morning: I received him in custody this morning, and brought bin' here in a cab. I charged him with having, on the sth said tember, attempted to murder his wife Cecilia. He sald reply: "I did not intend to kill her. I have something too' to say, but I will say it to the magistrates." Prisoner, who spoke very low and indistinctly, said it was most untrue what his wife and Mrs. Morris had said, and the the lads' evidence too. It was a made up thing among :L os Prisoner was committed to take his trial. 15 t d removed to Kirkdale on Friday, Dr. Richmond having eta eA that if removed on Thursday he would be unable to sae' the fatigue.

WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL. FREE SCHOLARSHIPS. Al EXAMINATION, to elect four free scholars, will be held at the GRAMMAR &moot, at 10 a.m., on FRIDAY, DEC. 18th. 1881. Candidates mnsthe under 12 years of age on September toth, 1881. These schohrships are open only to boys who have been for three years under instruction at some public elemen- tary school within the school district cf Warrington. All applications for admission to the Examination must be sent in before Thursday, December Ist; and must be accom- panied with certificates of age, of character, and of three years' attendance at a public elementary school. For further par ticulas apply to the HEAD MASTER.

WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES.— In connection with the Science and Art Department, I Kensington and City and Guilds of London Institute. —Sessiei 17481-82.—The eighth Session has now commenced. SYLLABUS : Mondays : Inorganic Chemistry, 6-30 to 8,0,p.m.; Alkali Manufacture' 8-0 to 9.0 p.m. Tuesdays: Art —Freehand Drawing, 6-30 to 8-0 pm.; Machine Construction and Drawing, 8-0 to 6-0 p.m. Wednesdays: Art—Freehand Drawing, 6-30 to 8-0 pkin. ; Building Construction and Draw- ing, 8-0 to 9-0 p.m. Fridays: Sound, Light, and Heat, 7-0 to I'6-0 p.m.; Animal Physiology, 8-0 to 9-0 p.m. The Technologi- , cal (Mass (Alkali Manufacture) will include the manufacture of I Sulphuric Acid, Sulphate of Soda, Soda Ash, Caustic Soda, I Soda Crystals, and Bleaching Powder. Candidates eligible for I the Technological Class (Alkali Manufacture) must be actually employed in Chemical or other allied works, and they must have passed, or pass during the coming session, in two of the I following-tamed subjects :—Machine Cunstruction, Building Construction, Theoretical Mechanics, Applied Mechanics, Acoustics, Light and Heat, and Inorganic Chemistry. Fee, 3s. per class, payable in advance. No class will commence unless a sufficient number of students join. Those who intend to join these classes must do so before the end of October. JOSEPH MORRISON, Hon. Sec. Widnes, September 22nd, 1881.

BOROUGH OF SAINT HELENS. TO THE BURGESSES OF WINDLE WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—The period for which you last elected me, without a contest, as your representative to our Municipal Parliament will expire October 31st. Should it be your pleasure to repose in me the same confidence in the future, which you have generously done each time I sought your suffrage in the past, I shall be proud to continue such ser- vices, assuring you that nothing shall be wanting os my part to secure and protect the interests of Windle Ward, and the prosperity and welfare of this my native town. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, yours faithfully. T. C. WILCOCK. St. Helens, October 10th, 1881.

BOROUGH OF SAINT HELENS. TO THE ELECTORS OF HA.RDBITAW WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, 4 Vacancy having occurred in the representation of our Ward, through the retirement of Mr. Thomas Swift, I beg to offer myself as a Candidate. Should you be pleased to elect me, it will be my study to promote the best interests of the town, more especially to ob- tain a resident Alkali Inspector, the adoption of those clauses of the Public Health Act to abate the Smoke Nuisance in our midst, and any other measure which, without injury to any manufacturing industry, will improve the abominable condi- tion of t.. atmosphere of Bt. Helens. The neglect of railway accomm.. Don, and the excessive charges both for goods and passengers to and from Bt. Helens, require immediate atten- tion. Your obedient servant, A. JAMISON.

firtOR•OUGH OF SAINT HELENS. TO THE ELECTORS OF WEST SUWON WARD. LLDIES AND GENTLEMBN,—The retirement of Mr. Edward Owen from the Council will leave a vacancy In the representa- tion of your Ward. Having been asked to come forward by a number of influential ratepayers. I beg to place my services at your disposal. Should you do me the honour of giving me a seat in the Council Chamber, my best endeavours will be devoted to :the economical management of the affairs in the Borough, in the prosperity of which, from long association, I take a deep interest. Two of the most important questions at present are, an Increased Supply of Pure Water and the Sanitary Condition of the town. These matters would have my earnest attention. I have the honour to be, Ladies and Gentlemen. Your obedient servant. EDWARD JOHNSON. Elephant-lane, Sutton.

BOR OUG H OF SAINT HELENS. TO THE BIIGEBBES OF ECCLEBTON WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—Ify present term of office as one of your representatives in the Town Council will shortly expire, and I beg to seek a. renewal of the honour. My earnest desire during the nine years I have represented you has been to secure the best Interests of the town ; many important Questions concerning the supply of water, t.f gas, and the management of the Borough rates and Corporation estates have arisen, and I trust that my action has received your general support and approval. The pressing need of ensuring an stun- dant and pure supply of water, along with other matters of consequence, will require the tarly and most careful attention of the Council. ehould you again renew your confidence by electing me, you may rely upon my devotion to the interests of your Ward and of the Borough at large. I am, Ladles and Gentlemen, Ycur faithful servant. • RICHARD PLLKINGTON. Glasswotks, 13th October, 1881.

BOROUGH OF SAINT HELENS. TO THE OF OF EAST SUTTON WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—The term for which you elected me, as one of your representatives in the St. Helens Town ' Council, has now ,nearly expired, and I beg respectfully to again solicit your suffrages at the forthcoming Election. It is with satisfaction that I can announce that the expenditure dur- ing the past year, as compered with previous years, has been largely reduced, and that the rates for the ensuing year will be Twopence in the pound less than they were last year. Yet I think it necessary to draw your attention to the fact that very Important questions, such as Increased Market Accommoda- tion, an Increased Water Supply, the General Eewerage of the :Borough, and other proposed improvements, all likely to in- vol :a large outlays of money, are still under the considelatiot of the Coulson, and will have to be decided very shortly. Should you again return me to the Council, I beg to assure you that it shall be my constant study to give to the discussion of these questions what practical experience I possess; and t 3 carefully watch all matters affecting the well-being of your Ward, and the general interests of the Borough. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, your obedient servant, A. HANSON. Chursh-street, St. Helens, October 17th, 1881.

TO SEWER CONTRACTORS.—The WIDNES LOW, BOARD is prepared to receive TENDERS for the construc- tion of a New Main Sewer, comprising about 245 yards of sft. by 31t. 3M. pitch pine sewer, and about 1,284 yards of ffit. by 41t brick sewer, extending from near the present outfall of the Marsh Brook to Moor-lane, the whole to be carried out in ac- cordance with plans, specification, general conditions, and form of tender, which may be seen at the Local Board Offices. Alforde-street, Widnes, on and after Tuesday, the Ist day of November, 1881. Copies of the specification, bill of quantities, schedule of prices, and form of tender may be obtained, on payment of three guineas in each case, to the undersigned, which will be returned on receipt of a bond fide tender, ccom- panted by the bill of quantities, schedule of prices, specifica- tion, and the receipt given ft' the three guineas deposited. Sealed tenders endorsed "Tender for Construction of Nevt Main Sewer, contract No. 1," must be addressed to the Chair- man of the Joint Highway and Health Committee, and delivered at the office of the undersigned not later than 12 o'clock on Thursday, the Ist day of December, 1881. Tenders will not be accepted unless made out on the form above- named, with all the items in the bill of quantities and schedule of prices, fully priced and moneyed out. The person whose tender is accepted will have to provide two reasonable sureties and be required to enter into a contract which will be prepared by a solicitor appointed by the Board. The Widnes Local Board does not bind itself to accept the lowest or any tender, or to defray any expenses incurred in furnishing such tenders.—By order JAB. T. ALLEN, Clerk. Widnes Local ioard Offices, Alforde Chambers, Alforde- street, Whines.

MAKINSON AND WILCOCK, in returning their sincere thanks to their numerous atrons and the public generally for the very kind and liberal support they have hitherto received, hope, by strict attention to the interests of their clients, and the prompt and faithful discharge of their duties, to continue to merit the same; the more so, as they are able to offer ad- vantages not generally enjoyed by those engaged in the same business, Mr. Makinson having had from early youth practical experience of the English Timber, Stone and Building Trades, and of Farming in all its branches, being at the present tine a farmer himself on a large scale; and, in addition, having served his apprenticeship to the ENGINEERING and MILLWEIGIIT busi- ness, besides having had, during the last TEN years, consider- able practice in Valuing and Selling Coliery, Quarry, and other Machinery and Working Plant, Growing nd Fallen Timber, Farming Stocks, Growing and Gathered Produce, Stocks-in- Trade, Household Furniture Innkeepers' Effects, Houses, Buildings, Landed Estates and Property generally, and also in cases involving Damage and Trespass. Mr. WILCOCK, also, has had the advantage of being brought up to Farming, together with that of having served an appren- ticeship to an eminent Veterinary Surgeon, combined with the experience he has had since his connection with this firm, enables him to give judicious and valuable ath;ce in all cases In which he may be consulted. In conclusion, M. and W. beg their friends and the public generally to note that they have a trustworthy and efficient staff of assistants in their employ, who have been carefully trained to watch over the interests of those who favour the firm with their patronage ; whilst last, but not least, their system of advertising, and the facilities they possess of ensuring an extensive circulation, enable them to offer the utmost pos- sible e übllcity to any sales entrusted to their management.
